findings.title: Extend FirestorePermissionDeniedException conversion beyond the 2 read call sites it currently covers
findings.rule: Nygard lens (mandatory for this area) — permission-denied at every I/O point; EH-2 typed-exception boundary

evidence.quote: Thrown when a Firestore operation returns PERMISSION_DENIED.

findings.why: _guardPermission (firestore_gateway_impl.dart:1197-1215) is the ONLY code in the app that ever throws FirestorePermissionDeniedException, and it wraps exactly 2 of this gateway's ~30 Firestore I/O methods — fetchPage (524) and fetchChildPage (1051), both reads, both with operation hardcoded to 'read'. None of the ~23 push* (write) methods route through it: pushStreak/pushSettings/pushTrack (288-337) issue raw .set() calls with no try/catch at all, and pushCompletionsBatch (246-285) wraps any commit failure — including permission-denied — as a generic SyncPushException instead. Traced end to end: OutboxProcessor absorbs every push failure internally (never rethrows to any AsyncValue/UI, so this is not a UI-facing bug), but the dedicated permission_denied analytics event in sync_orchestrator.dart (gated on `e is FirestorePermissionDeniedException`) therefore fires only from the pull path and never from an outbox push. The write path's only detector of this failure class is outbox_dao.dart's reviveIdentityDeadLetters, which pattern-matches raw persisted error text (`lastError.like('%permission-denied%')`) instead of a structured type — a duplicated, Firestore-SDK-wording-dependent re-derivation of the exact fact this exception exists to represent. This repo's own docs (on-device-preflight-cheatsheet.md, bug-hunt-findings-2026-05-31.md) call permission-denied on writes 'a known recurring failure mode in this project,' yet the typed signal for it covers roughly 1 in 15 of the gateway's I/O surface.
findings.recommendation: Route every push*/fetch* method in firestore_gateway_impl.dart through _guardPermission (or an equivalent shared wrapper) with an accurate operation value (read/write/delete) instead of only the 2 fetch methods, so FirestorePermissionDeniedException becomes the single source of truth for 'this failure was permission-denied' on both read and write paths. findings.title: Defensively copy SyncPushException.committed so the partial-commit invariant can't be violated by a future caller
findings.rule: Evans lens — invariant enforced in one place, not by caller convention
findings.why: SyncPushException.committed exists specifically so OutboxProcessor can tell which outbox rows genuinely landed before a batch failed, so committed rows are 'never re-pushed or dead-lettered' (per this file's own docstring, H3). That invariant currently holds only because the single production call site remembers to wrap the list in List.unmodifiable(pushed) before throwing — the exception class itself accepts any List<String>, including a live mutable reference, with no internal defensive copy. A future call site (or a test double standing in for one) that passes a growable list it keeps appending to after constructing the exception would silently corrupt the partial-commit accounting this type exists to protect, with no compiler or runtime signal that anything went wrong.
findings.recommendation: Copy defensively inside the constructor (e.g. an initializer that wraps committed in List.unmodifiable(committed)) so the guarantee doesn't depend on every future caller remembering to do it themselves.
acceptance_criteria: a new unit test constructs SyncPushException with a growable list, mutates the original list after construction, and asserts .committed is unaffected

findings.title: core/time/local_day_clock.dart's currentLocalDayClock global has no compiler-enforced set/reset pairing for tests
findings.rule: SM-7 spirit (no global/static mutable singletons) / TQ-6 hermetic tests
findings.why: This mutable top-level variable backs DateTimeFactory, which is called from 15+ production sites across DAOs/repositories/mergers (e.g. track_dao.dart, a churn hotspot, calls it 8 times). Test isolation relies entirely on every caller of useLocalDayClock() remembering to pair it with `tearDown(resetLocalDayClock)` per the doc comment's 'MUST' — nothing in the type system enforces this. A test file that calls useLocalDayClock() without the tearDown pairing would silently freeze time for every later test in that file/isolate, producing flaky failures unrelated to the code under test. I checked the two actual test files that use it (only outbox_processor_test.dart and one other) and both correctly pair set/reset via `tearDown(resetLocalDayClock)`, so this is a latent, convention-enforced risk rather than a demonstrated failure today.
findings.recommendation: Add a shared test helper (e.g. `withFakeClock(seed, body)`) that calls `addTearDown(resetLocalDayClock)` itself so individual tests can't forget the reset, and migrate the existing 2 call sites to it.

findings.title: Fix unsafe `as int?`/`as num?` casts in TrackCodec.decode and GoalCodec.decode that throw instead of returning null
findings.rule: EH-2/EH-4 decode() null-on-malformed contract + Nygard partial-failure
findings.why: entity_codec.dart's decode() contract states it 'Returns null when required fields are missing or malformed — the merger must skip malformed rows rather than crash.' Every other numeric field read across all 15 files in this batch goes through FirestoreCodec.parseInt, built specifically because Firestore fields can arrive as String (its own docstring says so). These 3 sites bypass it with a bare `as` cast: if profile_id/track_id/target_percent ever arrives as anything but exactly int (or num, for target_percent)/null — e.g. a String from a hand-edited doc, an import script, or a legacy document — `as int?`/`as num?` throws instead of returning null. TrackConfigMerger.merge() and GoalMerger.merge() call `_codec.decode(row)` inside a `for` loop with no try/catch, and MergeRouter.dispatch (merge_router.dart:55) awaits merger.merge() with no try/catch either, so one malformed row throws out of the whole pull page mid-iteration, silently dropping every row after it and aborting the sync pass instead of just skipping the bad row.

findings.title: Route LearningLedgerCodec.encode's completedAt through FirestoreCodec.encodeDateTime instead of raw toIso8601String()
findings.rule: Evans consistency (single documented UTC-safe conversion path) / data-integrity
findings.why: Every other DateTime field in all 14 sibling codecs — and every other field in this very file (see decode() at line 84-86) — is pushed via FirestoreCodec.encodeDateTime, which forces `.toUtc()` before serializing so the wire string always carries a 'Z' suffix. This one call skips it. entry.completedAt is read back from Drift's `dateTime()` column which, per the pinned drift-2.31.0 source (lib/src/runtime/types/mapping.dart:174, default storeDateTimesAsText=false, not overridden anywhere in this repo), decodes via `DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(unixSeconds*1000)` with no isUtc:true — producing a **local**, non-UTC-flagged DateTime even though the original value came from DateTimeFactory.nowUtc(). `.toIso8601String()` on a non-UTC DateTime omits the 'Z'/offset entirely. When a different device (a parent or tutor on a different device/timezone — an explicitly supported flow in this app, see tutor_grant_codec.dart in this same batch) pulls the row, FirestoreCodec.parseDateTime's `DateTime.tryParse(raw)?.toUtc()` (used by learning_ledger_merger.dart) reinterprets the offset-naive string using the READING device's local offset rather than the writer's, shifting completedAt by the delta between the two devices' UTC offsets — potentially moving a ledger entry onto the wrong calendar day on the syncing device.
findings.recommendation: Change line 67 to `'completed_at': FirestoreCodec.encodeDateTime(model.completedAt),` to match every sibling codec.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: encode a LearningLedgerRow with a non-UTC-flagged completedAt (isUtc:false, simulating the Drift round-trip) and assert the resulting 'completed_at' string ends in 'Z' and represents the correct UTC instant.

findings.title: Correct FirestoreCodec.encodeDateTime's false claim that the Firestore SDK auto-converts ISO-8601 strings to Timestamp
findings.rule: AG-8-adjacent doc/code truth + Evans (one place for an invariant)

evidence.quote: The Firestore SDK converts ISO-8601 strings into Timestamp objects on write, so this format is safe to use in push documents.
in Firestore Security Rules a `string <= timestamp` comparison is `false`, which would deny EVERY completion create.
timestamp), so a `created_at <= request.time` guard compared a string to request.time and was rejected at the type level —

findings.why: The claim is false — the SDK does not auto-convert a Dart String to a Timestamp. That's exactly why firestore_gateway_impl.dart carries a dedicated `_timestampifyCompletedAt` patch (lines 158-219) that rewrites `completed_at`/`purged_at` from String/DateTime to a real Timestamp AFTER every codec's encode() output runs, and exactly why streak_events' equivalent `created_at <= request.time` rule check was deleted after it denied every write in production. The real fix for a timestamp-compared field lives two layers away from the codec, in a hand-maintained per-field allowlist inside firestore_gateway_impl.dart — a mechanism entity_codec.dart's own 'Responsibilities' docstring never mentions. The next engineer who adds a new entity kind with a `<= request.time` rule, trusts this codec's comment, and skips the gateway patch will reproduce the exact 'permission-denied on every create' incident this codebase has already hit twice (completions, streak_events).
findings.recommendation: Fix the doc comment to state the SDK does NOT auto-convert and cross-reference firestore_gateway_impl.dart's `_timestampifyCompletedAt` as the actual mechanism. Consider moving that per-field patch logic into the codec/EntityCodec layer (or documenting it explicitly in entity_codec.dart's 'Push encoding — SyncWriteFacade territory' note) so the full push contract for a timestamp-compared field lives in one discoverable place instead of three.
acceptance_criteria: encodeDateTime's doc comment no longer claims SDK auto-conversion; it states the true behavior and points to the gateway patch.
A note is added (in entity_merger.dart's 'adding a new entity kind' checklist, or equivalent) that a request.time-compared field needs a gateway-side Timestamp conversion, not just a codec change.

findings.title: Make MergeStore.upsert + persistUpdatedAt atomic to stop a stale LWW shadow-timestamp surviving a mid-merge crash
findings.rule: DB-2 (>1 write runs inside a single transaction()) / Nygard: process death mid-write

evidence.quote:
await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);
      await _store.persistUpdatedAt(

await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);
      await _store.persistUpdatedAt(
await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);

await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);
      await _store.persistUpdatedAt(

await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);
      await _store.persistUpdatedAt(
await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);

await _store.upsert(kind: kind, profileId: profileId, fields: row);
      await _store.persistUpdatedAt(

findings.why: Every natural-key LWW merger applies the remote row (_store.upsert, which writes the entity table including its own updatedAt column) and THEN separately persists the SyncKv shadow timestamp (_store.persistUpdatedAt) as two independent awaited Drift writes with no enclosing db.transaction(). If the process dies between the two — an OS kill or force-quit on mobile is routine, not exotic — the entity row is left holding the remote's updatedAt while SyncKv still holds the pre-merge value. Any local edit made before the next successful sync now races a STALE local timestamp: a re-pulled, unchanged remote row will look newer than the stale SyncKv record and DriftMergeStore.remoteIsNewer will silently let it overwrite the user's genuinely-newer local edit — no exception, no log, nothing to retry against. This is DB-2's 'crash mid-sequence leaves the DB half-written' failure applied to the LWW bookkeeping itself.
findings.recommendation: Add a MergeStore.applyRemote(...) that wraps the entity write and its SyncKv persistUpdatedAt in one db.transaction() (or expose a transaction-scoped variant), and switch all 8 callers to it.
acceptance_criteria: Fault-injection/unit test: call upsert() alone (simulating a crash before persistUpdatedAt commits), then perform a legitimately-newer local edit to the same row, then re-merge the identical stale remote row — assert the local edit survives.
New transaction-wrapped MergeStore method has a unit test asserting both writes roll back together when the second write is forced to fail.

findings.title: Fix StudyDayConfigMerger to use DriftMergeStore.remoteIsNewer instead of the pre-Phase-3 merge_rules.remoteIsNewer
findings.rule: FB-2 (server-timestamp / clock-skew LWW ordering, never client-clock-only)
findings.why: Every other LWW merger in this batch (bookmark, track_config, settings, stage_definition, learning_order, profile_program, goal, learner_profile, gamification_settings, notification_settings, ui_preferences — 11 of 12 natural-key/singleton mergers) was upgraded in the documented 'Phase 3' pass to call `_store.remoteIsNewer`, which adds the ±5s clock-skew window plus Firestore server-timestamp (synced_at) tie-break specifically to fix FB-2's 'faster clock always wins' problem (see drift_merge_store.dart:34-38, 111-152, including the D15 fix). StudyDayConfigMerger alone still calls the plain free function from merge_rules.dart, which has neither: it is a strict `remoteUpdatedAt.isAfter(localUpdatedAt)` with no skew tolerance and no server-timestamp fallback. A device whose clock runs even a few seconds fast will have its study-day-config edits always win the comparison, silently discarding a genuinely newer edit made on a second device.
findings.recommendation: Give StudyDayConfigMerger a MergeStore dependency (constructor param, like every sibling merger) and call store.remoteIsNewer with the row's synced_at; drop its import of merge_rules.dart.
acceptance_criteria: Unit test: two devices' clocks 3s apart, both writes inside the ±5s window, no synced_at on one side — StudyDayConfigMerger resolves identically to DriftMergeStoreTest's D15 clock-skew group, not via strict remote.isAfter(local).

findings.title: Fix LearningLedgerMerger's fallback ULID generator to avoid a permanent same-millisecond collision loss
findings.rule: Nygard: silent, non-self-healing data loss on a manufactured natural-key collision
findings.why: This fallback (only used when a pulled row has no `ulid` — 'legacy data' pre-migration docs, per the file's own comment) is deterministic with zero entropy: two ledger rows completed in the same millisecond with no ulid produce the IDENTICAL synthetic id. LearningLedgerDao dedups on ulid via INSERT OR IGNORE, so the second row is silently dropped — permanently, since a retry regenerates the same colliding id every time (unlike the rest of this merge layer's failures, which self-heal on the next pull because the underlying condition changes). A bulk-mark flow (bulk_mark_screen.dart is a named churn hotspot) writing several legacy-shaped completions together is a plausible trigger.

findings.title: Fix hand-rolled test _FakeMergeStore.remoteIsNewer implementations to match DriftMergeStore's clock-skew/D15 semantics

evidence.quote:
// Mirror DriftMergeStore semantics: strict `remote > local` outside
    // the ±5 s window; inside the window, server timestamp decides.

findings.why: mergers_test.dart's fake claims to 'Mirror DriftMergeStore semantics' but omits the D15 fallback (drift_merge_store.dart:140-146): inside the clock-skew window with no decisive synced_at on both sides, the fake unconditionally prefers remote, whereas the real store first falls back to comparing raw updated_at (protecting a newer un-pushed local edit from being clobbered by an older remote). notification_settings_merger_round_trip_test.dart's fake is simpler still — no clock-skew window at all. acceptance_criteria: A within-skew-window / no-syncedAt / older-remote test case added to either file fails before the fix and passes after, or the fake is proven identical to DriftMergeStore.remoteIsNewer by delegation (making such drift structurally impossible).

findings.title: Strip row.entityKey out of the outbox dead-letter analytics event (leaks profileId + sefariaRef)
findings.why: For OutboxEntityKind.completion rows the outbox entityKey is literally `${profileId}:${sefariaRef}:${stageId}:${trackType}:${curriculumId}` (completion_writer.dart:747). findings.title: Give OutboxProcessor's single-flight guard a generation token so stale-reclaim can't run concurrent drains

evidence.quote: // reclaim only inspects the *same instance's* private state we also

findings.why: The single-flight guard is two plain fields (_draining/_drainingSince) with no per-invocation identity. In production, OutboxProcessor is built with unmodified defaults (outbox_providers.dart:98-105: pushTimeout/drainStaleAfter never overridden) and sync_orchestrator.dart fires a periodic drain every 60s forever (Timer.periodic(_periodicDrainInterval, ...)) while drainStaleAfter is 90s. Non-completion kinds are pushed one row at a time, individually awaited (up to 50 rows x ~18 kinds) — a real multi-kind backlog on a slow connection easily exceeds 90s. When that happens, the next periodic (or connectivity/lifecycle) trigger sees the guard as 'stale', resets it, and starts a second, genuinely concurrent `_doDrain()` while the first is still running — the code comment at line 206-211 only reasons about two *reclaimers* racing each other synchronously; it never accounts for the *original* stale-but-still-running drain's own `finally` unconditionally zeroing `_draining`/`_drainingSince` once it eventually completes, which can then let a THIRD trigger barge in on top of the second. This directly breaks the documented contract ('collapses them to one push round' / sync_orchestrator.dart:568 'the OutboxProcessor's single-flight guard collapses races with other triggers'), producing duplicate concurrent Firestore pushes and racy interleaved deleteRow/markAttempted calls that can double-count a row's attempts and dead-letter a recoverable failure roughly twice as fast as _maxAttempts=10 implies. The R6-13 regression test that targets exactly this code path never builds true overlap: every scenario releases and awaits the 'wedged' pipeline to full completion before the next drain runs (its own comment admits the limitation at line 1392/1396), so the actual race is untested.
findings.recommendation: Replace the boolean+timestamp guard with a construct that can tell 'my invocation' apart from a later reclaimer — e.g. a monotonically increasing generation counter captured at acquire time, checked before `finally` clears state (`if (_generation == myGeneration) { _draining = false; ... }`), or switch to chaining onto the in-flight Future (a late caller awaits/joins the existing drain rather than racing a flag).
acceptance_criteria: New/updated unit test keeps the first drain's pipeline call parked on a Completer, advances the clock past drainStaleAfter, drives a second (reclaiming) drain to full completion, then completes the first — and asserts the pipeline was invoked exactly once for the outstanding rows, or that DAO state is never corrupted by true overlap.
Guard implementation carries a generation token (or equivalent) so a finally block from an earlier invocation cannot clear state established by a later one.

findings.title: Move _decodePayload() calls inside outbox_processor.dart's per-row try blocks so one bad payload can't abort the whole drain

evidence.quote:
// Continue draining other rows — don't abort the whole batch on
          // a single failure.

findings.why: _decodePayload throws FormatException when a row's payload isn't a JSON object (DB corruption, a future write bug, or jsonEncode(null)). Both call sites sit OUTSIDE any try/catch: line 292 is inside the eligibleCompletions loop before the try at line 306, and line 383 is immediately before the per-row try at line 384. A single malformed row therefore throws all the way out of _drainForProfile → _doDrain → drain()'s try/finally (the finally still clears the single-flight guard, but nothing catches or converts the error), skipping every other pending completion, every remaining non-completion kind, AND the profile-0 account sweep in _doDrain — on every one of the 5 wired drain triggers, forever, until the row is fixed out of band. This directly contradicts the code's own stated invariant quoted above.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each _decodePayload call in its own try/catch (or catch FormatException specifically) so a bad payload is treated like any other per-row failure: logged, markAttempted (or immediately dead-lettered, since it can never succeed), and does not block sibling rows or other kinds.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: insert one outbox row with a non-JSON-object payload (e.g. payload: 'null') alongside a valid row of a different kind; drain() must not throw, the valid row must still be pushed, and the bad row must be marked attempted without blocking siblings.
Same test repeated for a malformed completion-kind row.

findings.title: Batch OutboxProcessor's post-commit deleteRow/markAttempted cleanup instead of awaiting it per row

evidence.quote:
for (final id in ids) {
            await _dao.markAttempted(id, error: failedError.toString());

findings.why: pushCompletionsBatch exists specifically 'to eliminate the N-round-trip problem' by pushing up to _completionDrainCeiling=100000 rows in ≤500-op Firestore batches, but the local cleanup after that push still runs one awaited Drift statement per outbox row. acceptance_criteria: New bulk DAO method(s) wrapped in a single transaction()/batch(); OutboxProcessor calls it once per outcome group.

'pushLedgerEntriesBatch writes all entries with ULID doc IDs',

if (tasks.length > 500) {

findings.why: pushCompletionsBatch (lines 245-285) correctly loops in <=500-item chunks via _writeBatchLimit and catches per-chunk failures into SyncPushException(committed:...). findings.title: Stop FirestoreGatewayImpl.pushGoal from using non-idempotent add() for id-less goals

evidence.quote:
final id = goal['id']?.toString() ?? goal['goal_id']?.toString();
    if (id != null) return id;

findings.why: Every other push* method here (pushCompletion, pushStreak, pushTrack, pushLedgerEntry...) derives a deterministic Firestore doc id so an outbox retry after a lost ack is a safe overwrite via set(merge:true). pushGoal is the one method that falls back to collection.add() -- a fresh random doc id -- whenever the payload carries no id/goal_id. outbox_sync_write_facade.dart's own _goalKey fallback (a composite curriculum_pct_timestamp key) proves this null case is real, not theoretical: it exists specifically to dedupe local enqueues of such goals. If the server commits the add() but the client never sees the ack (timeout, dropped connection -- exactly what the outbox's at-least-once retry exists to survive), the retry calls add() again and creates a second, permanent duplicate goal document in Firestore, which the pull path then merges back down as a duplicate goal locally.
findings.recommendation: Assign every goal a stable id before it is ever enqueued (mirror the ULID pattern already used for streak/ledger/points-ledger entries) and have pushGoal always do doc(id).set(merge:true); delete the add() branch.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: call pushGoal twice with an id-less payload against a fake/emulator Firestore; assert exactly one document exists afterward.
pushGoal's add() branch is removed or provably unreachable.

findings.title: Fix FirestoreGatewayImpl.deleteUserData to target real nested Firestore paths instead of empty top-level ones

evidence.quote: // Step 1: delete Firestore data via gateway (client-side best-effort)

findings.why: deleteUserData(uid) queries users/{uid}/<name> directly for 10 of its 12 hardcoded names (completions, bookmarks, settings, streaks, profiles, goals, rewards, sync_queue, learning_order, stage_definitions) -- but per this same file's own doc comment two lines above the class declaration, all of that data actually lives two levels deeper at users/{uid}/learner_profiles/{profileId}/<collection>. The wrong-path queries return zero docs and delete nothing, silently -- an empty result looks identical to 'already deleted'. Two names are also stale ('streaks' vs the real 'streak_events'; 'profiles'/'rewards'/'sync_queue' match no real collection). account_lifecycle_service.deleteCloudAccount() calls this as 'Step 1' with a comment ('execution order is critical ... NEVER deletes local before cloud succeeds') that assumes this step does real, potentially-failing work; in practice it only removes the learner_profiles parent docs and diagnostic_logs, leaving every real child subcollection (completions, streak_events, learning_ledger, curriculum_tracks, goals, bookmarks, preferences/*, points_ledger, reward_redemptions...) orphaned in Firestore. Account deletion is not actually broken today only because Step 2 (deleteCurrentFirebaseUser) fires the onUserDeleted Cloud Function, which does a correct db.recursiveDelete of the whole users/{uid} tree -- making this entire client-side step dead weight that documents a guarantee it doesn't provide.

acceptance_criteria: Emulator test seeds users/{uid}/learner_profiles/{id}/completions (and siblings) and asserts deleteUserData(uid) actually removes them, or the step is deleted and the doc/comment updated to match.

findings.title: Write server timestamps for LWW ordering fields in FirestoreGatewayImpl's push* methods (FB-2)

evidence.quote: Every cross-device LWW ordering field is written as `FieldValue.serverTimestamp()`, never a client clock.

findings.why: docs/sync-conflict-resolution.md names `updatedAt` as the LWW comparison field for curriculum_tracks, goals, bookmarks and settings. pushTrack (line 337), pushSettings (316), pushBookmark (369) and pushGoal (562) all spread the caller's `data` -- which carries whatever client-clock `updated_at` the local write set -- straight through, and only add a separate `synced_at: FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` field that isn't the one the merger compares. pushLearnerProfile (line 417) shows the codebase already knows the right pattern: it explicitly overwrites `updated_at` itself with `FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` before sending. FB-2's own stated rationale is exact: 'two devices with skewed clocks writing client timestamps make last-write-wins non-deterministic -- the faster clock always wins and silently overwrites newer data.' A device with a fast or wrong clock editing a track/goal/bookmark/setting can have its stale edit incorrectly beat a genuinely later edit from another device, with the loss silent (no error, just the wrong value persisting until the next edit).
findings.recommendation: Apply the pushLearnerProfile pattern (server-side overwrite of the merger's LWW field) to pushTrack, pushSettings, pushBookmark, pushGoal and any other push* method whose entity is LWW-merged by a client-set timestamp field; confirm against core/sync/merge/*.dart which exact field each merger compares before changing it.
acceptance_criteria: Emulator test (per FB-2's own 'Enforce' note) asserts the persisted field each merger actually compares is a server Timestamp, not a client-supplied value, for tracks/goals/bookmarks/settings.
Audit grep: no client-clock value reaches a field a merger uses for cross-device LWW comparison, across firestore_gateway_impl.dart's push* methods.

findings.title: Wire onError (and a recovery-pull path) into TutoredListenerSupervisor's inner ListenerSupervisor

evidence.quote:
onError: (Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
          _onError?.call(channel, error, stackTrace);

findings.why: TutoredListenerSupervisor.attach() builds its ListenerSupervisor with only `source` and `onEvent` -- no `onError`, no `recoveryPullTriggers`. Inside ListenerSupervisor.start(), a stream error calls `_onError?.call(...)`, which is a silent no-op when `_onError` is null. Firestore terminates a `.snapshots()` stream on error (e.g. permission-denied when a parent revokes the grant while the tutor's 15 tutored channels are live, or any transient stream fault) -- so that one channel goes permanently dark for the rest of the session, with zero AppLogger entry, zero Crashlytics record, and no resubscription, while sibling channels keep working. The parallel own-profile path in sync_orchestrator.dart wires `onError: _onListenerError` (logs, forwards to Crashlytics, fires analytics) and `recoveryPullTriggers` (recovers from at-limit snapshots) -- the tutored path has neither, so it is both less observable and less self-healing than the path it was copied from.
findings.recommendation: Pass `onError` (log via AppLogger at minimum, consider triggering TutoredPullService.pull() on permission-denied) and `recoveryPullTriggers` into the ListenerSupervisor built in TutoredListenerSupervisor.attach(), mirroring SyncOrchestratorImpl.start().
acceptance_criteria: Unit test: a ListenerSource stub that emits a stream error during an attached tutored session asserts the error reaches a logger/callback, not silently dropped.
TutoredListenerSupervisor.attach() passes a non-null onError to ListenerSupervisor(...).

findings.title: Close the TutoredListenerSource channel gap and de-duplicate the two hand-maintained channelToKind switches

// The channel set mirrors the pull set in PullPipeline.pullForTutoredProfile
// (same collections, same order-field conventions) so listeners and the initial

findings.why: TutoredListenerSource's own doc comment claims its channel set 'mirrors the pull set in PullPipeline.pullForTutoredProfile' -- but PullPipeline's tutored collection list includes `learning_order` (pull_pipeline.dart:276) while TutoredListenerSource.openChannels()'s returned map does not. findings.title: Type the catch/catchError clauses across sync_orchestrator.dart, pull_pipeline.dart and tutored_listener_supervisor.dart (EH-4)
findings.why: All 16 sites catch without an `on <Type>` clause, so each also catches Error subtypes (TypeError, StateError, RangeError, NoSuchMethodError) as if they were the transient I/O failures the surrounding code is designed to shrug off. Every one of these swallows-and-logs (the pull_pipeline.dart and tutored_listener_supervisor.dart sites don't rethrow at all; most of the sync_orchestrator.dart sites log a warning and return/fall through). Concrete cost: if a future change introduces a null-dereference or bad cast inside a merger reached from the 60s periodic drain, a recovery-pull trigger, or a listener dispatch, it gets caught here, logged once per occurrence as an ordinary 'drain failed'/'listener error' warning, and never crashes or reaches Crashlytics as a fatal -- masking a real regression indefinitely instead of surfacing it. (Two other sites -- sync_orchestrator.dart:768 and :939 -- were deliberately excluded from this list: :768 delegates to a typed `_isLocalDatabaseError` classifier before deciding to swallow, and :939 rethrows after converting to a status; both already behave like the fix this finding asks for elsewhere.)
findings.recommendation: Narrow each listed catch to `on Exception catch` (Exception still covers FirebaseException/TimeoutException/SocketException etc.) so Error subtypes propagate to the zone's uncaught-error handler instead of being absorbed; use sync_orchestrator.dart:768's classifier-based pattern as the template for guards that need to stay broad on purpose.
acceptance_criteria: Enable avoid_catches_without_on_clauses + avoid_catching_errors once dart run custom_lint is unblocked; all 16 sites pass.
A test that injects a StateError into a merger/dispatch call reached from one of these paths shows the error propagating (not silently logged-and-continued).

findings.title: Fix TutoredPullService.pull()'s misleading on-Exception comment / uncaught upsert failure

evidence.quote:
// A failure outside the per-collection guards (e.g. the synthetic-profile
      // upsert) — surface as a soft error; do NOT wipe (not a revocation).

findings.why: upsertTutoredProfile is awaited on line 83, before the try block opens on line 97. The `on Exception` catch's own comment (line 118) says it covers failures like 'the synthetic-profile upsert' -- but that call already ran to completion (or threw) before the try even starts, so a real upsert failure (DB busy, unique-constraint violation on grantId, disk I/O) is not caught by this method at all; it propagates straight out of pull(), unlike every other failure path here, which returns TutoredPullResult.error. A maintainer trusting the comment would wrongly assume upsert failures degrade softly like the rest of this method.
findings.recommendation: Either move the upsertTutoredProfile call inside the try (returning TutoredPullResult.error on failure, consistent with the rest of the method), or correct the comment to state plainly that upsert failures propagate uncaught to the caller.
acceptance_criteria: A test that makes profileDao.upsertTutoredProfile throw asserts pull() either returns TutoredPullResult.error or the method's doc explicitly says it throws.

findings.title: Resolve profileId live, not by snapshot, when wiring OutboxSyncWriteFacade/LocalDataUploadService/PointsBalanceDao.syncSink in syncOrchestratorProvider
findings.rule: sync push/pull invariant (docs/sync-conflict-resolution.md) / Nygard-lens: stale capture
findings.why: syncOrchestratorProvider is a keepAlive singleton that (by explicit design, per its own comments and resolveProfileIdProvider's doc) survives a profile switch without rebuilding, reacting only via `ref.listen(activeProfileIdProvider, ...)` to restart listeners. But `profileId` at line 79 is a one-time ref.read snapshot baked into OutboxSyncWriteFacade/LocalDataUploadService and into pointsBalanceDao.syncSink — not the lazy `resolveProfileId` the same function already builds at line 68 for the orchestrator's own calls. OutboxSyncWriteFacade._enqueue (features/sync/data/outbox_sync_write_facade.dart) stamps every outbox row's `profileId` column from this captured field for every entity kind it handles except learner-profile-delete (bookmarks, settings, goals, learning order, curriculum tracks, notification/gamification/UI-preference snapshots, streak events, study-day configs, and — via PointsBalanceDao._pushRedemption calling sink.enqueueRewardRedemption — reward redemptions). OutboxProcessor._doDrain only sweeps the currently-active profileId plus account-level 0 (confirmed in outbox_processor.dart and explicitly documented for the analogous deleteLearnerProfile case: 'the drain only sweeps the ACTIVE profile + 0... orphans the row'). So after a household profile switch (Bug #1/R1 already proves this happens mid-session without an orchestrator rebuild), every write of the affected kinds for the newly-active profile gets tagged with the stale boot-time profileId and is never drained until — if ever — that exact stale profile becomes active again. Concretely: parent app open with childA active, orchestrator built (profileId=A); parent switches to childB; childB redeems a reward or a bookmark/goal/track change is made; the outbox row is stamped profileId=A; the orchestrator's periodic/lifecycle/connectivity drains all resolve the live profileId (=B) and never pick up the A-stamped row. That data silently never reaches Firestore / other devices.
findings.recommendation: Change OutboxSyncWriteFacade and LocalDataUploadService to take an `int Function() resolveProfileId` (reuse resolveProfileIdProvider) instead of a captured `int profileId`, reading it at each call instead of at construction. Re-wire pointsBalanceDao.syncSink and re-run reEnqueueUnsyncedLedgerRows whenever the active profile changes, not just once at orchestrator build.
acceptance_criteria: OutboxSyncWriteFacade/LocalDataUploadService read the active profile id live at write time rather than at construction time.

Regression test: build a ProviderContainer, go cloud-born with profile A active, switch activeProfileIdProvider to B, perform a write that reaches OutboxSyncWriteFacade, and assert the resulting outbox row's profileId column equals B, not A.
Existing sync_orchestrator_providers.dart comments documenting the resolver-vs-snapshot distinction (Bug #1/R1) are updated to cover this fix.

findings.title: Add error handling and logging to resetFirestoreNetwork's disable/enable sequence in firestore_instance_provider.dart

evidence.quote:
final reset = resetFirestoreNetwork;
      if (reset != null) await reset();

findings.why: resetFirestoreNetwork disables then re-enables the Firestore network with no try/catch and no AppLogger call. If enableNetwork() throws after disableNetwork() succeeds (plugin channel error, terminated instance, or exactly the flaky-network condition this function exists to recover from), the network is left force-disabled with no automatic retry and zero diagnostic trail. The connectivity-trigger caller in sync_orchestrator.dart (line ~611) does wrap this in try/catch+log, but the lifecycle/foreground-resume caller in lifecycle_observer.dart:147-148 does not — an exception there aborts the rest of the resume sequence (redetectTimezone, invalidateSacredCache, triggerPull) as an unhandled async error, silently skipping the resume pull.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the disable/enable pair in try/catch inside resetFirestoreNetwork itself (so every caller gets the protection for free), log failures via AppLogger with a stable event code, and consider a bounded retry for enableNetwork() specifically so a mid-sequence failure doesn't leave the channel permanently disabled.
acceptance_criteria: resetFirestoreNetwork catches and logs failures from disableNetwork()/enableNetwork() instead of letting them propagate unhandled.

Unit test: stub FirebaseFirestore so enableNetwork() throws after disableNetwork() succeeds; assert the exception is caught/logged and does not abort the lifecycle-resume sequence (timezone redetect, sacred-cache invalidation, resume pull still run).

findings.title: Resolve outboxProcessor lazily in syncOrchestratorProvider instead of capturing it by value
findings.rule: SM-6 lazy-resolver consistency / Nygard-lens: stale capture across DB swap
findings.why: Every other volatile build-time dependency in this same constructor call (gateway, merge router, outbox DAO, identity status) is deliberately passed as a lazy `() => ref.read(...)` resolver specifically — per the inline comments at lines 136-137, 161-163 — 'so a DB swap (multi-account flow) is picked up without rebuilding the orchestrator singleton.' outboxProcessor is the one exception: it's read once (line 129) and stored as a plain value field. outboxProcessorProvider (outbox_providers.dart) watches userDatabaseProvider and rebuilds on a DB swap; database_provider.dart confirms userDatabaseProvider swaps via the independently-mutable accountDbFileNameProvider, decoupled from authStateProvider (the only thing syncOrchestratorProvider itself watches). If a DB swap can occur without authStateProvider's watched value also changing in the same tick, the orchestrator keeps draining through an OutboxProcessor bound to the pre-swap, superseded UserDatabase/outboxDao while its other lazily-resolved collaborators (gateway, merge router) may already be pointing at the new account — a split-identity state. Confirming this needs tracing whether the app's account-switch flow (account_actions.dart) can complete a DB swap before authStateProvider's emitted value settles to the new account.
findings.recommendation: Change the outboxProcessor parameter to a lazy `resolveOutboxProcessor: () => ref.read(outboxProcessorProvider)` resolver, matching resolveGateway/resolveMergeRouter/resolveOutboxDao, so it can't go stale relative to its siblings.
acceptance_criteria: syncOrchestratorProvider resolves outboxProcessor via a lazy resolver rather than a captured value.

Regression/integration test: trigger a userDatabaseProvider swap while syncOrchestratorProvider stays alive (authState unchanged) and assert the next drain operates against the new outboxDao's pending rows, not the pre-swap instance.

findings.title: Add ref.mounted guards to SignInController's post-await state writes and a dispose-mid-flight regression test
findings.rule: SM-4 (check ref.mounted after await in a Notifier before touching ref/state)
findings.why: signInControllerProvider is autoDispose and its methods await many things (registry lookups, Firestore fetches, SharedPreferences, sync-orchestrator pulls with 8s timeouts) with zero `ref.mounted` checks anywhere in the ~1000-line file, then keep calling `_ref.read(...)` / `state = ...` afterward. If the user navigates away (dialog dismissed, screen popped) while a sign-in is in flight, the provider can be disposed mid-await and the next `state = ...` throws Riverpod 3's UnmountedRefException in the app's most security-critical flow. None of the 5 sign-in notifier tests in this batch dispose the container between an await and the following state mutation, so this path is completely unexercised. (This gap is systemic — only 3 of ~32 autoDispose notifiers in lib/features use ref.mounted at all — so the fix likely belongs to a broader SM-4 sweep; flagged here specifically because this batch's test suite is the one place positioned to catch it for the highest-stakes notifier.)
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` (or equivalent) after each await inside signInWithEmail/signInWithGoogle/_navigateAfterSignIn/etc. before the next state or ref.read, and add a test that disposes the container mid-flight (e.g. between two awaits in a stubbed slow authRepo call) and asserts no unhandled exception surfaces.

findings.title: Fix the cross-feature-deep-import checker (Makefile audit 15/15) — its awk logic can never fire

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'

findings.why: The awk derives BOTH the importing-file's feature name and the imported feature name from $0, which is the full grep -rn output line beginning with the FILE PATH — so match($0,...) always finds the importer's OWN feature name (from the path prefix) before ever reaching the import statement, making a[1]!=b[1] always false. Verified by feeding the exact grep -rn output line for pending_local_signup.dart through the isolated awk: it printed 'SUPPRESSED (bug present)'. Because of this, Rule 2 has zero real enforcement repo-wide despite 'make audit' reporting 15/15 clean, and two concrete violations sit undetected in this batch alone: pending_local_signup.dart (a domain/services file) reaches directly into a different feature's presentation/providers instead of a barrel — profiles' own barrel (features/profiles/profiles.dart) is an empty stub with nothing exported, so there was no barrel path available — and onboarding_screen.dart in a different feature deep-imports account's onboarding_intent_screen.dart because account.dart's barrel doesn't export it.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to extract the imported-feature name from the import-statement TEXT only (e.g. split the grep -rn line on the first ':' twice to isolate the content, or use grep -oP 'features/\K[^/]+' scoped to the substring after the import path's package: prefix) so it stops reading the file-path prefix. Then resolve the two concrete violations: export a currentAccountId-style accessor from features/profiles/profiles.dart and import through it, and export OnboardingIntentStep from features/account/account.dart. Add a tiny fixture-based regression so a bad cross-feature import always reproduces a checker failure.
acceptance_criteria: Feeding a synthetic 'file/features/A/x.dart:N:import ...features/B/y.dart' line through the fixed awk prints the line (not suppressed)
make audit check 15/15 stops being silently no-op and either fails on the two known violations or passes because they were fixed

findings.title: Add ref.mounted guards and Timer disposal to SignInController's autoDispose async flows

evidence.quote:
final watchdog = Timer(const Duration(seconds: 15), () {
      if (state is SignInSubmitting) {

findings.why: This 1016-line Notifier<SignInState> is registered autoDispose and performs 84 awaited operations per file (multi-second retries, 8s Firestore timeouts, 350ms polling loops) yet contains zero occurrences of 'mounted' anywhere in the file — every method touches `state`/`_ref` after an await with no disposal guard. If the user backs out of the sign-in screen mid-request (a completely ordinary action while a 'signing in...' spinner shows), autoDispose tears the notifier down; when the pending await resolves and the code does `state = SignInError(...)` or `_ref.read(...)`, Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException. The watchdog Timer compounds this: it is only cancelled in signInWithEmail/signInWithGoogle's own `finally` block, never via ref.onDispose, so if the notifier is disposed mid-flight the Timer keeps running and fires `state = ...` against an already-disposed notifier up to 45s later. The codebase already has an established ref.mounted convention elsewhere (dashboard_providers.dart, notification_providers.dart, sacred_location_provider.dart all use it), so this file's total omission is an inconsistency, not a repo-wide non-issue.
findings.recommendation: After every await that precedes a `state =` or `_ref.read(...)` write, add `if (!ref.mounted) return;`. Register `ref.onDispose(watchdog.cancel)` immediately after each Timer is created (both the 15s and 45s watchdogs).
acceptance_criteria: A notifier test that disposes the ProviderContainer (or pops the route) while signInWithEmail/signInWithGoogle is mid-await asserts no exception escapes and no post-dispose state write occurs
Watchdog Timers are cancelled by ref.onDispose in addition to the existing finally-block cancel

findings.title: Cache the account list Future instead of constructing it fresh inside AccountPickerScreen.build()
findings.why: registry.getAllAccounts() is called directly inside `Widget build()`, which returns a brand-new Future object on every rebuild. FutureBuilder tracks futures by identity, so any unrelated rebuild of this ConsumerWidget (a ref.watch(accountDbFileNameProvider) change from switching accounts, a locale/theme change, or any ancestor rebuild) restarts the FutureBuilder into ConnectionState.waiting — flashing the loading spinner over the already-rendered account list and re-querying the device registry — the textbook 'Future-in-build' Flutter anti-pattern.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the fetch behind a FutureProvider/AsyncNotifier (e.g. deviceAccountsProvider watched via ref.watch), or convert to ConsumerStatefulWidget and cache the Future in State so its identity is stable across rebuilds.
acceptance_criteria: A widget test triggers an unrelated provider rebuild while AccountPickerScreen is mounted and asserts the list does not revert to the loading spinner and getAllAccounts() is not invoked a second time

findings.title: Watch reactive auth state instead of ref.read-ing currentUser inside _AccountTileState.build()
findings.why: SM-3 requires ref.watch in build and ref.read only in callbacks, precisely because a ref.read snapshot of a mutable getter (`.currentUser`, which changes on sign-in/out/re-auth without the authRepositoryProvider instance itself changing) is only re-evaluated when something else this widget DOES watch happens to force a rebuild — not when the underlying session actually changes. The tile's 'valid session' vs 'sign in again' pill/warning-icon can go stale after an auth event (e.g. a sibling tile's re-auth flow) that doesn't independently invalidate this tile.
findings.recommendation: Replace with a watched, narrow selector, e.g. `ref.watch(authStateProvider.select((s) => s.currentUser?.firebaseUid))`, so the tile is reactive to session changes.
acceptance_criteria: A widget test changes the live Firebase session via a provider override while the picker is mounted and asserts the affected tile's badge updates without an unrelated rebuild trigger

findings.title: Make AppUser/AuthState/AuthUser @freezed instead of hand-rolled classes without value equality

findings.title: Fix Makefile check 15's awk logic — it structurally can never flag a cross-feature deep import
findings.area: tooling/Makefile (Rule 2 checker) — surfaced while verifying content_browsing layering

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'
awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}';

findings.why: match($0, ...) scans the whole `path:line:content` string and returns the FIRST `features/X/` match — which is always inside the file-path prefix, identical to what match($1, ...) already extracted from the path alone. So a[1] and b[1] are always equal and `if(a[1] != b[1])` never fires, regardless of input. Verified by running the exact pipeline against the live tree: it returns 0 lines. Yet real cross-feature deep imports exist and bypass their feature's providers.dart barrel — e.g. lib/features/content_browsing/presentation/widgets/hierarchy_selection_panel.dart:14 imports 'package:learning_tracker/features/tracks/setup/domain/entities/add_track_result.dart' directly, and a broader scan turned up 40+ more instances just under lib/features/tracks/. This is a different, more severe problem than the already-documented 'checks 14-15 are warn-only' backlog: check 14 (Rule 1) is warn-only but does enumerate its ~32 known edges every run; check 15 (Rule 2) has never printed a single violation and would stay silent even on a brand-new cross-feature deep import introduced today, so Rule 2 currently has zero live detection, not merely non-blocking detection.
findings.recommendation: Fix the second match() to search only the substring after the file path's own feature segment (e.g. split $1 out of $0 first, or anchor the second regex to the import-statement portion of the line only), then re-run and baseline the newly-real violation list the same way check 14 already documents its known edges.
acceptance_criteria: make audit check 15 prints hierarchy_selection_panel.dart:14 (and other live cross-feature deep imports) as WARN output on the current tree.

findings.title: Guard ref.watch/ref.read after in-flight awaits in dashboard_providers.dart (SM-4)
findings.why: dashboardTrackCompletionPercentage, dashboardCompletionPercentage, stripStockMilestonesEffect, and dashboardPaceStatus each call ref.watch/ref.read after an earlier await (a Drift DB read) with no ref.mounted check in between. If any of these autoDispose family providers loses its last listener while that DB read is still in flight — e.g. the user swipes the active-tracks carousel past a card or leaves the dashboard mid-load — the later ref call throws UnmountedRefException, an uncaught exception inside the async provider body. The same file's dashboardChildNextReward provider (line 343) already guards this exact hazard with `if (!ref.mounted) return null;`, proving the team knows the failure mode; it just isn't applied consistently.
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return <default>;` immediately after the await that precedes the later ref access in each of the four functions, mirroring the existing guard in dashboardChildNextReward.

findings.title: Inject LocalDayClock into ParentDashboardAggregator instead of hardcoding SystemLocalDayClock
findings.why: compute({DateTime? now}) documents now as 'pass explicitly for testability', and every other metric (pace, engagement, recent-completions window) honors it — but the streak sub-computation always builds StreakStateProvider with a hardcoded SystemLocalDayClock(), which reads real DateTime.now() regardless of the now argument. findings.title: Fix make audit check 15/15's self-comparing awk so cross-feature deep imports are ever detected
findings.rule: Rule 0 (checker must detect what it claims); Rule 2; AG-11
findings.why: match($1,...) extracts the feature name from the FILE PATH ($1, e.g. 'dashboard'). match($0,...) is meant to extract the feature name of the IMPORTED module, but $0 is 'path:line:content' and $1 is a literal prefix of $0, so match($0,...) finds that same 'dashboard' substring inside the path prefix before it ever reaches the import statement — a[1] and b[1] are therefore always identical and 'if (a[1] != b[1])' can never be true for any input. I confirmed this by piping track_stat_grid.dart's real cross-feature import (dashboard deep-importing scheduler's daily_task.dart, not via a barrel) through the literal pipeline (0 lines out) and by isolating the awk step directly (a[1]=dashboard, b[1]=dashboard). A rough repo-wide count of the same import shape this check should be flagging runs into the hundreds (e.g. tracks→scheduler ×31, dashboard→scheduler ×26, settings→account ×23 lines by a similar grep). `make audit PASSED` reads as 'Rule 2 is at least being warned about'; in reality check 15 has never printed a single violation since it was written, so the 'warn-only, pending Wave-2 fix' backlog it exists to size has been completely invisible the whole time — new cross-feature deep imports can be added freely with zero signal.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to extract the imported feature from the import string specifically (e.g. operate on a field after stripping the 'path:line:' prefix, or grep the 'package:learning_tracker/features/X/' substring in the import text only) rather than re-scanning the whole line. Add a fixture test: one known cross-feature-deep-import line must warn, one same-feature multi-segment import must not.
acceptance_criteria: make audit check 15/15 prints a WARN line citing lib/features/dashboard/presentation/widgets/track_stat_grid.dart:8 (or the fix documents an explicit, reviewed barrel exemption for domain models) on the current tree
a shell/unit test pins the checker against a same-feature multi-segment import fixture and asserts it produces no false positive

findings.title: RewardForm is a hand-written state class with no @freezed/== override, so Riverpod can never skip a rebuild on it
findings.rule: naming/placement — 'Domain/state models are immutable @freezed classes... never hand-write ==/hashCode'

evidence.quote: hand-rolled equality drifts from the fields and silently breaks rebuild-skipping.

findings.why: RewardForm is held directly as RewardConfigController's Notifier state (per its own doc comment) but has no @freezed codegen and no == /hashCode override anywhere in the file, so it falls back to identity equality. Every copyWith() call — including a no-op one — produces a referentially distinct instance that Riverpod's default identity-based updateShouldNotify always treats as changed, so any widget watching this provider rebuilds on every field mutation regardless of whether the visible state actually changed. This is exactly the failure mode coding-standards.md cites as the reason for the @freezed rule.
findings.recommendation: Convert RewardForm to @freezed, or at minimum hand-write a field-wise == / hashCode.

findings.title: Fix physical Positioned(right:) badge on AchievementTierCard so it doesn't overlap the title in Hebrew RTL
findings.rule: AX-1 (EdgeInsetsDirectional/AlignmentDirectional required in this RTL app; no physical left/right)
findings.why: The title is positioned with AlignmentDirectional.topStart and padded with EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(end: 96) -- both direction-aware, so in Hebrew (RTL) the title anchors to the physical right and reserves 96px on the physical left. The TrackTagChip badge, however, is pinned with plain Positioned(top:0, right:0) -- direction-UNAWARE, so it stays on the physical right in both locales. In LTR this is correct (title occupies the left zone, badge sits in the reserved right zone). In RTL the title now ALSO occupies the right zone (topStart flips), so the badge renders directly on top of the milestone title text on every achievement card for every Hebrew-locale user. This exact bug class was already found and fixed once in this feature (progress_summary_card.dart's PositionedDirectional comment explicitly describes the identical failure mode), and a dedicated regression test already exists for this widget under Hebrew locale (gamification_screen_l1_test.dart, 'R6-16: AchievementTierCard under RTL has no Directionality(ltr) wrapper') but it only asserts the absence of a forced-LTR Directionality wrapper -- it never checks rendered geometry, so it passes today despite the overlap. point_config_screen.dart:428,445 have the same Positioned(right:) pattern but on purely decorative, content-free background circles (IgnorePointer, low opacity) -- same root cause, cosmetic-only impact.
findings.recommendation: Replace Positioned(right: 0) with PositionedDirectional(end: 0) at achievement_tier_card.dart:108-112 (and the two decorative sites in point_config_screen.dart for consistency). Extend the existing R6-16 test to pump under Locale('he') and assert the TrackTagChip's rendered Rect does not intersect the title Text's Rect.
acceptance_criteria: achievement_tier_card.dart uses PositionedDirectional(end:) instead of Positioned(right:) for the TrackTagChip badge
gamification_screen_l1_test.dart's R6-16 test (or a new sibling test) asserts non-overlapping geometry between the badge and title under Locale('he'), not just absence of a forced Directionality

findings.title: Stop achievementsOverviewProvider and _pointConfigDataProvider writing to Drift/SharedPreferences and pushing to Firestore from inside FutureProvider build
findings.rule: SM-2 (provider build is pure: no writes/requests/side effects)
findings.why: Both providers exist to compute a read-only view model (achievements list / per-track point config rows), but their build functions mutate persisted state (SharedPreferences milestone config, Drift PointConfigs rows) and push a network sync write as an unguarded side effect of simply being watched. Riverpod rebuilds these providers on every dependency change (achievementsOverviewProvider re-runs on every completionCommittedProvider tick; _pointConfigDataProvider re-runs whenever activeTracksProvider emits) -- so opening the achievements screen or the point-settings screen can silently trigger writes and a Firestore push purely from reading state, with no user action and no guard against concurrent/duplicate invocation. This also makes both providers impossible to unit test as pure read logic without a working sync facade and DB write path.
findings.recommendation: Move the strip-stock-templates / seed-default-configs mutations out of the read providers into an explicit one-shot action (invoked once from a screen lifecycle hook or a dedicated Notifier method with SM-4-safe mounted checks), leaving the FutureProviders as pure reads.
acceptance_criteria: achievementsOverviewProvider's build function performs no writes; a separate, explicitly-invoked action performs stripStockTemplateMilestones + push
_pointConfigDataProvider's build function performs no writes; seeding defaults happens in a separate action
A ProviderContainer.test() test watches each read provider twice and asserts the mutation/sync-push call count is 0 (or exactly 1, deliberately) rather than growing with rebuilds

findings.title: Add ref.mounted/context.mounted guards after awaits in RewardConfigController and the pending-redemptions fulfil/decline handlers
findings.rule: SM-4 (after any await in a Notifier method/async callback, check ref.mounted before touching ref/state)
findings.why: RewardConfigController is an autoDispose Notifier (confirmed via reward_config_controller.g.dart: isAutoDispose: true) whose saveReward/toggleEnabled/deleteMilestone/_persistAndSync methods each await one or more DB/network calls and then read `state` or call `ref.invalidate`/`ref.read` afterward -- with zero ref.mounted checks anywhere in the file (grep confirms). If the user saves/toggles/deletes and the screen is popped (e.g. the success dialog's own navigation, or a fast back-gesture) before the await resolves, Riverpod 3 throws when a disposed Ref is touched. The same shape recurs in parent_pending_redemptions_screen.dart's _fulfil/_decline: `ref.invalidate` runs BEFORE the `context.mounted` check that appears one statement later in the same function -- the check exists, it's just ordered too late. By contrast, every other async flow in this exact feature (child_redemption_screen.dart, achievement_unlock_celebration.dart, reward_configuration_screen.dart) consistently checks mounted immediately after every await, so this is a real, demonstrated-known-pattern that these two files skip. No test in reward_config_controller_test.dart exercises container/widget disposal mid-await (grep for 'Unmounted'/dispose-mid-call found nothing).
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` immediately after every await in RewardConfigController's mutation methods before touching state/ref again; in parent_pending_redemptions_screen.dart move `ref.invalidate(...)` after the `context.mounted` check, not before it.
acceptance_criteria: Every await in RewardConfigController's saveReward/toggleEnabled/deleteMilestone/_persistAndSync is followed by a ref.mounted check before further ref/state use
parent_pending_redemptions_screen.dart's _fulfil/_decline check context.mounted before ref.invalidate, not after
A widget/provider test disposes the container or pops the screen mid-await and asserts no uncaught disposed-ref exception

findings.title: Log RewardMilestoneService.getAllMilestones/getAllUnlocks JSON-decode failures instead of silently returning an empty list that can later overwrite cloud data
findings.rule: EH-3 (log-less catch is a pending violation; every catch rethrows, converts, or logs via AppLogger)
findings.why: If the SharedPreferences-stored reward config JSON is unreadable (process death mid-write, storage corruption, cross-version format mismatch), getAllMilestones/getAllUnlocks silently treat 'corrupt' the same as 'genuinely empty', with zero AppLogger call. That empty result then flows straight into exportCloudPayload(), which is what pushGamificationSettingsSnapshot() uploads as the authoritative reward_settings snapshot on the next sync -- silently overwriting the family's real, previously-configured reward list on every other synced device, with no diagnostic trail to explain why rewards 'disappeared'. The existing test suite (reward_milestone_service_test.dart 'getAllMilestones edge cases', lines 536-574) exercises invalid/blank/non-list JSON but only ever asserts the method returns empty -- it pins the silent-swallow as the specified behavior rather than testing that the failure is surfaced or logged.
findings.recommendation: Log via AppLogger.error (or similar) inside both catch blocks before returning the fallback list, including enough context (profileId, key) to diagnose; consider whether a corrupt-vs-genuinely-empty distinction should block the next cloud push instead of silently exporting empty.
acceptance_criteria: Both catch(_) blocks in getAllMilestones/getAllUnlocks call AppLogger before returning the empty fallback
A test seeds corrupted JSON, calls the method, and asserts the logger recorded the failure (fake/spy AppLogger sink)

findings.title: Fix mergeCloudPayload treating a non-empty remote payload with a missing/unparseable updated_at as unconditionally newer than local
findings.rule: EH-2 / Nygard lens (LWW ordering must not silently clobber on ambiguous input; mirrors FB-3's null-timestamp guard even though this path is SharedPreferences-based, not core/sync)
findings.why: The short-circuit `remoteUpdatedAt != null && ...` means: when the remote payload is non-empty but its 'updated_at' fails to parse (missing key, malformed string, cross-version format drift), the early-return guard never fires, so the method falls through and unconditionally overwrites local milestones/unlocks with the remote payload -- treating 'timestamp unknown' as 'always newer' instead of the safer 'cannot prove newer, keep local'. This is the exact malformed-timestamp branch never exercised by either reward_milestone_service_test.dart's mergeCloudPayload group (only null/empty/older/newer-with-valid-ISO-dates are tested) or test/sync/merge/gamification_reward_merge_test.dart (same gap, confirmed by grep -- only valid ISO8601 updated_at values appear in that file too).
findings.recommendation: Change the guard so a null/unparseable remoteUpdatedAt is treated as NOT provably newer (skip the merge, same as the older-timestamp branch) rather than falling through to an unconditional overwrite.
acceptance_criteria: mergeCloudPayload with a non-empty milestones/unlocks payload and a missing or garbage 'updated_at' leaves existing local data untouched
A new test in the mergeCloudPayload group covers this exact case and fails against the current code

findings.title: Fix the Makefile check-15 awk pipeline so cross-feature deep-import detection can actually fire
findings.rule: Rule 0 / Rule 2 / AG-11 (a standard ships with a deterministic checker; checker failures print file:line and exit non-zero -- a check that structurally cannot fire is a broken guardrail)

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'

findings.why: $1 (awk field 1, the file path column) and $0 (the whole grep output line, which starts with that same file path) are both matched against the identical regex `features/([^/]+)/` -- since the file's own path is always the leftmost occurrence of that pattern in $0 too, `a[1]` and `b[1]` are always extracted from the SAME text (the importing file's own feature folder), so `a[1] != b[1]` can never be true and the check prints nothing, always, regardless of what's actually imported. I reproduced the exact pipeline directly: the grep -P pre-filter stage alone finds 70+ candidate cross-feature import lines (including at least 10 genuine features/{dashboard,learning,notifications,sync,content_browsing}/** files deep-importing into features/gamification/**), but piping through the full check-15 awk command yields exactly 0 output lines. Unlike check 14 (which lists its ~32-edge backlog so it's at least visible for future cleanup), check 15 gives zero visibility into the Rule 2 backlog size today, and -- more importantly -- will never flag a brand-new cross-feature deep import added by any future change, even once the check is flipped from warn-only to enforcing.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk script to compare the importing file's feature folder against the IMPORTED path's feature folder specifically (e.g. split $1 and the import-statement portion of $0 separately, or use two distinct match targets), then re-run make audit and confirm it lists the real backlog the way check 14 does.
acceptance_criteria: Running the check-15 pipeline against the current tree (unchanged) prints the real cross-feature deep-import edges instead of nothing
A synthetic new deep import added between two features is caught (non-zero WARN output) after the fix

findings.why: Both are classic (non-@riverpod) family providers with no `.autoDispose` -- in this Riverpod version, a manually-declared provider not marked autoDispose is kept alive for the container's lifetime once first read. findings.title: Convert RewardMilestone/RewardUnlockRecord to @freezed data classes
findings.rule: Naming/placement (domain/state models are immutable @freezed classes; never hand-write ==/hashCode for data classes)
findings.why: Both classes are hand-written data holders with a hand-rolled copyWith/toJson/fromJson but no == / hashCode override at all, so they fall back to identity equality -- two RewardMilestones with identical field values are not `==`. Current call sites happen to compare by `.id` field rather than object equality (so no live bug was found), but this is fragile: any future code that puts RewardMilestone in a Set, uses List.contains, or relies on Riverpod .select()-style equality skipping would silently misbehave. The sibling model in the same feature (StreakRecoveryInfo) already follows the correct @freezed convention, showing the pattern is known and used elsewhere in this exact directory.
findings.recommendation: Convert RewardMilestone and RewardUnlockRecord to @freezed classes (keeping the existing toJson/fromJson as named factory/method overrides if the generated ones don't match the custom snake_case JSON shape).
acceptance_criteria: RewardMilestone and RewardUnlockRecord are @freezed with generated equality
Existing reward_milestone_test.dart suite passes unchanged (or updated only for the freezed toString/copyWith surface)

findings.title: Use ICU-parameterized l10n instead of raw 'label: value' string interpolation for chip/subtitle text

findings.title: Override userDatabaseProvider/coarsePacedTrackIdsProvider/contentIndexProvider in LearningScreen widget tests — real Drift DB is being constructed on every pump

Every ProviderScope in these tests opens a NEW real UserDatabase instance sharing the same QueryExecutor/file name, i.e. real shared mutable state across nominally-isolated tests — the exact thing TQ-6 forbids. findings.title: Narrow and log the catch-all in CompletionRepositoryImpl._appendStreakEvent

evidence.quote:
} catch (_) {
      // Defensive: never let a telemetry tee block the primary write.

findings.why: catch (_) swallows every exception from BOTH the streak_events Drift insert and the outbox enqueue (facade.enqueueStreakPayload) with no AppLogger call anywhere in this file — a codec bug, closed-DB race, or genuine corruption is indistinguishable from the expected benign duplicate-key case this comment is defending against. This is also EH-4-adjacent (catches Error subtypes, not just typed Exceptions) and evades the Rule-0 'no empty catch blocks' Makefile grep (`catch\s*(_\?\w*)\s*{}`), which only matches a literal same-line `{}` — this multi-line comment-only body is functionally empty but textually invisible to that checker. Per the file's own header comment, the outbox enqueue here is what 'closes the gap' where a second device sees a frozen streak; if enqueueStreakPayload throws, that gap silently reopens with zero diagnostic trail and no retry.
findings.recommendation: Catch a specific expected type (e.g. the Drift unique-constraint exception) for the benign-duplicate case and let everything else propagate or be logged via AppLogger.instance.warning/error before swallowing, so a genuine failure is at least visible in Crashlytics/Talker.
acceptance_criteria: The catch narrows to the specific expected exception type; every other path logs via AppLogger before returning; a regression test that makes enqueueStreakPayload throw asserts the failure is logged, not silently dropped.

findings.title: Wrap LearningLedgerRepositoryImpl's ledger insert and outbox enqueue in one transaction
findings.why: recordCompletion inserts the learning_ledger row (line 104) and then enqueues its outbox row (line 127) as two separate, unwrapped statements; recordCompletionsBatch commits all N ledger rows inside one _database.transaction() (closes at line 195) but then loops the outbox enqueue afterward, outside that transaction, one row at a time. A process death or crash between these steps leaves a ledger entry (e.g. a manual siyum mark from the Lifetime Marking screen) permanently local-only — nothing re-derives a missing outbox row from an existing ledger row, so it never reaches Firestore or a second device. The sibling CompletionWriter (completion_writer.dart) explicitly wraps its analogous completion_events + outbox insert in one Drift transaction for exactly this reason (its docs call this 'Both rows commit or both roll back' — the FR15/RC1 fix); LearningLedgerRepositoryImpl doesn't follow the same discipline for the same class of append-only sync-critical data.
findings.recommendation: Move the outbox enqueue for recordCompletion inside the same transaction as the ledger insert (or into one atomic Drift batch, as CompletionWriter does); for recordCompletionsBatch, move the per-item enqueueLedgerEntry calls inside the existing transaction block instead of running them afterward in a separate loop.

findings.title: Stop relying on find.byKey(...).last for time-row lookups in notifications_screen_l1_test.dart and notifications_screen_test.dart
findings.why: _SettingsTimeRow (learning_tracker/lib/features/notifications/presentation/screens/notifications_screen.dart:306, `return ListTile(key: key, ...)`) forwards its own key onto the inner ListTile it builds, so Key('reminder_time')/Key('streak_alert_time') each match 2 elements in the tree. All 8 sites paper over that with `.last`, trusting find.byKey's traversal order to put the ListTile after its wrapper -- an implementation detail, not a documented Flutter API contract -- while the very same file already uses a robust, order-independent alternative for the Switch rows (e.g. l1_test.dart:218-220, `find.descendant(of: reminderRow, matching: find.byType(Switch))`). If the match order ever flipped, `.last` would silently resolve to the wrapper widget and the ensuing `tester.widget<ListTile>(...)` cast would throw, breaking otherwise-unrelated tests with a confusing error.
findings.recommendation: Match the ListTile the same way the Switch rows already do -- e.g. `find.widgetWithText(ListTile, l10n.notifReminderTime)` or, on the production side, stop forwarding `key` to the inner ListTile in _SettingsTimeRow and instead expose a distinct key for it -- so the finder resolves to exactly one widget without depending on registration order.
acceptance_criteria: Time-row assertions no longer call `.last` on a byKey finder with 2 matches.

findings.title: Harden or test the failure path of the unawaited CompletionDetectionService call in CompletionRepositoryImpl.markComplete
findings.rule: EH-2/EH-3 (errors converted/logged, no log-less catch) + Nygard (partial I/O failure) -- surfaced via this batch's tests

evidence.quote:
// Wait for any fire-and-forget unawaited futures to settle.

findings.why: completion_detection_service.dart and learning_ledger_repository_impl.dart contain zero try/catch blocks (grep-confirmed), and the call site wraps them in unawaited(...) with no .catchError, so any exception during siyum detection (closed DB mid profile-switch, disk-full write, a malformed content lookup) becomes an unhandled Future error with no retry and no user-facing signal -- the completion itself still records, but the documented B1 policy ('a learner who bulk-marks a complete masechta still earns the siyum') silently fails to hold for that unit, permanently, with no reconciliation job anywhere in lib/ to catch the gap. findings.recommendation: Wrap the unawaited call in a .catchError (or add an internal try/catch inside checkAndRecordCompletions) that logs via AppLogger per EH-3; add a test that forces the detection service to throw (e.g. a ContentRepository stub that throws) and assert markComplete still returns successfully while the failure is logged.
