findings.title: Check ref.mounted/State.mounted before touching state after await in onboarding async flows
findings.why: Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException when a disposed Notifier's ref/state is touched, and Flutter throws on setState() after dispose(). OnboardingController is @riverpod (autoDispose); if the wizard screen holding it is popped while current.save(ref) (a DB-touching step save) is in flight, advance() resumes and unconditionally reads/writes state, crashing. bulk_mark_screen.dart demonstrably knows the correct pattern -- _loadPreExistingCompletions checks mounted twice -- yet _proceedToConfirmation and both branches of _executeBulkMark omit it after their own awaits, so backgrounding the app or hitting back during a multi-hundred-item bulk-mark write reproduces the same crash class.
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` / `if (!mounted) return;` immediately after every await that is followed by a state=/setState/provider touch, matching the pattern already used correctly elsewhere in the same files.
acceptance_criteria: a notifier/widget test that disposes the provider/widget mid-await (pump then pop before the fake repository's Future completes) passes without throwing
a grep-based Rule-0 checker (or the fixed custom_lint) flags `state =`/`setState(` appearing after an `await` in a Notifier/State method without an intervening mounted guard

findings.title: Wrap multi-statement Drift writes in transaction() in the wizard stage-apply and prior-completion expunge paths
findings.why: A process death (OOM kill, backgrounding) between the delete and the insert loop in applyWizardResult leaves a track with zero or partial review stages, breaking the B6 'every configured stage needs a completion row' invariant documented in bulk_prior_completion_service.dart's own docstring -- for both first-run onboarding and the edit-track flow. StageDao already ships a transactional `replaceStagesForTrack` (stage_dao.dart:83-93, wraps the identical delete+insert in db.transaction()) and a generic `runTransaction` helper, but applyWizardResult calls the raw untransacted DAO methods instead. Separately, expungePriorCompletions tombstones completion_events, deletes prior_completion_imports, then loops outbox inserts as three independently-awaited steps with no enclosing transaction; a crash after the tombstone UPDATE but before the outbox inserts land leaves the local device showing an item as unmarked while every other synced device still shows it complete, because the tombstone never reaches Firestore.
findings.recommendation: Call the existing StageDao.replaceStagesForTrack/runTransaction helper from applyWizardResult instead of raw delete+insert; wrap expungePriorCompletions's update+delete+insert sequence in _database.transaction().
acceptance_criteria: a test that throws inside the stage-insert loop (fake DAO) asserts zero stages remain afterward (rollback), not a partial set
a test that throws after the tombstone UPDATE in expungePriorCompletions asserts the prior_completion_imports row still exists (rollback) instead of a half-tombstoned state
a DB-2 Rule-0 grep checker flags >1 awaited mutation in a service method with no enclosing db.transaction()

findings.title: Stop surfacing PinService's raw ArgumentError.message as OnboardingParentPinStep's error text
findings.why: The domain layer's exception message is an English literal that reaches the presentation layer verbatim and unlocalized (PinService throws ArgumentError('PIN must be exactly 4 numeric digits') at pin_service.dart:65,135,199), so a Hebrew-locale parent sees this exact English sentence when setting up a child's PIN. It is also brittle cross-layer coupling: ArgumentError.message is typed Object?, so the `as String?` cast is only safe because every current throw site happens to pass a String -- changing any one of the three pin_service.dart throw sites to ArgumentError.value(...) would turn a benign validation failure into an unhandled TypeError in this catch block.
findings.recommendation: Give PinService a typed error (enum or sealed class per EH-2/EH-6) instead of ArgumentError(String), and resolve the display string in the widget via AppLocalizations.
acceptance_criteria: PinService validation failure exposed as a typed value/enum, not ArgumentError with a formatted message
a test asserts the PIN-mismatch/invalid-PIN error text is resolved via AppLocalizations for both en and he locales

findings.title: Log the swallowed exception in BulkMarkScreen._loadPreExistingCompletions's catch block

evidence.quote:
} catch (_) {
      // Non-fatal: if pre-tick loading fails just open with unticked state.

findings.why: The B7 pre-tick feature (pre-checking previously-completed items when the bulk-mark screen opens) fails completely silently on any exception -- DB error, malformed hierarchy data -- with zero telemetry. If pre-ticking breaks in production (e.g. after a schema change), nobody will know; users will see every item as unticked and may re-mark (and re-earn siyum credit for) content already completed, with no log line to diagnose why.
findings.recommendation: Log via AppLogger.instance.warning(event: ..., exception: e, stackTrace: st) before falling through to the unticked-state fallback, matching the pattern already used in _expungeRefs's .catchError a few lines below in the same file.

findings.title: Await BulkMarkScreen._expungeRefs's expunge writes before invalidating dependent providers
findings.why: The loop fires expungePriorCompletions (which internally does multiple awaited DB writes) without awaiting it, then immediately calls ref.invalidate on the dashboard/progress providers. Because those providers are manually invalidated rather than backed by a reactive .watch() stream, the invalidated providers can refetch before the un-awaited expunge write lands, showing the user a stale (pre-expunge) completion count right after unticking a previously-marked item. Confirming this needs a widget test with a deliberately delayed fake CompletionRepository asserting the provider's value immediately after _toggleItem completes.
findings.recommendation: await Future.wait(refs.map((r) => service.expungePriorCompletions(...))) before the ref.invalidate calls, or move invalidation into a .whenComplete() continuation.
acceptance_criteria: a test with an artificially delayed expunge write asserts the dashboard provider reflects the post-expunge count immediately after the awaited toggle completes, not the pre-expunge count

findings.title: Hoist EmptyLoginScreen's getAllAccounts() future out of build()
findings.why: future: is evaluated fresh on every rebuild of EmptyLoginScreen (theme change, locale change, any ancestor rebuild), so FutureBuilder restarts from its loading/no-data state each time, re-querying the device registry and making the account-switch icon flicker/disappear-and-reappear on unrelated rebuilds instead of staying stable.
findings.recommendation: Move the Future into a @riverpod FutureProvider (e.g. allDeviceAccountsProvider) and ref.watch it, or cache it in a late final in a stateful wrapper.
acceptance_criteria: a widget test that triggers an unrelated rebuild of EmptyLoginScreen asserts getAllAccounts() is called exactly once, not once per rebuild

findings.title: Guard ref.mounted after awaits in PinFlowController._handleSetup/_handleChange/_handleVerify (SM-4)
findings.why: PinFlowController is @Riverpod(keepAlive: true), so it survives normal widget disposal, but keepAlive doesn't prevent explicit container disposal (app teardown, ref.invalidate, hot-restart, or a route pop mid-flight) while a bcrypt verify/hash is in flight — bcrypt is deliberately slow, widening this window. Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException from a post-await `state = ...` write if the container is gone by then. None of the 4 awaited PinService call sites (_handleSetup confirm-save, _handleChange verifyCurrent and confirm-save, _handleVerify) check ref.mounted first, and none of the 628 lines in pin_flow_controller_test.dart dispose the container between firing an async PIN action and that action resolving — every async test either awaits full completion or uses a never-resolving Future, so this path is never exercised. Runtime confirmation needs a test that disposes mid-await and checks the outcome is clean rather than an uncaught exception.
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` immediately after each of the 4 awaited PinService calls, before the subsequent state write. Add a regression test that disposes the container after the 4th digit triggers the async handler but before the pending PinService future resolves.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the 4 sites has a ref.mounted guard after its await.

findings.title: Guard ref access after await in notification_providers.dart effect providers (SM-4)
findings.why: allProfilesReminderBootstrap, reminderSyncEffect and streakAlertSyncEffect all touch ref (read/watch) immediately after an await with no ref.mounted guard. If any of these keepAlive FutureProviders is invalidated or disposed while suspended past its first await (profile switch, container teardown during navigation/tests, hot-reload), the next ref access throws UnmountedRefException uncaught, leaving the provider's AsyncValue stuck in .error and silently freezing that profile's notification (re)scheduling until something else forces a rebuild.
findings.recommendation: Add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` immediately after each await, before any further ref access, in all three functions.
acceptance_criteria: A test that invalidates a watched dependency mid-flight (e.g. activeProfileIdProvider while profileListStreamProvider.future is pending) asserts the effect settles instead of throwing UnmountedRefException.
A Rule-0 grep/lint flags ref.read(/ref.watch( on a line whose nearest preceding statement in the same async function contains await with no intervening ref.mounted check.

findings.title: Route sacred_window_repository.dart through the sacred_time barrel instead of deep cross-feature imports (Rule 2)

evidence.quote: match($1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print

findings.why: features/notifications reaches directly into features/sacred_time's domain internals instead of features/sacred_time/sacred_time.dart (itself an empty stub barrel with no exports), so a refactor inside sacred_time's domain layer can silently break notification scheduling with no barrel-boundary warning. Separately, make audit check 15's awk pattern always compares a feature name against itself: it runs match() against $0 (the whole grep -rn line, which starts with the FILE PATH), so the first 'features/X/' match in $0 is always the same X captured from $1 -- a[1] and b[1] can never differ, so check 15 can never print a warning for ANY file. findings.title: Wrap SacredWindowEntries clear+insert in one transaction (DB-2)
findings.why: The table is briefly empty between clearAll() completing and insertAll() starting; neither call is awaited by any caller and neither is wrapped in a transaction. invalidate()'s own separate unawaited clearAll() (line 50) can also interleave with _persistToDb()'s clear-then-insert pair (line 167) in either order. The class's own doc says this cache exists so 'background notification-fire-time checks can read them on cold-start without the Flutter engine' -- a background read landing in the empty gap, or after invalidate() wins a race against a slower insertAll(), sees no Sacred Time windows and could fail to suppress a notification during Shabbos/Yom Tov, the entire point of DNI-367. Confirming the full consequence requires reading the background notification-fire-time isolate handler, which is outside this batch.
findings.recommendation: Wrap clear+insert in one db.transaction(...) and await it from both invalidate() and _persistToDb(), or add an explicit generation-counter guard so a stale clear can't stomp a newer insert.
acceptance_criteria: A DAO-level test that races invalidate() against a concurrent _persistToDb() cycle never observes SacredWindowEntries transition through an empty state once a non-empty write has committed.

findings.title: Use a clock-skew-safe timestamp, not client clock, for notification_settings updated_at LWW field
findings.why: This client-computed timestamp becomes the payload's updated_at field pushed via enqueueNotificationSettings; core/sync/merge/notification_settings_merger.dart (outside this batch) parses remote['updated_at'] to arbitrate LWW. If two devices' clocks disagree, the device with the faster/wrong clock can push a stale settings change that looks 'newer' and wins over a genuinely newer change made on a correctly-clocked device, silently reverting the user's real edit with no error surfaced anywhere. Confirming the full blast radius requires reading the outbox-drain write path (outside this batch) to see whether it overwrites this field with FieldValue.serverTimestamp() before commit.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether the write path already substitutes a server timestamp before commit; if not, do so, or route the push side through the same clock-skew arbitration MergeStore.remoteIsNewer already implements for the pull side.
acceptance_criteria: A sync test with an artificially-skewed local clock demonstrates the genuinely later settings write wins regardless of which device has the faster clock.

findings.title: Test the real _persistNotificationSettingsToCloud signature logic, not a hand-copied reimplementation
findings.why: _persistNotificationSettingsToCloud's M2 no-op-skip logic (skip pushing when the settings signature hasn't changed, to avoid bumping updated_at and clobbering a newer remote under LWW -- the exact mechanism the client-clock finding depends on) is a private function, so G1-G4 reimplement its string format by hand in the test file instead of exercising it. If a future edit to the real signature-building code drops a field or changes the separator, breaking the no-op-skip contract, G1-G4 keep passing because they never call the real function.
findings.recommendation: Extract the signature-building into an internal @visibleForTesting function the tests can call directly, or drive it end-to-end via notificationSettingsCloudSyncEffectProvider with a fake outbox facade asserting enqueue is/isn't called across setting changes.
acceptance_criteria: A mutation check confirms G1-G4 (or their replacement) fail when a field is removed from the real signature-building code in notification_providers.dart.

findings.title: Convert ReminderPreferences to @freezed instead of hand-rolled ==/hashCode/copyWith
findings.why: Matches the coding standard's explicit rule to never hand-write ==/hashCode for data classes. The 7 fields are consistent between == and hashCode today, but every future field addition is a manual 3-way sync across the constructor, ==, hashCode and copyWith -- an easy place to introduce a silent equality bug (a field present in the constructor but missed in == makes two logically-different instances compare equal).
findings.recommendation: Convert to @freezed class ReminderPreferences with _$ReminderPreferences.
acceptance_criteria: dart run build_runner build generates the freezed file and existing tests (e.g. notification_providers_deep_test.dart groups H/A-E) keep passing unmodified.

In these 3 files, _buildApp (and _buildAppLoading/_buildAppError, which have no db: parameter at all) construct one via `db ?? inMemoryDb()` whenever the optional db: is omitted, and the large majority of testWidgets in parent_settings_screen_l1_test.dart and parent_track_management_screen_l1_test.dart (~30 of ~40 across the two files) do omit it, so each test run leaks a native sqlite3 in-memory connection nothing ever closes — the caller has no reference to the db, so it can't be closed even in a teardown. evidence.quote:
try {
          final ok = await pinService.verifyProfilePin(profileId, pin);

state = state.copyWith(busy: true, errorMessage: null);
        await pinService.setProfilePin(profileId, pin);

try {
      final ok = await pinService.verifyProfilePin(profileId, pin);

findings.why: Per SM-4 (and the digest's own note that Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException), every `await` in a Notifier method must be followed by a `ref.mounted` check before touching `state`. None of the four PIN-transition handlers in this @Riverpod(keepAlive:true) notifier do this — `_handleSetup`, `_handleChange` (twice), and `_handleVerify` all assign `state = state.copyWith(...)` immediately after an `await pinService.*Pin(...)` with no guard. The confirm-step of `_handleChange` (line 350-351) is worse: it has no try/catch at all around `setProfilePin`, unlike its own sibling handlers. If the provider is invalidated/torn down while a bcrypt hash/secure-storage write is in flight (e.g. rapid navigation away, container disposal), the resulting exception is unguarded and, for the confirm-step case, has no catch clause to even convert it to a value.
findings.recommendation: After each await in _handleSetup/_handleChange/_handleVerify, add `if (!ref.mounted) return;` before assigning state; wrap the confirm-step setProfilePin call in the same try/catch pattern used by _handleSetup.

findings.title: Guard ProfileRepositoryImpl.deleteProfile's cloud-sync push the same way create/update/ensureDefaultProfile do
findings.why: createProfile, updateProfile, and ensureDefaultProfile all wrap their `_syncEngine?.push*` call in try/catch with an explicit 'offline-first, cloud push is non-fatal' comment. deleteProfile does not: `await _syncEngine?.deleteLearnerProfile(id)` runs bare, after the local cascade-delete transaction has already committed across ~12 tables. Both push and delete enqueue through the same outbox `_enqueue` mechanism (a local Drift insert), so they carry the same theoretical failure mode (e.g. disk-full, DB-locked). If that insert throws, the whole deleteProfile Future rejects even though the profile is already gone locally — and neither of deleteProfile's two callers in this batch (profile_edit_delete_actions.dart's deleteProfileFlow, profile_picker_screen.dart's _showDeleteDialog) catch it either, so the exception surfaces as an unhandled error in a button's onPressed handler while the delete has, in fact, already succeeded — contradicting the offline-first invariant this same file documents for every other mutation.
findings.recommendation: Wrap `await _syncEngine?.deleteLearnerProfile(id)` in the same non-fatal try/catch (with logging per the previous finding) used by createProfile/updateProfile/ensureDefaultProfile.

findings.title: Fix the always-passing awk comparison in Makefile check 15/15 (no-cross-feature-deep-imports)

evidence.quote: match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print

findings.why: match($0, ...) scans the whole 'path:lineno:content' grep line and matches the FIRST 'features/xxx/' occurrence, which is always inside the file-path prefix — identical to what match($1, ...) already extracted. a[1] and b[1] are therefore always equal and the filter never prints, regardless of which feature is actually imported. Running the exact command directly against the current tree confirms 0 output even though the 18 cross-feature-import lines cited in the paired finding (and ~26 total repo-wide) exist. Rule 2 has had zero real enforcement, even as a warning, since this check was written.
findings.recommendation: Match the import path portion only (e.g. split on the literal single-quote around the package path before matching, or grep the content field explicitly by re-slicing on the first two colons). Add a fixture case to the audit's own coverage so a future edit to this check can't silently break it again.

findings.title: Make scheduler STUDYDAY-* regression tests exercise the real screen/provider code they claim to guard
findings.rule: TQ-8 (regression test must pin the actual bug, not a re-derivation) / Feathers testability lens

evidence.quote: 'upsertDayConfig result is immediately visible to getConfigsByTrack '

findings.why: Each file's docstring and reason: strings claim to prove/document a specific screen-layer bug fix — STUDYDAY-CHAZARA-GATE-12's threshold in the private `_curriculumTrackHasChazaraProvider`, STUDYDAY-TOGGLE-RACE-14's invalidate-after-write ordering in `_toggleDay`, STUDYDAY-COMPANION-10's null-trackId guard in `_toggleDay` (all in study_day_config_screen.dart) — but none of the three files ever reference `_toggleDay` or `_curriculumTrackHasChazaraProvider`. They call only the DAO directly, or re-type the guard's `if (trackId != null)` inline in the test itself. If a future edit changes the private provider's threshold (e.g. `count > 1` to `count >= 1`) or reintroduces `track?.id ?? 0`, these three files stay green — they would not notice. findings.title: Replace fixed Future.delayed sleeps with a deterministic await in scheduler provider tests
findings.rule: TQ-6 (hermetic tests, no timing-based synchronization) / Fowler flaky-test smell
findings.why: Every one of these sites follows the same pattern: `c.listen(skippedTasksProvider, (_, __) {})` then a hardcoded 100-200ms sleep, hoping SkippedTasks._loadFromPrefs() (fired via `unawaited()` inside build()) finished first — instead of awaiting the load itself, because the notifier exposes no future to await. Under a loaded CI runner or slower SharedPreferences-mock resolution the guess can be wrong: assertions then run against the stale initial `{}` state, or (in the several tests that call `.skip()`/`.undoSkip()` immediately after the sleep) a late-resolving `_loadFromPrefs()` can overwrite `state` with old prefs data right after the test's own mutation, silently clobbering it. The result is an intermittent, hard-to-reproduce CI failure with no diagnostic pointing at the real cause, plus 3+ seconds of pure sleep time paid on every run across these 4 files.
findings.recommendation: Give SkippedTasks a way to be awaited deterministically (e.g. an internal `Future<void>` the notifier tracks that a test helper can await via `container.read(...notifier).debugReadyForTest`), or restructure as an AsyncNotifier so tests can `await container.read(skippedTasksProvider.future)`. Replace all fixed-delay call sites with that await.
acceptance_criteria: No `Future<void>.delayed` remains in test/features/scheduler/presentation/providers/*.dart used purely to wait for provider initialization.
A test that artificially slows the fake SharedPreferences resolution (e.g. via a delayed Future in the mock) still passes, proving synchronization is no longer time-based.

findings.why: A stray level1 ledger row targeting a composite curriculum's synthetic container (e.g. tanach/level1/'Torah' — created by a since-fixed bug and, per the code's own comment, never cleaned up on already-upgraded devices because the v32 migration only runs once) makes every leaf under that curriculum register as learned. lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart's lifetimeDataProvider defends against this by dropping synthetic-container level1 rows before building the tree (comment there explicitly calls it a 'P0 (composite over-credit) READ-TIME guard'). items_learned_providers.dart's computeLifetimeViewSummary reimplements the identical ledger-to-learned-refs algorithm from scratch in a private _learnedLeafRefs function, but never applies the guard. Since the Lifetime Knowledge screen's default tab is 'All sources' (_filter = allSources), which routes to computeLifetimeViewSummary via lifetimeViewSummariesProvider, a user with exactly one Chumash book bulk/lifetime-marked can open the app and see 'Tanach 100% learned' by default — a silent, high-visibility corruption of the app's core progress-tracking claim. The one regression test written for this exact invariant (lifetime_tree_builder_composite_test.dart) only calls LifetimeTreeBuilder directly, so it gives zero protection against this duplicate path.
findings.recommendation: Delete the duplicate _learnedLeafRefs/_buildCompletionTree/_levelKey/_hebrewForLeafGroup functions in items_learned_providers.dart and have computeItemsLearnedSummary/computeLifetimeViewSummary call LifetimeTreeBuilder (computeLearnedLeafRefs/buildTree) directly, exactly as lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart already does, so the guard and any future fix apply to both surfaces from one implementation.
acceptance_criteria: A test mirroring lifetime_tree_builder_composite_test.dart's single-book scenario, but driven through computeLifetimeViewSummary/lifetimeViewSummariesProvider, asserts the composite curriculum's learned count equals the single book's leaf count, not the whole curriculum's.
items_learned_providers.dart contains no second implementation of the ledger-scope-to-learned-refs algorithm; grep for '_learnedLeafRefs' in that file returns nothing after the fix.

findings.title: Fix Makefile check 15/15 cross-feature-deep-import detector — awk comparison always matches a feature against itself
findings.rule: Rule 0 (deterministic checker) / Rule 2 (no cross-feature deep imports) / AG-11
findings.area: tooling (learning_tracker/Makefile `make audit` check 15/15) — found while triaging this batch's cross-feature imports against the Rule-2 baseline
findings.why: match($0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b) scans the WHOLE grep -n line ('path:line:content'), so it always matches the importing file's own features/<name>/ segment first — the identical substring match($1,...) already captured into a[1] — because the file path precedes the import statement in that line. a[1] and b[1] are therefore always equal and the WARN branch can never fire, for any input; verified empirically by piping a real progress-to-learning cross-feature import line through the exact awk one-liner, which prints nothing instead of the intended warning. The check is warn-only so this never flipped CI either way, but it means the tool meant to enumerate the Rule-2 backlog has never actually enumerated it: lib/features/progress alone has a dozen-plus real deep cross-feature imports (chart_data_service.dart -> features/learning/domain/entities/completion_tier_filter.dart; lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart -> features/content_browsing/..., features/dashboard/..., features/tracks/...) that should appear in the WARN list and never will. 'make audit ... PASSED — all 22 greps clean' and this audit's own baseline note that 'ALL current cross-feature deep-import edges are baselined' cannot be verified against reality for Rule 2 — the source list is empty by construction, not by absence of violations.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to compare the import target's feature against the importing file's own feature — e.g. restrict the second match() to substr($0, length($1)+1) so it only scans the import-statement portion of the line — then re-run make audit and reconcile the resulting edge count against the digest's baseline claim, which today only actually covers check 14.
acceptance_criteria: Feeding a synthetic cross-feature import line through check 15's grep+awk pipeline prints the WARN line; feeding a same-feature deep-import line does not.
make audit's check 15 output, run against current HEAD, lists a non-empty (or explicitly justified empty) set of real cross-feature deep-import edges.

findings.title: Log the 5 silent catch blocks in items_learned_providers.dart and lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart (EH-3 log-less catch)
findings.why: Each swallows any exception (content-asset load failure, calendar-position lookup failure) with zero diagnostic trail, so when a curriculum silently drops out of Items Learned / Lifetime View, or a track's due/overdue badge silently reads zero, nothing in the logs explains why. The same two files already contain the correct pattern twice: _safeLoadLeaves (lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart:577) and _safeHeLabelLookup (:598) both log via AppLogger.instance.warning under a documented 'F20' fix ('surface content-asset load failures so a missing/corrupt asset is diagnosable instead of silently producing an empty tree') — but that fix was never applied to these 5 other catches doing the identical kind of fallback-on-failure.
findings.recommendation: Route all 5 catches through AppLogger.instance.warning with the same event/fields shape as the F20 fix in _safeLoadLeaves, before returning the fallback value.
acceptance_criteria: grep for log-less catch blocks (or the custom_lint no_raw_logevent/empty-catch equivalent once fixed) reports zero hits in these two files.
A test that forces repo.getContentForCurriculum to throw asserts a warning is logged, for at least one of the 5 sites.

findings.title: Collapse chart_data_service.dart's *Live methods — byte-identical duplicates of their non-Live counterparts

findings.title: Stop interpolating raw error.toString() into localized error messages across progress screens
findings.rule: EH-5 / custom_lint no_e_to_string_in_ui (currently enforcing nothing repo-wide)
findings.why: error.toString() on a Dart/Firebase/Drift exception is always in English (e.g. 'Bad state: ...', 'SqliteException: ...') and not ICU-pluralizable; interpolating it into an otherwise-Hebrew ARB string means a Hebrew-locale, RTL user who hits any of these error states sees a sentence that switches to raw untranslated English mid-string. recent_activity_screen.dart in the same directory shows the correct pattern (l10n.chartFailedToLoad with no error interpolation, 4 uses) — the other 4 screens in this same feature diverge from it.
findings.recommendation: Replace error.toString() interpolation with the generic localized failure string (as recent_activity_screen.dart already does) and, if diagnostic detail is genuinely needed, log error.toString() via AppLogger instead of rendering it to the user.
acceptance_criteria: None of the 4 screens' AsyncValue.error branches call .toString() on the error object inside a Text/l10n call.

findings.title: Replace hand-rolled ==/hashCode on PaceCalculator, LifetimeLeafProvenance and RecentActivityWindow with @freezed or a record
findings.rule: naming/placement — domain/state models are @freezed; never hand-write ==/hashCode for data classes
findings.why: Three separate hand-written equality implementations exist in this one feature slice alongside a fourth model file (journey_view_model.dart) that correctly uses @freezed for the same kind of value object, and alongside sibling family-key records elsewhere in this same batch (e.g. lifetime_knowledge_providers.dart's ({int profileId, CurriculumId curriculumId})) that get structural equality for free. Hand-rolled equality is exactly the boilerplate freezed exists to generate and keep in sync; PaceCalculator's == only compares 6 of its 13 fields (the derived ones are excluded) which is easy to get wrong silently the next time a field is added, since nothing forces == and hashCode to be touched together.
findings.recommendation: Convert PaceCalculator and LifetimeLeafProvenance to @freezed classes (both fit the private-const-factory-plus-named-computing-factory pattern already used elsewhere for derived-field value objects); convert RecentActivityWindow to a named-field record (({DateTime startDate, DateTime endDate, String? curriculumId})) to match the record-based family keys already used in this same feature.
acceptance_criteria: grep -rn 'bool operator ==' lib/features/progress/ (excluding .freezed.dart/.g.dart) returns no hits.

findings.title: Fix make audit check 15/15's awk logic — it can never detect a cross-feature deep import
findings.rule: Rule 2 (no cross-feature deep imports) / Rule 0 (checker must actually detect violations)
findings.area: Makefile `make audit` tooling (discovered via a features/scheduler test import)
findings.why: match($0, ...) scans the WHOLE grep -rn output line (`path:line:content`), so it always matches the leftmost `features/<X>/` substring — which is the FILE's own path segment — identical to what match($1, ...) already captured. b[1] therefore always equals a[1] and `if(a[1] != b[1])` can mathematically never be true. Verified with an isolated repro piping the real scheduler_engine.dart grep-rn line through the exact awk expression: both captures resolve to 'scheduler', differ=0. Consequence: check 15/15 has never printed a single violation on any `make audit` run regardless of how many real cross-feature deep imports exist in lib/features/ — it currently misses both lib/features/scheduler/domain/services/scheduler_engine.dart:11 and test/features/scheduler/domain/services/scheduler_engine_schedule_types_test.dart:12, which both import features/tracks/stages/domain/models/schedule_type.dart directly instead of via a tracks.dart barrel. `make audit`'s 'PASSED — all 22 greps clean' banner therefore gives false assurance specifically for Rule 2: an unbounded amount of cross-feature coupling could accumulate with zero signal to any developer or CI run.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the awk step to derive b[1] from the import-statement text only (e.g. strip the `path:line:` prefix with a field split on the first two colons before matching, or match specifically on `package:learning_tracker/features/([^/]+)/`), and add a regression fixture (a deliberately cross-feature-importing line) that the check must catch so this can't silently regress again.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture cross-feature import line makes `make audit` check 15/15 print a WARN; a test/CI step proves the check fails closed when the fixture is present.

Re-run `make audit` after the fix and triage the resulting real violation list, starting with scheduler_engine.dart:11 and scheduler_engine_schedule_types_test.dart:12 — route through the tracks.dart barrel or add to a documented baseline.

findings.title: Add regression tests for GoalRepositoryImpl's not-found and delete-sync payload paths
findings.rule: EH-2 (typed exceptions surfaced correctly) / TQ-8 (every reachable error branch needs a red-first test)

evidence.quote:
if (existing == null) {
        throw ArgumentError('Goal not found: $goalId');

findings.why: (a) updateGoal throws ArgumentError when goalId doesn't exist (e.g. the goal was deleted from another device and the sync merge already removed the local row before this device's in-flight edit lands) — no test in this file ever calls updateGoal with a nonexistent id, so nothing pins whether it throws, what it throws, or that a future refactor doesn't silently swallow/change it. (b) The file's own 'sync payload completeness (R4-6)' group exists specifically because create/update once shipped without profile_id/id in the outbox payload — but that hardening was never extended to deleteGoal: _RecordingGoalSyncFacade.deleteGoal is a blind no-op with no payload recorder (unlike goalPayloads for pushGoal), and the sole 'deleteGoal removes the goal' test uses the sync-less `repo` instance, so _syncDeleteGoal's {firestore_id, curriculum_id} payload is completely unverified. A key rename or dropped field in _syncDeleteGoal would ship silently — the exact class of bug R4-6 was written to catch for create/update.
findings.recommendation: Add a test asserting updateGoal(goalId: <nonexistent>) throws ArgumentError; add a deletePayloads recorder to _RecordingGoalSyncFacade and a test asserting deleteGoal() pushes the expected firestore_id/curriculum_id payload, mirroring the existing R4-6 create/update tests.
acceptance_criteria: New red-first test fails against a deliberately-broken updateGoal (e.g. the null check removed) and passes against current code.
New deleteGoal-payload test fails if _syncDeleteGoal's field names are renamed or dropped, mirroring the existing R4-6 create/update tests.

findings.title: Replace the hardcoded trackId:1 literal with the captured track id in two scheduler tests
findings.why: Both files insert a real curriculumTracks row and capture its autoincrement id into a `trackId` local specifically so downstream code can reference the real id — and both then ignore that variable and hardcode `trackId: 1` in the ScheduleConfig/generator.generate() calls that drive the assertions, while still correctly using the captured `trackId` variable a few lines away for the StageDefinitions/CompletionEvents inserts. It works today only because a fresh in-memory DB's first insert is always id 1 (verified: neither seedProfile nor seedProfileZero touch curriculumTracks). If either helper is ever extended to seed a track, or a second track is inserted earlier in a shared setUp, config.trackId/DailyTask.trackId would silently diverge from the row the stages/completions actually reference, and no assertion in either file would catch it since nothing currently checks task.trackId's value.

findings.title: Drop the hard-coded 500ms wall-clock assertion from scheduler_engine_performance_test.dart

evidence.quote:
final stopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();
      final tasks = await engine.generateDailyTasks(config);

findings.why: This test asserts a hard wall-clock budget (elapsedMilliseconds < 500) for a 5,000-item/10,000-completion synchronous computation, running inside the same hermetic unit suite as every other file in this batch (no @Tags/exclusion). It passed on this run, but pass/fail now depends on host CPU speed and contention from parallel test-runner isolates/CI-runner noise, not on SchedulerEngine's correctness — a classic Nygard/Fowler 'erratic test.' A spurious failure on a busy CI runner produces a false-negative unrelated to the diff under review, and the natural response ('just rerun it') erodes trust in the suite over time.
findings.recommendation: Tag it out of the default hermetic run (e.g. `@Tags(['perf'])`, matching how the repo already tags story-acceptance suites) so it runs in a dedicated, less contention-sensitive job, or replace the absolute threshold with a much wider safety margin / relative-regression check.
acceptance_criteria: Test is excluded from the default `flutter test` sweep, or its threshold is widened enough (e.g. 5-10x measured baseline) to tolerate CI contention while still catching a genuine algorithmic regression (e.g. an accidental O(n^2) reintroduction).

findings.title: Replace DateTime.now() with a fixed clock value in scheduler test fixture seeding
findings.why: TQ-6 requires hermetic tests with no wall-clock. All three files otherwise correctly drive their actual scheduling assertions off a fixed `DateTime.utc(...)` 'now'/'today' constant — but the CurriculumTracksCompanion.insert(...) calls that seed the track row use the real system clock for stateChangedAt/activatedAt instead of that same fixed constant. No current assertion reads these two columns, so it doesn't flip any test's pass/fail today, but it's an easy trap: the moment a future test (or the production code these tests exercise) starts reading track state-change recency, these three tests will intermittently disagree with their own fixed 'now' by however many days/years separate the two clocks.

findings.title: Stop ProfileRepositoryImpl.updateProfile silently swallowing tutor Cloud-Function write failures
findings.rule: EH-2/EH-3 (typed errors must reach a boundary as values, no log-less catch) + Nygard lens (retry-assumption mismatch across facade implementations)

evidence.quote:
} catch (_) {
      // no-op: cloud push failure is non-fatal; local write already succeeded (offline-first)

/// When a tutor session is active ([activeTutoredProfileSelectionProvider] !=
/// null) the outbox facade is wrapped by a [TutoredWriteRouter]

} catch (_) {
      // no-op: cloud push failure is non-fatal; local write already succeeded (offline-first)

} catch (_) {
      // no-op: cloud push failure is non-fatal; local write already succeeded.

findings.why: ProfileRepositoryImpl wraps every _syncEngine?.pushLearnerProfile(...) call in a blanket catch(_) {} (createProfile:104-109, updateProfile:157-161, self-heal:321-336), on the premise that 'local write already succeeded (offline-first)' and the push will retry later. That premise only holds when _syncEngine is the durable OutboxSyncWriteFacade. Per sync_providers.dart:75-78, when a tutor session is active, _syncEngine is instead a TutoredWriteRouter that turns pushLearnerProfile into a one-shot, non-retryable Cloud Function RPC (tutorEditProfile). When that RPC fails (network drop, CF timeout, or the tutor's grant expiring mid-session), the failure is discarded: updateProfile still returns its local model as if the push succeeded, so the tutor's own local mirror shows the rename/mode/avatar change permanently while the owner's actual Firestore profile was never touched — a silent, non-retryable divergence between what the tutor sees and what actually persisted, with zero error surfaced. This also makes editProfileFlow's dedicated 'on TutorWriteException catch' (profile_edit_delete_actions.dart:46) dead code: repo.updateProfile can only ever let StateError or DuplicateProfileNameException (line 134) escape to its caller, and editProfileFlow doesn't catch the latter at all, so even a same-account name collision on the Edit flow throws unhandled — unlike ProfilePickerScreen's own separate rename dialog, which does catch DuplicateProfileNameException. profile_edit_delete_actions_test.dart exercises neither path (zero references to TutorWriteException or DuplicateProfileNameException in the whole file).
findings.recommendation: Only swallow pushLearnerProfile failures when the underlying facade is genuinely durable/retryable (OutboxSyncWriteFacade); let a TutorWriteException-shaped failure propagate (or convert it to a typed Result the caller must handle) so editProfileFlow's existing catch becomes reachable and can tell the tutor the edit didn't save. Add a catch for DuplicateProfileNameException in editProfileFlow mirroring profile_picker_screen.dart's _showRenameDialog.
acceptance_criteria: ProfileRepositoryImpl no longer unconditionally swallows pushLearnerProfile failures when the sync facade is the tutor-routed (non-durable) path

findings.title: Fix the tautological awk comparison in make audit check 15 so cross-feature deep imports are ever reported
findings.why: awk's match() finds the leftmost occurrence of `features/([^/]+)/` in $0, which for a `file:line:content` grep line is always inside the FILE PATH itself (it precedes the content). So a[1] (from $1, the path) and b[1] (from $0) are always derived from the same leading match and are always equal — `a[1] != b[1]` can never be true. I reproduced this directly: piping the real repo through the exact pipeline yields 0 lines even though 1186 lines match the pre-filter pattern, and manually evaluating the awk on a scheduler_providers.dart import line prints `a=scheduler b=scheduler` for an import that is unambiguously FROM `features/learning/`. Rule 2 is marked [E] (enforced) but its checker is structurally incapable of ever printing a violation or failing, regardless of how much cross-feature coupling exists — `make audit PASSED` gives false assurance for this rule specifically (distinct from the already-documented 'warn-only' gap, which assumed the check merely doesn't fail the build, not that it is inert).
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the check-15 pipeline to compare the importing file's own feature (parsed once from $1) against the imported feature (parsed from the import statement/content portion only, e.g. by stripping $1 and the line number before matching), and add a fixture test (a temp file with a deliberate deep cross-feature import) asserting the check's exit/output actually flags it before merging any fix.
acceptance_criteria: `make audit` check 15 prints at least one file:line when a deliberate cross-feature deep import is introduced in a throwaway test fixture.
A regression test or CI fixture pins this behavior so the check cannot silently regress to a no-op again.

findings.title: Normalize config.currentDate before delay-stage due-date arithmetic in SchedulerEngine
findings.why: config.currentDate flows in unnormalized: allDailyTasksProvider sets `now = ref.watch(clockProvider)` (a raw timestamp with time-of-day) and _buildFreshPlan passes it straight through generator.generateAll(activeCurricula, now, ...) -> ScheduleConfig(currentDate: date). previousCompletedAt also carries a real time-of-day (completion timestamps are never normalized — confirmed via completion_writer.dart). Duration.inDays truncates toward zero, so when the true calendar-day gap is exactly 1 day but the elapsed wall-clock time is <24h (e.g. item completed at 20:00 five days ago, now it's 02:00 the next calendar day — only 6h elapsed), daysUntilDue computes 0 instead of -1: a chazara item that is genuinely 1+ calendar days overdue is shown in 'due today' (scheduledTasks) instead of 'overdue' (overdueTasks), silently under-reporting overdue-ness by up to a day. This is the same class of bug (R4-1) this codebase has explicitly fixed elsewhere in the very same feature (local_calendar_engine.dart's UTC-midnight handling, goal_setup_screen.dart's daysRemaining guard, and _buildProjectionTasks's pervasive DateUtils.extractLocalDate use) — just missed in the delay-stage path.
findings.recommendation: Normalize both previousCompletedAt/currentCompletedAt and config.currentDate to calendar-date-only (e.g. via DateUtils.extractLocalDate) before computing daysUntilDue in _processDelayStage, matching the pattern already used in _buildProjectionTasks.
acceptance_criteria: New unit test: a delay-stage item whose previous-stage completedAt time-of-day is later than the current query's time-of-day, with a true 1-calendar-day gap, asserts the task lands in overdueTasks (not scheduledTasks).

findings.title: Guard SkippedTasks.build()'s fire-and-forget prefs load with ref.mounted
findings.why: build() kicks off an un-awaited async side effect (SM-2 forbids side effects in build). _loadFromPrefs() then does `await SharedPreferences.getInstance()` and further awaits before writing `state = ...` twice, with no `ref.mounted` check (SM-4) anywhere in the method. If the provider is disposed (e.g. the user navigates off the Scheduler screen quickly) before the load resolves, the post-await `state = ...` throws Riverpod 3's UnmountedRefException — which the surrounding try/catch swallows and logs via `AppLogger.instance.error(event: 'Failed to load skipped tasks', ...)`, i.e. a routine dispose race gets misreported as a genuine load failure in production logs/Crashlytics breadcrumbs, obscuring real failures of the same code path.
findings.recommendation: Check `ref.mounted` immediately before each `state = ...` assignment in _loadFromPrefs, and return early (without logging) when unmounted, matching Riverpod 3's documented SM-4 pattern used elsewhere in the codebase.
acceptance_criteria: _loadFromPrefs checks ref.mounted before both `state = refs.toSet()` and `state = {}`.

findings.title: Wrap the DB write in StudyDayConfigScreen._toggleDay with catch/log and a consistent mounted guard

findings.recommendation: Wrap the DB write in try/catch with an AppLogger.error call and user-facing feedback on failure; check `context.mounted` (or equivalent) before the `ref.invalidate` call, matching the guard already present for the SnackBar.

findings.title: Migrate scheduler-adjacent tests off the deprecated LearningProgramRepository.instance singleton
findings.why: This static singleton is exactly the 'global/static mutable singleton' SM-7 prohibits, and it has zero production (lib/) call sites — but 30+ test files across the suite (test/core/services/*, test/story_acceptance/*, test/features/tracks/*, test/features/onboarding/*, etc.) construct their fixtures via `LearningProgramRepository.instance` instead of overriding `learningProgramRepositoryProvider`. findings.recommendation: Migrate test fixtures to override learningProgramRepositoryProvider via ProviderContainer overrides instead of reading the singleton directly; once the fan-out is gone, delete the singleton entirely.

findings.title: Fix Makefile check-15 cross-feature-import grep — it can structurally never detect a violation
findings.rule: Rule 2 (cross-feature deep imports) / Rule 0 checker correctness / AG-11

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'

findings.why: match($0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b) re-scans the WHOLE line (path:linenum:import-text) for the leftmost 'features/X/' substring, which is always inside the file-path field that a[1] already captured — so b[1] is always identical to a[1] and the check can never print a WARN, no matter how many real cross-feature deep imports exist. I reproduced the exact pipeline against a real offending line and confirmed a[1]=b[1]='progress' even though the import target feature is 'content_browsing'. As a direct, concrete consequence, siyumim_grouped_view.dart:10 deep-imports content_browsing's provider file instead of the (currently empty) content_browsing.dart barrel, and make audit reports check 15 as clean regardless. The correctly-written custom_lint equivalent (no_feature_cross_import, ERROR severity) would catch this, but that tool currently crashes on every run — so both enforcement layers for Rule 2 are simultaneously non-functional, for two unrelated reasons, and nobody would know new violations are accumulating.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the awk to isolate the imported feature name from the import-URI field only (not re-scan $0), add a Makefile-test fixture proving check 15 fires on a synthetic cross-feature deep import and stays silent on a same-feature one, then re-run make audit to see and triage the real (likely multi-file) backlog this uncovers across lib/features/.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture cross-feature deep import makes check 15 print a WARN; a same-feature deep import does not.

findings.title: Stop keying GoalEntity.firestoreId on mutable targetPercent — every goal-percent edit orphans a Firestore document instead of updating it
findings.rule: Evans invariant (aggregate identity must be stable across normal mutation); adjacent to the FB family's stable-natural-key principle

evidence.quote: test('two goals with different createdAt have different firestoreIds', () {

findings.why: firestoreId = curriculumId + '_' + targetPercent.toStringAsFixed(1) + '_' + createdAt.millisecondsSinceEpoch. updateGoal preserves createdAt but allows targetPercent to change, so any 'adjust my goal target %' edit (a routine, expected user action) computes a DIFFERENT firestoreId and _syncGoal pushes a brand-new Firestore document instead of updating the original — the original document is never touched again and deleteGoal only ever removes the CURRENT firestoreId's doc, so the old one is orphaned forever. GoalMerger happens to key its LWW arbitration by track_id rather than firestoreId, so the local state pulled on other devices generally self-heals to the latest edit — but Firestore itself accumulates one permanent garbage document per percent-edit for the life of the account, silently inflating every future full pull of that profile's goals collection. The test suite tests firestoreId's format exhaustively (contains curriculumId / contains targetPercent / contains createdAt, in TWO separate near-duplicate files) and even exercises the exact repro (create at 50.0, update to 75.0) but never asserts the one invariant that matters: the id must stay the same across that edit.
findings.recommendation: Derive firestoreId only from fields that cannot change through updateGoal (drop targetPercent from the id, or key on the DB row id / trackId+curriculumId+createdAt) so an update always resolves to the same document.
acceptance_criteria: GoalEntity.firestoreId no longer includes targetPercent (or any other field updateGoal can change).
New regression test: create a goal, call updateGoal changing only targetPercent, and assert the pushed sync payload's id/firestoreId is identical to the create call's.

findings.title: Add a profileId ownership check to GoalRepositoryImpl.updateGoal/deleteGoal and unify its profileId source
findings.rule: profileId-in-PK / multi-profile isolation invariant (repository as last line of defense); naming/placement (single source of truth)
findings.why: getGoals() filters by the constructor-injected _profileId field, but createGoal takes its own explicit profileId parameter that is never cross-checked against _profileId — the interface lets a caller create a goal 'for' a different profile than the repository instance represents, which would then be invisible to that same instance's getGoals(). Independently, updateGoal and deleteGoal load the existing row by bare goalId and mutate/delete it with no ownership check at all — updateGoal even copies existing.profileId straight back into the write (line-133, not separately confirmed) without ever comparing it to _profileId. None of this is proven to be hit by today's UI (all current call sites happen to pass matching profileIds), but the repository adds zero defense-in-depth on top of the DAO layer (which itself does not scope goalDao.updateGoal/deleteGoal/getGoalById by profile) — the next screen or bug that supplies a mismatched id/profileId pair silently edits or deletes another profile's goal.
findings.recommendation: Pick one source of truth for 'which profile owns this repository instance' and have updateGoal/deleteGoal verify existing.profileId against it before mutating, throwing a typed error on mismatch.
acceptance_criteria: createGoal derives profileId from the same single source as the rest of the class (drop the redundant parameter or validate it against _profileId).
updateGoal and deleteGoal verify existing.profileId == _profileId before mutating/deleting, throwing a typed error otherwise.

match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print

findings.title: Resolve the ambiguous stageId/stageOrder dual-interpretation in SchedulerCompletionRepositoryImpl.resolveStageOrder
findings.rule: Evans lens — a single field pattern-matched against two overlapping ID spaces with no way to tell them apart

evidence.quote:
final stageOrderMap = {for (final s in stages) s.id: s.stageOrder};
    final knownStageOrders = {for (final s in stages) s.stageOrder};

findings.why: The comment says newer completion rows store a stage's stageOrder in c.stageId while older rows store the stage's DB id; resolveStageOrder tries to guess which format a given row used by checking 'does rawStageId match some CURRENT stage's stageOrder' first. Stage id (a table-wide autoincrement) and stageOrder (a small 1..N per-curriculum ordinal) share the same small-integer space, especially for the first curriculum/stages ever created in a fresh install or test DB (id and stageOrder can be identical by coincidence, e.g. 1,2,3). When they collide, an OLD-format row that really means 'stage id 3' gets misread as 'stageOrder 3' and silently resolves to the wrong stage — which would misreport a chazara/review stage as complete (or vice versa) with no error. I have not constructed a concrete seed scenario proving the collision fires against real data (id values grow globally across curricula, so the window narrows over an install's lifetime), so this is reported as SUSPECTED, not CONFIRMED — a runtime/unit test seeding a stage whose id equals a different stage's stageOrder plus an old-format completion would confirm or rule it out.
findings.recommendation: Give completion rows an explicit format marker (or normalize all stored stageId values to stageOrder in a one-time migration) instead of guessing per-row from an ambiguous value.
acceptance_criteria: A targeted unit test seeds two stages where one stage's DB id equals another (or the same) stage's stageOrder, adds an old-format completion using the id, and asserts resolveStageOrder resolves to the correct stage rather than the coincidentally-matching one.
If the test confirms a collision, resolveStageOrder no longer disambiguates by value coincidence (explicit format tag, or a completed one-time backfill removes the dual-format need).

findings.title: Guard ref.mounted after await in SacredLocationNotifier/InIsraelNotifier mutator methods
findings.why: detect() awaits a GPS fix with a 15-second timeout then unconditionally writes state/invalidates ref on success; setManualCity, setManualCoords and InIsraelNotifier.setInIsrael likewise touch state/ref after an await with no ref.mounted check. This file's own _load() methods DO guard (comment: 'an account switch rebuilds it. Never write state on a disposed notifier'), and the paired test file carries a regression test titled 'was a race' proving the team already hit a real race in this exact provider once. If the notifier is disposed while one of these four unguarded methods is mid-await (profile/account switch during a slow GPS fetch is the obvious trigger), Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException, which nothing in the call chain catches (the caller's try/finally in sacred_time_settings_card.dart has no catch clause).

findings.title: Fix vacuous cross-feature deep-import check (Makefile check 15) and route Sacred Time's cross-feature imports through a real barrel

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'

findings.why: check 15's awk does `match($0, ...)` against the WHOLE grep line (file:line:content); since the file path always starts with the importing file's own 'features/<x>/' prefix, that regex always matches the file's OWN feature name first, so a[1] (from the file path) and b[1] (also latched onto the same leading path) are always equal and the print condition never fires. I ran the exact pipeline against the current tree and confirmed 0 output despite real violations. sacred_time.dart is the feature's designated barrel but exports nothing (7 lines, no export statement) and nobody imports it; meanwhile 6 files — 1 in this batch, 5 across settings/onboarding/notifications — deep-import sacred_time internals directly (one reaches into sacred_time's data/services/ layer). coding-standards.md's current Rule 2 text also says the barrel must be named providers.dart, but no feature in the repo, including sacred_time, has ever adopted that filename — every barrel and the checker itself still use the pre-revision <feature>.dart convention, so doc and code disagree about what's even being enforced. Net effect: the one guardrail meant to bound this feature's blast radius is silently non-functional, and where it would apply is already routinely bypassed — a future sacred_time internal refactor breaks 6 unrelated files with zero warning today.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to isolate the import target (e.g. split on the quote character or operate on a field after the import keyword) before comparing feature names; then either populate sacred_time.dart's exports and migrate the 6 call sites to import through it, or accept <feature>.dart as the real convention and correct coding-standards.md's Rule 2 text to match.
acceptance_criteria: make audit check 15 flags a deliberately cross-feature-deep-import test fixture (regression-proves the awk fix)
coding-standards.md Rule 2 names the barrel filename that actually exists in the repo
sacred_time.dart either exports its public surface and is used by the 6 identified external call sites, or is removed if the feature intentionally has no barrel yet

findings.title: Narrow LocationService's `on Object catch` clauses so programming errors aren't swallowed
findings.why: `on Object` catches everything Dart can throw, including Error subtypes (TypeError, NoSuchMethodError, StateError, ...) that only_throw_errors-compliant code elsewhere in the app throws for genuine programming bugs. A plugin-level type mismatch or null-safety violation inside geolocator/geocoding would silently become 'location fetch failed' (or a silently-null country code) forever, with no crash report and no log line — exactly the bug-masking EH-4 exists to prevent.

findings.title: Fix ZmanimWindowService polar-fallback candle-lighting/tzais to use the target location's time, not the device's
findings.why: DateTime(y, m, d, 17) (no .utc) constructs a device-local wall-clock time; .toUtc() then converts using the DEVICE's current timezone offset, not the offset of latitude/longitude — an arbitrary location the user picked, which the feature explicitly lets differ from the device's own timezone (manual city/coords). The doc comment above promises 'a wide local-time window' at the target, but the fallback is local to whichever timezone the device (or test runner) happens to be in. It only fires at extreme (polar) latitudes when getCandleLighting()/getTzais() return null, and zmanim_window_service_test.dart has no test forcing that branch, so it has never been exercised.
findings.recommendation: Compute the fallback from a fixed offset derived from longitude (or explicitly switch to UTC and correct the 'local-time' claim in the comment) instead of relying on DateTime's device-local constructor.

findings.title: Scope DataExportImportService.importData()'s 16 bare table deletes to the imported profile, not every profile on the device

evidence.quote:
/// Per-profile import: deletes all existing rows and re-inserts from the
  /// export payload. Does not hard-delete accounts not present in the export

findings.why: Every delete in importData() (lines 517-532, one per user-data table) calls Drift's `delete(table).go()` with no `.where()` clause, which executes an unconditional DELETE FROM on that table. On a device with more than one local account or learner profile (the app's own account-switcher/registry and sibling-profile model), importing ONE profile's exported JSON silently erases every OTHER profile's/account's rows in all 16 tables first -- directly contradicting the method's own doc comment. The multi-account round-trip test (epic_26_story_23_data_export_round_trip_test.dart) can't catch this because it manually wipes the ENTIRE database before calling importData(), so a scoped delete and this unscoped one are indistinguishable to that test. DataExportImportService has zero production callers today (grepped repo-wide across lib/), so no user is exposed yet, but it is fully implemented and covered by ~900 lines of tests across 8 test files -- clear signal a 'restore backup' UI hookup is imminent, at which point the first restore on a multi-child/multi-account device would silently erase a sibling's entire Torah-study history.
findings.recommendation: Thread profileId/accountId into importData() and scope every delete with `..where((tbl) => tbl.profileId.equals(profileId))` (account-level equivalent for accounts/learnerProfiles); extend the round-trip test to seed two profiles and import only one.
acceptance_criteria: New/updated test seeds profile A and profile B, exports+imports only A, and asserts profile B's rows in all 16 tables are byte-for-byte unchanged (not just non-empty).

Every _database.delete(...) call in importData() carries a matching .where(...) scoping clause -- checkable by a Rule-0 grep asserting no bare `delete(_database.` call lacks a following `..where(` in this file.

evidence.quote: for (final u in data['userProfiles'] as List) {

findings.why: Every one of the 16 imported tables is inserted row-by-row with an individual `await ...insert(...)` inside a for loop instead of Drift's batch()/insertAll for same-shape bulk writes (lines 538-901). The whole thing is correctly wrapped in one _database.transaction() (DB-2 satisfied), but each row still pays its own round-trip; a family with several years of daily completions (thousands of completionEvents/learningLedger rows) multiplies import wall-clock time by roughly the row count instead of running as a handful of batched statements. findings.recommendation: Replace each per-table loop with _database.batch((b) => b.insertAll(_database.<table>, rows)) inside the existing transaction.
acceptance_criteria: Import of a large fixture (1,000+ completionEvents) uses batch()/insertAll, verifiable by code review confirming no remaining bare `for` + `await ...insert(` loop in importData(), or by an insert-call-count assertion in a test.

findings.area: features/account domain service, tested from this batch's settings test tree

evidence.quote: // Log but don't rethrow — auth deletion + local cleanup still proceed.

findings.why: The comment claims 'Log but don't rethrow' but there is no AppLogger call anywhere in the catch body -- it is functionally empty. The Makefile's 'no empty catch blocks' grep (check 9/15) only matches a literal single-line `catch(...) {}`, so this multi-line, commented-but-logless catch is invisible to that checker (EH-3's 'log-less' half is explicitly Pending, not enforced). If the deleteAccountData Cloud Function fails during account deletion -- network error, quota, not-yet-deployed, permission-denied -- nothing is recorded anywhere (no Crashlytics, no Talker/AppLogger), so there is zero telemetry on failures of the primary Firestore-deletion path for a 'delete my account and my data' request. Verified account_management_service_test.dart has no test that stubs this call to throw and asserts on logging. The onUserDeleted Cloud Function trigger is a documented safety net that reduces the risk of the data actually surviving, but it does not restore visibility into how often the primary path fails.
findings.recommendation: Add an AppLogger.error(...) call (uid only, no other PII) inside the catch block; add a test that stubs a throwing httpsCallable and asserts the log call fired.
acceptance_criteria: Catch block calls AppLogger.error with the uid and exception.

findings.title: Fix docs/sync-conflict-resolution.md's LWW tie-break rule — it contradicts the implemented and tested behavior
findings.rule: AG-8 (doc/code parity); FB-2/FB-3 (LWW ordering, clock-skew handling)

evidence.quote:
> strictly newer timestamp wins. If both timestamps are equal the remote row
> is silently dropped (the LWW rule is `remoteTimestamp > localTimestamp`).

// The one true tie (equal `updated_at`, no decisive server timestamp) is
    // resolved by preferring remote so two devices that wrote the same value
test('exactly identical timestamps, no synced_at → remote wins', () {

findings.why: The canonical doc says ties are dropped in favor of local (strict `remoteTimestamp > localTimestamp`) and never mentions a clock-skew window. The actual implementation and its exhaustive, intentional test coverage do the opposite for the common case: outside a ±5s skew window ties do stay local, but *inside* the window — the realistic case for near-simultaneous writes from a user's own two devices — an exact tie goes to REMOTE (code comment: 'prefer remote... converge instead of bouncing'), and a `synced_at` server-timestamp tie-break exists that the doc never describes at all. An engineer implementing a new merger or debugging a 'my edit got overwritten' report will read the doc, get the tie-break backwards for the realistic case, and either mis-implement a new merger or chase a phantom bug.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the 'Push/pull invariant' section to describe the actual 3-tier rule in DriftMergeStore.remoteIsNewer: (1) outside ±5s skew, strict remote>local wins and ties stay local; (2) inside ±5s skew with both sides carrying synced_at, the server timestamp decides; (3) inside the window with no decisive synced_at, remote wins to force convergence. Point the doc at drift_merge_store.dart:113-152 so future changes are easy to diff against it.
acceptance_criteria: docs/sync-conflict-resolution.md's tie-break wording matches lib/core/sync/merge/drift_merge_store.dart:113-152 exactly, confirmed by re-reading both side by side

findings.title: Sync push payloads embed client-clock timestamps as the cross-device LWW ordering field instead of FieldValue.serverTimestamp()

evidence.quote:
the device with the
strictly newer timestamp wins.
// remote document carries a valid LWW timestamp. The merger

findings.why: docs/sync-conflict-resolution.md's own Push/pull invariant says the device with the 'strictly newer timestamp' wins LWW races. Every updated_at value this batch's push payloads carry comes from `_clock.nowUtc()` (LocalDayClock, ultimately the device's own system clock) or a Drift-stored value stamped by the device clock at write time -- never FieldValue.serverTimestamp(). coding-standards.md's own FB-2 rationale names the exact failure: 'two devices with skewed clocks writing client timestamps make last-write-wins non-deterministic -- the faster clock always wins and silently overwrites newer data.' A device with a wrong/stuck system clock (common on hand-me-down or long-offline tablets, which this family-learning app explicitly supports offline) will have every goals/curriculum_tracks/settings/gamification_settings push either always lose or always win LWW races regardless of actual edit recency, silently discarding another device's real edits with no error surfaced anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Route the LWW ordering field for mutable-document pushes through FieldValue.serverTimestamp() at the Firestore-gateway layer (the codebase already does this correctly for the separate synced_at field in firestore_gateway_impl.dart), keeping the client timestamp only as a local optimistic-ordering hint per FB-2's own wording. The fix site is core/sync/ (gateway + merge layer), outside this batch; these two files are the clearest evidence, not the fix location.
acceptance_criteria: FB-2 Rule-0 checker per coding-standards.md: audit grep asserting no DateTime.now()-derived value feeds a sync codec's ordering field, plus an emulator test asserting the persisted ordering field is a server Timestamp.
Extend test/integration/two_device_sync_test.dart (or add a sibling test) with a case that sets one device's local clock backward and asserts its genuinely later edit still wins the LWW race.

findings.title: outboxSyncWriteFacadeProvider mutates DAO state and fires a network re-enqueue from inside its Provider build function
findings.why: The code directly inside `Provider<OutboxSyncWriteFacade?>((ref) {...})` mutates pointsBalanceDao.syncSink and unawaited-fires reEnqueueUnsyncedLedgerRows(profileId) unconditionally on every build. This provider watches authStateProvider, activeTutoredProfileSelectionProvider, userDatabaseProvider, activeProfileIdProvider, and localDayClockProvider -- any of which changing (e.g. every profile switch in this multi-child app) reruns build and refires the recovery scan, which its own D14 comment says is meant to run once. SM-2 exists precisely because 'side effects in build race and get skipped or duplicated on rebuild' -- here they duplicate on every rebuild instead of running once.
findings.recommendation: Move syncSink wiring and the one-time ledger-recovery call out of build into a ref.listen/onDispose pairing or an explicit one-shot recovery triggered on cloud-conversion, leaving build to only construct and return the facade.
acceptance_criteria: riverpod_lint/custom_lint rule flagging DAO field mutation or unawaited async calls directly inside a Provider build body (SM-2 Enforce backstop).

findings.title: onEnqueueDrain closures in sync_providers.dart read ref after an await with no ref.mounted guard
findings.why: Both onEnqueueDrain closures (in syncWriteFacadeProvider and outboxSyncWriteFacadeProvider) do a ref.read after an await with no ref.mounted check, violating SM-4. Riverpod 3 throws UnmountedRefException if ref is used after its provider has rebuilt. Both providers watch activeProfileIdProvider/authStateProvider, which change on every profile switch or sign-out -- realistic during the network round-trip a drain takes. If that happens between the two awaits, the second ref.read(syncOrchestratorProvider)?.recordDrainAttempt() throws on a stale ref. The surrounding comment (sync_providers.dart:100-104) spells out the user-visible cost of skipping recordDrainAttempt: 'the badge stays at its old value (e.g. a stale Synced) ... a false-Synced when the push failed.' Because this closure runs inside unawaited(tee().catchError((Object _) {})) in outbox_sync_write_facade.dart, the resulting exception is silently swallowed (see the companion EH-3 finding), so this failure currently has zero observability.
findings.recommendation: Check ref.mounted after the first await in both closures before the second ref.read call, per SM-4; extract the duplicated closure body into one shared helper to fix both sites at once.
acceptance_criteria: custom_lint/riverpod_lint rule flagging ref use after an await without a mounted check (SM-4 Enforce backstop).
Provider test that rebuilds/switches the active profile mid-drain and asserts no UnmountedRefException reaches the caller and recordDrainAttempt either completes or is safely skipped.

findings.title: OutboxSyncWriteFacade._enqueue swallows every drain-tee failure with no log and no AppLogger field in the class
findings.why: OutboxSyncWriteFacade never declares an AppLogger field, so this catchError has no way to log even if it wanted to. Any exception from the drain tee -- including the UnmountedRefException from the companion SM-4 finding, or a genuine permission-denied/network failure -- is discarded with zero trace. Every push*/enqueue* method in this class, used for every sync write in the app, funnels through this one _enqueue, making it the single choke point where all fire-and-forget drain failures currently vanish silently. No test in this batch (including the 1184-line local_data_upload_service_test.dart, which never wires onEnqueueDrain) exercises this path either.
findings.recommendation: Inject an AppLogger into OutboxSyncWriteFacade (mirroring LocalDataUploadService's existing nullable _logger field) and log the swallowed exception at warn/error level inside catchError before discarding it.
acceptance_criteria: EH-3 Rule-0 checker (log-less catch grep) reports no hits in outbox_sync_write_facade.dart.

findings.title: LocalDataUploadService.pushAllLocalData enqueues every entity kind via a per-row awaited loop instead of a batched outbox write
findings.why: pushAllLocalData is explicitly a one-time bulk operation ('Called once after a local-born account is upgraded to cloud... so the user's offline learning history is immediately available') yet writes to the single Drift outbox table one row at a time across 7 loops, each await-ing OutboxSyncWriteFacade._enqueue -> OutboxDao.insertOutboxRow individually. Per outbox_sync_write_facade.dart:289-292, each insert also fires its own unawaited network drain-kick. A learner with a full year of history could have hundreds of completions/streak events/ledger entries; the one-time account-conversion flow does hundreds of sequential single-row DB writes plus hundreds of concurrent drain-kick Futures where a handful of batch inserts would do, extending how long this migration keeps the DB busy and widening the exposure window for the SM-4 race described in the companion finding.
findings.recommendation: Batch each entity kind's outbox rows via db.batch()/insertAll (build the list of OutboxCompanions first, one transaction per kind) instead of looping individually-awaited _enqueue calls; fire at most one drain-kick per pushAllLocalData call rather than one per row.
acceptance_criteria: DB-3 Rule-0 checker (audit grep for awaited per-row insert loops against the same table) reports zero hits in local_data_upload_service.dart.

findings.title: SyncStatus.error and RestoreStatus.error carry a free-text message instead of a stable code, inviting raw/untranslated text downstream
findings.why: EH-5 requires domain/data errors to carry stable codes/enums, never pre-formatted human messages, because this is an EN+Hebrew app where presentation must resolve text via AppLocalizations. findings.title: Repositories/services constructed inline instead of injected via a provider at three sync-path call sites
findings.why: SM-7 requires repositories/services/DAOs to be constructed only inside their @riverpod provider or a test override, so they stay swappable in tests without also having to fake the DB the constructor pulls in. All three sites construct a repository/service directly inside a plain method body, given only the already-available UserDatabase. A unit test of pushAllLocalData, buildGamificationSnapshot, or the reward-merge delegate cannot substitute a fake ParentAnalyticsRepositoryImpl/RewardMilestoneService without also faking the whole Drift database those classes read. findings.title: Set driftRuntimeOptions.dontWarnAboutMultipleDatabases in two_device_sync_test.dart's setUp, matching every other multi-device test
findings.why: Empirically reproduced by running `flutter test` on this batch: every test in this file prints Drift's 'created the database class UserDatabase multiple times... race conditions will occur and might corrupt the database' warning plus a full stack trace, because setUp creates deviceA and deviceB (two UserDatabase instances) without setting driftRuntimeOptions.dontWarnAboutMultipleDatabases. The warning is a false positive here (deviceA/deviceB use separate NativeDatabase.memory() instances, not a shared QueryExecutor), and the project already has an established, 20-file-strong convention of setting this flag for exactly this pattern — including its own sibling, test/integration/two_device_sync_test.dart:113. This file is the one multi-database test in the codebase (found via grep) that skips it, so it pollutes every CI run with a scary-looking but inapplicable corruption warning that could bury a real one.
findings.recommendation: Add `driftRuntimeOptions.dontWarnAboutMultipleDatabases = true;` to this file's setUp, matching test/integration/two_device_sync_test.dart:113.

findings.title: Rewrite TrackLearningOrderScreen 'race-safety' test to actually verify the _sedarimSaveSeq guard
findings.rule: TQ-8 (regression test weaker than what the source can do wrong) / Feathers seam lens
findings.why: Test '20. rapid successive reorders only persist the final order (seq guard)' claims to pin the _sedarimSaveSeq race guard, but its only assertions are that saveSedarimOrder was called twice and that some DraggableOrderItem still renders. Both saves are dispatched regardless of the guard (the guard only gates the *post-await* provider-invalidate/setState in _persistSedarim), so deleting the 'mySeq != _sedarimSaveSeq' checks entirely would not change either assertion's outcome — the test cannot fail if the guard regresses. Contrast with track_learning_order_reset_test.dart in the same batch, which correctly uses controlled Completers to prove which read 'wins'; that pattern is available and not applied here, so a future refactor could silently reintroduce the stale-continuation race (flicker/revert of the reordered list) with CI green.
findings.recommendation: Give the mocked repo.saveSedarimOrder two distinguishable outcomes (e.g. via Completers, as done in track_learning_order_reset_test.dart) so the first (slow) save's post-await continuation would visibly corrupt state if it ran; assert that only the second reorder's masechtos invalidation/refetch is reflected in the rendered order, and that the test fails when the mySeq guard is removed.
