findings.title: Close every inMemoryDb() Drift database opened by tracks/setup and track_order widget tests
findings.rule: TQ-6 (hermetic tests / no shared/leaked state) — violates drift_memory.dart's own documented contract

evidence.quote:
/// Callers MUST `await db.close()` in `tearDown` to free the native
/// resources.

findings.why: drift_memory.dart's own doc comment says callers MUST close every inMemoryDb() in tearDown to free native FFI/sqlite3 resources. step_starting_position_l1_test.dart creates 6 in-memory DBs (lines 222, 234, 251, 1017, 1075, 1127) and closes none. track_management_body_and_order_l1_test.dart creates 8 and closes only 3 (the other 5 — lines 158, 204, 304, 461, 929 — leak once per test invocation that hits them, i.e. ~13+ leaked native handles across that file's test run). track_management_hub_screen_l1_test.dart's shared default at line 120 leaks once per test that doesn't pass an explicit db (~10 tests). track_learning_order_reset_test.dart's single DB is never closed. Across a full CI run this accumulates open native sqlite3 handles per test file, risking slow teardown/fd pressure and contradicts the helper's explicit contract.
findings.recommendation: Add `addTearDown(() => database.close())` (or an explicit `await db.close()`) immediately after every inMemoryDb() call site listed, including the shared `db ?? inMemoryDb()` defaults in _buildBodyApp/_buildApp/_buildStartingPositionApp-style helpers.

findings.title: Fix learning_tracker/Makefile check 15/15 cross-feature-import awk — it can never detect a violation
findings.rule: Rule 0 (checker must actually fail) / Rule 2 (no cross-feature deep imports)

evidence.quote: awk -F: '{match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print}'

findings.why: grep -n emits 'path:line:content', so the file's own path (which always contains 'features/<owning-feature>/') appears in $0 BEFORE the import statement text. awk's match($0, /features\/([^/]+)\//, b) returns the FIRST match in the line — the file's own feature — not the imported feature, so b[1] always equals a[1] (both extracted from the same file-path segment) and the `a[1] != b[1]` guard can never be true. Reproduced directly: running the exact pipeline against lib/features/ yields 0 hits, and the committed baseline (docs/audits/standards-audit-2026-07-03/_work/baseline/make-audit.txt) shows check 15/15 printing no WARN block at all — a silent, false PASS. My batch alone contains ~50 real deep cross-feature import lines (dashboard/, scheduler/, sync/, onboarding/, content_browsing/, profiles/, settings/ providers imported directly instead of via a feature barrel) that this check should be listing as warn-only violations and never does.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to extract the imported feature name from the import token specifically (e.g. `grep -oP "features/[^/]+/" <<<"$import_part"` after splitting off the file:line prefix), verify it now emits the WARN list, then use it to start triaging the real cross-feature-import backlog per Rule 2.
acceptance_criteria: A synthetic fixture file importing a different feature's deep path makes `make audit` check 15/15 print a WARN/file:line for it
Running the fixed check against current lib/features/tracks/setup/** surfaces its real deep cross-feature imports instead of zero

findings.title: Fix the awk field-split bug in `make audit` check 15/15 that makes cross-feature-import detection a permanent no-op

evidence.quote: match($$1, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, a); match($$0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//, b); if(a[1] != b[1]) print

findings.why: Check 15/15's awk splits each `grep -rn` hit on ':' and calls match($1,...) for the file's own feature and match($0,...) for the import's feature, expecting them to differ on a real violation. But $0 is the whole line, and `grep -rn` always prints `path:line:content` first — since the file path itself contains 'features/<name>/', match($0, /features\/([^\/]+)\//) finds that occurrence (the file's OWN feature) before ever reaching the import text, so a[1] and b[1] are always equal and `if(a[1] != b[1])` never fires. Reproduced by hand: piping step_chazara.dart's onboarding import through the exact command yields a1=tracks b1=tracks. The captured baseline (docs/audits/standards-audit-2026-07-03/_work/baseline/make-audit.txt) confirms this: check 14/15 (core→features, different/working logic) lists 32 edges, check 15/15 prints nothing at all. A hand grep across just this 30-file batch turns up 25 real cross-feature deep imports across 13 files (onboarding, scheduler, settings, content_browsing, profiles, sync, progress, dashboard) — none of which the 'audit PASSED' result reflects.
findings.recommendation: Fix the awk to derive the file's own feature from a fixed prefix match on $1 only, and the import's feature from the substring AFTER the 'package:learning_tracker/features/' marker in the import text specifically (not the first 'features/' in the whole line) — e.g. split on the import URI, not on ':'. Then run it for real, triage the resulting list the same way the 32 known core→features edges were baselined, and decide per-edge whether to introduce features/<Y>/providers.dart barrels or accept/document the exception.
acceptance_criteria: `make audit` check 15/15, run against the current tree, prints at least the 25 known violations found in this batch (not zero).
A regression fixture (a deliberately-added cross-feature deep import in a scratch file) causes check 15/15 to fail non-zero, then passes again once removed.

findings.title: Surface reorder/reset save failures to the user in the learning-order screens instead of silently swallowing them
findings.rule: EH-2 (no raw exception reaches presentation without becoming a value) + Nygard I/O-failure-halfway lens
findings.why: None of these 5 call paths (2 persist + 1 reset in track_learning_order_screen.dart; 1 reorder + 1 reset in learning_order_screen.dart) has a try/catch or .catchError. The UI has already applied the optimistic reorder to local widget state before the write lands, so if saveSedarimOrder/saveMasechtosOrder/saveOrder/resetToDefault throws (DB busy, disk full, offline outbox push failure) the screen keeps showing the new order as saved with zero error affordance and no rollback — the user believes it persisted; it silently didn't, and it reverts on next app load. Sibling screens in the same feature (edit_track_screen.dart, add_track_flow_screen.dart, track_management_hub_screen.dart) all wrap the equivalent save call in try/catch + ScaffoldMessenger SnackBar; this pair is the outlier.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each persist/reset call in try/catch (or move the mutation into a proper AsyncNotifier using AsyncValue.guard), show a SnackBar/retry matching the add_track_flow_screen.dart pattern, and revert _local*/_localOrder to the pre-optimistic value on failure.
acceptance_criteria: Widget test: stub the repository/use-case to throw on saveSedarimOrder/saveMasechtosOrder/saveOrder/resetToDefault and assert a visible error affordance appears and local state reverts
No unawaited(...persist...) or bare .then(...) without an adjacent catch remains in these two files

findings.title: Stop LearningOrderRepositoryImpl.getOrder from writing to the DB as a side effect of a FutureProvider build call
findings.rule: SM-2 (provider build is pure — no writes/side effects)
findings.why: getOrder is invoked directly from learningOrderProvider's FutureProvider.family build callback, yet it performs a DB write (_stampReorderAt) whenever the stored learningOrderVersion is stale — and nothing else ever updates learningOrderVersion except an explicit user reorder/reset. So on every cold start or provider invalidation while the version mismatch persists, merely reading the curriculum's order silently re-stamps lastReorderAt = now, which is exactly the reorder-amnesty trigger — overdue-item detection for that curriculum stays silently suppressed after any content reseed until the user happens to manually reorder or reset, defeating a named product invariant via a function that looks like a pure read.
findings.recommendation: Move the version-mismatch re-amnesty write out of getOrder into an explicit, one-shot repair step (run once at app start or as part of the content-reseed pipeline) so provider build stays a pure read.
acceptance_criteria: Test: call getOrder() twice in a row with a stale learningOrderVersion and assert lastReorderAt is stamped at most once, not on every call

findings.title: Wrap saveOrder/resetToDefault's reorder-amnesty stamp in the same transaction as the order write
findings.rule: DB-2 (>1 write = one transaction()) + Nygard partial-failure lens
findings.why: _stampReorderAt does its own read+write OUTSIDE the transaction that persists the order change, in both saveOrder and resetToDefault. A process death or DB error between the two calls leaves the new order committed but the overdue-amnesty stamp missing (or the delete committed but the stamp missing on resetToDefault) — the code's own comment about wrapping upserts 'so a mid-loop crash cannot leave a half-shuffled state' shows the author cared about exactly this class of bug but didn't extend it to the second write.

findings.title: Inject FakeLocalDayClock into TrackCreationService's B3 back-date tests instead of reading the wall clock

evidence.quote: expect(daysBack, 5, reason: 'offset:5 must be exactly 5 days in the past');

findings.why: Neither B3 test overrides LocalDayClock, so DateTimeFactory.nowUtc() reads the real system clock both for the test's 'before' and again inside the SUT's _parseProgramStartingRef moments later. Duration.inDays truncates: (Duration(days:5) - Duration(microseconds:1)).inDays == 4, verified directly in this Dart VM; an empirical 200k-iteration back-to-back DateTime.now() sample in this same environment showed roughly 4% of pairs returning a non-zero gap (up to 70us), meaning daysBack can legitimately compute to 4 instead of 5 and fail expect(daysBack, 5, ...) for reasons unrelated to any real regression. This is exactly the flakiness class LocalDayClock/FakeLocalDayClock exists to eliminate, and the sibling provision_track_use_case_test.dart correctly uses FakeLocalDayClock for the equivalent B3 assertions — this file is the outlier.
findings.recommendation: Thread a FakeLocalDayClock(seed) into TrackCreationService/_parseProgramStartingRef so the test's 'before' and the SUT's 'now' are the identical fixed instant, making daysBack deterministic.

It slipped past `make audit` because check 15's awk comparison is a no-op: match($0,...) scans the whole grep line (file-path:linenum:content), so it always matches the FIRST 'features/X/' occurrence, which is in the file-path prefix — identical to match($1,...) — making a[1] and b[1] always equal regardless of what is actually imported. Verified empirically: piping all 1186 non-barrel deep-import candidate lines in lib/features/ through the exact Makefile command yields 0 matches. `make audit` reports 'PASSED — all 22 greps clean' for a check that structurally cannot ever fail, so any current or future cross-feature deep import (this one included) ships silently.
findings.recommendation: Swap the import in tutor_pin_reset_screen.dart to package:learning_tracker/features/account/account.dart. Separately, fix the check-15 awk logic to compare the source file's feature name against the TARGET import's feature name specifically (e.g. match on the import statement field, not $0), then re-run against this known-bad line as a regression fixture to confirm it now fails.

findings.title: Catch and log exceptions around TutorPinService calls in the PIN entry/setup async handlers
findings.why: _onPinComplete (gate) and _onConfirmPinEntered (setup) wrap their await in try/finally with no catch clause. TutorPinService.verifyTutorPin/setTutorPin only converts PinLockoutException — an underlying secure-storage failure (a real class of Android keystore/PlatformException issue this environment has hit before per the App Check debug-token flakiness on wipes) propagates as a raw, uncaught exception. Because _onPinComplete is invoked fire-and-forget (not awaited) from _appendDigit, the failure is swallowed by whatever global handler exists, with zero AppLogger call from this site and zero user feedback: _isVerifying resets to false in the finally block but _errorMessage stays null and _digits stays at 4 filled dots, leaving the user staring at a stalled numpad with no explanation and no way to retype until they notice backspace still works.
findings.recommendation: Add a typed catch around the await that logs via AppLogger and sets a generic, localized _errorMessage (consistent with EH-2's 'no raw exception reaches presentation').

findings.title: Type and log the catch block in TutorPinResetScreen._sendResetEmail
findings.why: The bare `catch (e)` has no `on X` type, so per Dart semantics it catches everything thrown — including Error subtypes (StateError, TypeError, NoSuchMethodError from a programmer bug) — and silently converts all of them into the same generic 'send failed' UI message with zero AppLogger call. A real programming defect elsewhere in the call chain would present identically to a normal network failure, with no trace to diagnose it.
findings.recommendation: Catch a specific exception type (or at least log via AppLogger.instance.error before setting the UI message) so Error subtypes are not silently masked and failures are traceable.

findings.title: Stop misreporting a failed local PIN clear as a failed reset email in TutorPinResetScreen
findings.why: sendPasswordResetEmail and clearTutorPin are two sequential awaits inside one try block with one shared catch that always sets the l10n key tutorPinResetSendFailed ('Failed to send reset email...'). If the email send succeeds but the subsequent local-PIN-clear throws (a real possibility given documented secure-storage flakiness in this environment), the user is told the email failed when it actually sent — they will retry, triggering a second real password-reset email, while the actual failure (local PIN not cleared) goes unaddressed and unreported.
findings.recommendation: Split the two operations into separate try/catch blocks (or at minimum track which step failed) so the error message and retry behavior match what actually happened.

findings.title: Check TutorGrantResult before treating revoke/resign/rescind as successful in manage_tutors_screen.dart and manage_grants_screen.dart
findings.why: All three handlers await the use case's Future<TutorGrantResult> and discard the return value, then unconditionally run the success branch (wipe local mirror, invalidate the grant list, send a lifecycle email) inside `if (mounted) { ... }`, with only a generic `catch` around thrown exceptions. FirestoreTutorGrantRepository.revokeGrant/resignGrant/rescindInvite never rethrow FirebaseFunctionsException — they always return TutorGrantFailure. So when the Cloud Function genuinely rejects the call (permission-denied, already-revoked race, offline), the UI still shows success, wipes the tutor's local mirror, and — worst case for _revoke — emails the tutor 'your access was revoked' while the grant is still active server-side, giving the parent false assurance that access was cut off. The sibling screens (invite/accept/decline) all correctly `switch` on the same result type, proving the pattern is known but was missed here.
findings.recommendation: Assign the awaited call to a `result` variable and exhaustively switch on TutorGrantSuccess/TutorGrantFailure/TutorGrantPreconditionError exactly as invite_tutor_screen.dart/accept_invite_screen.dart/decline_invite_screen.dart already do; only run the mirror-wipe/invalidate/notify side effects on Success, and surface a localized error (not e.toString()) otherwise.

findings.title: Convert TutorPermissions to @freezed instead of hand-writing ==/hashCode
findings.why: coding-standards.md is explicit: domain value objects must be `@freezed` with generated `==`/`hashCode`/`copyWith`, specifically because hand-rolled equality drifts from the field list. TutorPermissions — its own doc-comment calls it 'Immutable value object' / 'VO' — hand-writes both operators across 9 fields, plus a separately hand-written constructor, copyWith, toFirestore, and fromFirestore: 5 places a future field addition must be updated by hand. The drift risk is already visible today: `canMarkLiveCompletion` is deliberately excluded from both `==` and `hashCode` (harmless only because it is hardcoded false for every instance) — exactly the kind of silent omission @freezed generation would make structurally impossible.
findings.recommendation: Convert TutorPermissions to a @freezed class (keeping canMarkLiveCompletion as a computed getter rather than a constructor field, or a private default so it can't be set), and delete the hand-written ==/hashCode/copyWith.
acceptance_criteria: TutorPermissions.freezed.dart is generated; no hand-written operator == or hashCode remains in tutor_permissions.dart.
Existing TutorPermissions unit tests (defaults/readOnly/toFirestore round-trip) still pass unmodified.

findings.title: Handle mid-loop failure in TutoredWriteRouter.pushStageDefinitions (tutored_write_router.dart)
findings.rule: Nygard (partial I/O failure) / DB-6 offline-first parity
findings.why: pushStageDefinitions awaits one Cloud Function call per stage sequentially and _handleResult throws immediately on the first TutorWriteFailure. If a tutor edits several stages at once and the network drops partway through, the earlier stages are already committed server-side while the remaining ones are simply lost — the thrown TutorWriteException names only the failing stage, not which stages already succeeded. Unlike the normal (non-tutored) write path, tutored writes deliberately bypass the local outbox (per this file's own header comment), so there is no retry queue to pick the dropped stages back up on reconnect — the class's offline-first guarantee (DB-6, exercised everywhere else in this app) does not hold here. This is architectural/edge-case reasoning, not a reproduced runtime failure.
findings.recommendation: Either batch the per-stage calls into a single CF invocation (atomic on the server) or collect per-stage results and surface a structured partial-failure summary (which stages succeeded/failed) so the caller can retry just the failed subset instead of losing silent state.
acceptance_criteria: A test that fails the 2nd of 3 stage upserts asserts the caller learns which stages succeeded (not just a single opaque exception).
Documented decision (in tutored_write_router.dart's header) on whether partial multi-stage failure is an accepted risk or gets a retry path.

findings.title: Guard int.parse(sel.profileId) in tutored_write_router.dart
findings.rule: EH-3/EH-4 (unhandled exception type breaks the class's stated contract)
findings.why: The class doc says 'CF failures... are re-thrown as TutorWriteException so callers can surface a clear snackbar,' but int.parse(sel.profileId) is called unguarded at 10 sites before any CF call happens. If profileId is ever non-numeric (malformed TutoredProfileSelection, future ID-scheme change), a raw uncaught FormatException propagates instead of the documented TutorWriteException — no AppLogger context, and callers that specifically catch TutorWriteException per this class's contract won't catch it. No test in s1_tutored_write_router_test.dart exercises a non-numeric profileId, so this is unconfirmed in practice.
findings.recommendation: Parse once via a small helper (e.g. `_profileIdOrThrow(sel)`) that logs via AppLogger and throws a typed TutorWriteException on failure, matching the class's documented error contract; call it once instead of int.parse at each of the 10 sites.
acceptance_criteria: A test that constructs a TutoredProfileSelection with a non-numeric profileId and calls any pushX method asserts a TutorWriteException (not FormatException) is thrown and logged.

findings.title: Add ref.mounted guards after awaits in manage_tutors_providers.dart's incomingTutorGrantsProvider
findings.why: incomingTutorGrantsProvider watches `authStateProvider.select((s) => s.currentUser?.firebaseUid)` and then awaits two network/DB calls before touching `ref.read` three more times (lines 118, 124, 131). If the watched uid changes mid-flight (e.g. the tutor signs out while this fetch is in progress — the exact account-switch race this file's own comments say it must defend against), Riverpod 3 tears down this build invocation and a subsequent `ref.read` throws UnmountedRefException instead of the intended AsyncError/graceful outcome. No `ref.mounted` check guards any of the three post-await reads.
findings.recommendation: Check `if (!ref.mounted) return const <TutorGrant>[];` (or equivalent) immediately after each await before touching ref again, mirroring the SM-4 pattern used elsewhere in Notifier methods.
acceptance_criteria: A test that invalidates authStateProvider's uid while incomingTutorGrantsProvider's future is pending does not throw UnmountedRefException.

findings.title: Rewrite regression_invariants_test.dart N7 to call the production code it claims to guard

evidence.quote: group('N7: pace-goal projected finish anchors to createdAt, not now', () {

findings.why: The file header names N7 as the regression anchor for historical bug F1 (pace-goal forecast drifted because the projected-finish date was anchored to DateTime.now() instead of goal.createdAt). The N7 test never imports or calls the real fix site (_estimatedFinish in track_detail_screen.dart, or any PaceCalculator/goal service) — it re-types the exact same date-math formula twice inline and asserts the two copies agree with each other and differ from a third, also inline, now-based computation. If a future edit reverts track_detail_screen.dart:568 from `goal.createdAt.add(...)` back to `DateTimeFactory.nowLocal().add(...)`, reintroducing F1, this test keeps passing, because there is no production code in its call path to break. The file's own stated contract ('a failing test is fixed by changing production code only — never by weakening the assertion') cannot be honored by a test with no production code to fail.
findings.recommendation: Extract the date-math core of _estimatedFinish into a small `@visibleForTesting` pure function (or call it via a testable service) and have N7 import and invoke that exact symbol with a fixed goal.createdAt, asserting the result stays anchored to createdAt across two calls made with different injected 'now' values via the existing fake-clock pattern (FakeLocalDayClock, already used correctly in epic_08_gamification_test.dart).

findings.title: Delete or replace compile-time-tautological assertions across Epic 1/2 acceptance tests
findings.why: In null-safe Dart, `expect(SomeClass, isNotNull)` on a Type literal, a non-nullable getter, or a non-nullable top-level provider constant is guaranteed true by the type system before the test ever runs — the same is true for a bare `expect(true, isTrue)`. None of these 42 assertions, spread across 6 of Epic 1's 12 stories (1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7, 1.9) and 3 of Epic 2's AC blocks, can fail for any runtime reason; they only prove the referenced symbol resolves at compile time, which flutter analyze / the test file's own import block already guarantees. Story 1.3, for example, consists of exactly these two assertions and nothing else, yet the file header claims 'All 12 stories are DONE and actively tested,' and CLAUDE.md frames `make test-story-X.Y` passing as the story's acceptance gate ('always validate it before marking it done'). A regression in AuthGuard's guard logic, AppRouter's routes, SyncOrchestrator's wiring, or any of the 11 DAOs' real behavior ships green through that gate.
findings.recommendation: For each site, either delete the assertion (documenting that the import block is the only intended check) or replace it with a behavioral assertion that calls a representative method/route/guard and checks its actual return value — the pattern Stories 1.2, 1.6, 1.11, 1.12 and the rest of Epic 2 already use in the same files.
acceptance_criteria: No `expect(X, isNotNull)` remains where X's static type is non-nullable, and no standalone `expect(true, isTrue)` remains, in epic_01_foundation_test.dart / epic_02_content_test.dart
Each surviving test in the affected groups exercises at least one real method call or return value

findings.title: Inject a fake clock instead of comparing against real DateTime.now() in completion/restore timing assertions
findings.why: Both assertions pin correctness to a 5-second window measured against the real wall clock at assertion time, rather than the FakeLocalDayClock/DateTimeFactory override the codebase already provides and uses correctly elsewhere (e.g. epic_08_gamification_test.dart Story 8.2). On a slow or contended CI runner, a stall of more than 5 seconds between the write and the assertion — plausible for a cold Drift/sqlite3 open — flakes the test for a reason unrelated to the code under test.
findings.recommendation: Install a FakeLocalDayClock (or equivalent) before the write and assert equality/near-equality against the fake's fixed instant, matching the pattern already used in epic_08_gamification_test.dart Story 8.2.
acceptance_criteria: Both assertions compare against a fixed/fake clock value, not a DateTime.now()/DateTimeFactory.nowUtc() call made at assertion time

findings.title: Give ParentDashboardAggregator's streak test a fixed/injectable clock instead of mixing UTC-anchored seed data with SystemLocalDayClock's local-day read

evidence.quote:
for (var i = 4; i >= 0; i--) {
        final day = now.subtract(Duration(days: i + 1));

findings.why: The test seeds streak events using a UTC-anchored 'today' (now = DateTime.now().toUtc()), but ParentDashboardAggregator's internal StreakStateProvider is hardcoded to `SystemLocalDayClock()` in its constructor (lib/features/dashboard/domain/services/parent_dashboard_aggregator.dart:94-96) whose .today() reads the machine's LOCAL calendar day (lib/core/time/local_day_clock.dart's SystemLocalDayClock.today() calls plain DateTime.now(), not .toUtc()). compute()'s `now:` parameter is documented 'pass explicitly for testability' but is never forwarded to the streak read, so there is no override hook at all for this value. On any machine whose local UTC offset is nonzero, for the hours each day where the local calendar date and UTC calendar date disagree, the seeded 5-day run and the clock's 'today' land on different day boundaries, flipping currentStreak/maxStreak and failing the exact-match assertion `equals(5)` — a systematic, timezone-correlated failure window, not a rare race. The neighboring 'engagement metrics' test in the same group sidesteps the same hazard by using `greaterThan(0)`, an assertion too weak to catch an off-by-one day-boundary bug either way.
findings.recommendation: Add a constructor-injectable LocalDayClock to ParentDashboardAggregator (defaulting to SystemLocalDayClock) and thread it into StreakStateProvider instead of hardcoding it; then pass a FakeLocalDayClock fixed at a constant date from the test, mirroring StreakAlertService's existing streakClock: parameter already used correctly in epic_12_notifications_test.dart.

findings.title: Register onDispose when overriding userDatabaseProvider with inMemoryDb() in tracks_studydays_and_content_hierarchy_l1_test.dart

evidence.quote: /// Callers MUST `await db.close()` in `tearDown` to free the native

findings.why: The production userDatabaseProvider registers ref.onDispose(database.close) so the DB is closed when its ProviderScope is torn down; overriding the provider with a bare `(ref) => inMemoryDb()` replaces that entire body and drops the dispose registration, so none of the 4 fresh NativeDatabase.memory() instances created by this file's 27 widget tests are ever closed — a direct violation of drift_memory.dart's documented 'Callers MUST await db.close()' contract and a native-resource leak that scales with every widget test using this override pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add `ref.onDispose(db.close)` inside each override lambda (e.g. `userDatabaseProvider.overrideWith((ref) { final db = inMemoryDb(); ref.onDispose(db.close); return db; })`), or capture the db per-test and close it in the test's teardown.

findings.title: Move DB/temp-dir cleanup into addTearDown across epic_21_multi_account_test.dart so failed assertions don't leak resources
findings.rule: TQ-6 / Nygard lens (cleanup on the failure path)
findings.why: 20 of this file's ~30 tests acquire a DeviceRegistryDatabase/UserDatabase/temp Directory and release it as the very last statement of the test body instead of via addTearDown/tearDown -- the correct pattern the SAME file already uses in Stories 21.1, 21.3, and 21.4 (`tearDown(() => registry.close())` at lines 32/208/257). When an earlier expect() in one of the 20 ad-hoc tests fails, execution stops before the cleanup line runs: the temp directory and its .db file are never deleted, and the Drift database handle is never closed. On a local edit-test-rerun loop this leaks a fresh systemTemp directory on every failed run; a leaked open DB handle mid-suite risks 'database is locked'-style failures bleeding into unrelated tests later in the same run, muddying CI triage of an unrelated failure.
findings.recommendation: Replace every trailing `await registry.close()` / `await db.close()` / `await tempDir.delete(recursive: true)` with `addTearDown(() => ...)` registered immediately after the resource is created, mirroring the tearDown(() => registry.close()) pattern already used in this file's Stories 21.1/21.3/21.4 groups.
acceptance_criteria: No test body in this file calls .close()/.delete(recursive on a resource it created without a preceding addTearDown for that same resource

findings.why: Info.plist declares both `fetch` and `remote-notification` background modes, but AppDelegate.swift (6-18) implements no `application(_:performFetchWithCompletionHandler:)` or `application(_:didReceiveRemoteNotification:fetchCompletionHandler:)` override and never calls `registerForRemoteNotifications()`; pubspec.yaml has no `firebase_messaging` dependency; every reminder in NotificationGateway is scheduled locally via `zonedSchedule`. The keys were added wholesale in the initial iOS scaffold (b9d3a8b0) and never exercised. Concrete cost: Apple App Review Guideline 2.5.4 explicitly targets apps that declare background modes without a corresponding implementation (submission friction/rejection risk), and the stale declaration will mislead whoever next builds real push notifications into thinking server-side delivery already exists.
findings.recommendation: Remove the `UIBackgroundModes` key (and its two entries) from Info.plist since notification delivery is 100% local today. If server push is genuinely planned, land the capability declaration in the same change as the `firebase_messaging` dependency, the AppDelegate handler(s), and `registerForRemoteNotifications()` — not ahead of the implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Info.plist has no UIBackgroundModes key, or each remaining mode has a matching handler in AppDelegate.swift referenced by a Linear ticket.
grep -A2 'UIBackgroundModes' learning_tracker/ios/Runner/Info.plist returns nothing (or only modes with matching AppDelegate.swift handlers) — usable as a Rule-0 grep checker.

findings.title: Log the caught exception at 7 silent/overbroad catch sites across tool/ fetch-and-resolve helpers
findings.rule: EH-3 (log-less catch) / EH-4 (Error-subtype catch) — general lens applied to tool/
findings.why: None of these seven catch/except blocks log the caught error before discarding it — Dart sites return a generic error flag, Python sites `pass`/`continue`/`return None`. When a fetch or ref-resolution genuinely fails, the operator sees only an aggregate 'N errors'/'SKIP' count, never why (network error vs. malformed data vs. a real bug in the resolver itself), making failures expensive to diagnose. verify_seed_calendar.dart:202 additionally catches `Object` — broader than even `Error` — so it would also swallow a `TypeError`/`RangeError` from a bug in the tool's own JSON-parsing code and silently retry it up to 4 times before reporting the day as a generic 'live fetch failed', masking a real programming defect as a transient network blip.
findings.recommendation: Add a log line (print/stderr.writeln/sys.stderr.write) with the caught exception's message and ref/date context at each of the 7 sites before falling through to the existing error-flag return. Narrow verify_seed_calendar.dart:202's `on Object` to the specific exception types the HTTP client/JSON decoder can actually throw.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the 7 cited sites logs the caught exception before returning its existing failure value
verify_seed_calendar.dart:202 no longer catches bare Object

findings.title: Decode xz's stderr before interpolating it in seed_content_db.dart's failure message (currently prints a raw byte list)
findings.why: Process.runSync is called at line 312-317 with `stderrEncoding: null`, so ProcessResult.stderr holds raw bytes (a Uint8List), not a decoded String. String-interpolating it at line 319 invokes List.toString(), producing something like 'xz failed: [120, 122, 58, 32, ...]' instead of xz's actual human-readable stderr text — exactly when a maintainer most needs a readable error, during a failing release build.
findings.recommendation: Pass `stderrEncoding: systemEncoding` (or explicit `utf8`) to this Process.runSync call, or explicitly `utf8.decode(xzResult.stderr as List<int>)` before interpolating it into the thrown StateError.
acceptance_criteria: Triggering an xz failure (e.g. temporarily pointing dbPath at a nonexistent file, or aliasing xz unavailable) prints a human-readable message, not a numeric byte-list

findings.title: Add SR-1 changed-value-denied test to firestore_rules.test.mjs for completions/streak_events/learning_ledger/points_ledger

evidence.quote: SR-1 — Append-only collections (`completions`, `streak_events`, `learning_ledger`, `points_ledger`) deny value mutation on update: allow only idempotent identical replay.
Enforce: [Pending] deny-tests in `functions/test/firestore_rules.test.mjs`: changed-value update `assertFails`, identical replay `assertSucceeds`.
describe('streak_events — owner write, tutor read, delete denied', () => {

findings.why: Confirmed by grep: no `resource.data == request.resource.data`-style identical-replay guard exists anywhere in firestore.rules (447 lines, zero hits). Every SR-1-named collection's update branch is just `isOwner(uid)` (plus unrelated format checks on completions only) — an owner-authenticated client (a modified build, a compromised device, or a bug in the sync engine's outbox-retry logic) can silently overwrite an EXISTING completion's points, a streak event, or a ledger/points-ledger entry with any new value, and the rule accepts it as an ordinary update. firestore_rules.test.mjs is this repo's only server-side gate test for owner writes and its own header claims it 'locks the LOAD-BEARING security boundaries' — yet none of its 4 SR-1 describe blocks (completions:306, streak_events:337, learning_ledger:347, points_ledger:357) ever attempt a changed-value update and assert it fails; each only proves identical-value re-writes and tutor-writes are handled. This is exactly the risk coding-standards.md itself names for SR-1: 'a child's study record is tamperable' — and since points/streak/ledger entries feed reward_redemptions (real-world reward fulfilment), undetected mutation directly undermines the rewards economy's integrity, with zero test coverage to catch a regression today or after any future fix.
findings.recommendation: For each of completions/streak_events/learning_ledger/points_ledger, add a test that seeds a doc then attempts an owner update with a changed field value and asserts it fails; pair with a firestore.rules change adding `request.resource.data == resource.data` as an allowed alternative to full validation on update.
acceptance_criteria: firestore_rules.test.mjs adds one assertFails case per SR-1 collection where an owner updates an existing doc with a changed field value
`make test-rules` fails against today's firestore.rules and passes once firestore.rules adds an identical-replay branch for each SR-1 collection
docs/coding-standards.md SR-1 Enforce line flips from [Pending] to [Enforced] once the test lands

findings.title: Add SR-2/SR-3/SR-4/SR-5 + TQ-9 ruleCoverage pending hardening tests to firestore_rules.test.mjs

evidence.quote: SR-2 — Validate value types and cap string sizes in rules (`is timestamp`, `is number`, `s.size() <= N`), not just key sets via `hasOnly()`.
SR-3 — Every event create requires a server-bounded timestamp: present, `is timestamp`, and `<= request.time`.
SR-4 — Cap `list` queries on per-profile event collections: `allow list: if <cond> && request.query.limit <= 500`.
SR-5 — Tutor cross-user access checks state and expiry in the rule itself (`state == 'active' && expires_at > request.time`...).

findings.why: coding-standards.md (2026-07-02) lists SR-2..SR-5 and TQ-9's ruleCoverage clause as [Pending], each with an 'Enforce' line naming the exact test pattern this file should carry. None exist. (1) SR-2: the only type/size check anywhere is `points: '50'` on completions (line 318) — no oversized-string test, no wrong-type test on any other field in any of the 12 hasOnly/open-bag collections. (2) SR-3: streak_events/learning_ledger/points_ledger accept a timestamp field of any value including far-future dates with zero test coverage — the deprecated test/firestore-rules/ suite used to test exactly this for 2 of these 3 collections before the schema migration; that coverage was lost, not carried forward. (3) SR-4: the file's own Firestore import list (line 33-40) never imports `getDocs`/`query` — it is structurally impossible for any test here to issue a list/collection query, so an owner or active tutor enumerating a child's entire event history in one unbounded query is completely untested. (4) SR-5: beforeEach (line 106-122) always seeds an 'active' tutor_grants/tutor_active_access pair; no test seeds a revoked or expired grant to prove tutor access is actually cut off, so a bug in the Cloud Function that deletes tutor_active_access on revoke would go undetected. (5) TQ-9: the emulator's own `ruleCoverage` report (flags rule expressions never evaluated by any test) is never fetched or asserted anywhere in the repo (zero grep hits for 'ruleCoverage'), so dead/unreachable branches in the 447-line rules file can accumulate silently.
findings.recommendation: Track as a backlog against SR-2..SR-5 + TQ-9: each lands its named assertFails/assertSucceeds pattern in firestore_rules.test.mjs; SR-4/SR-5 additionally need firestore.rules changes (an allow-list split with a limit cap, and a state/expires_at field) since nothing in the current rule is testable yet; TQ-9's ruleCoverage check is a Makefile/ci.yml addition that curls the emulator's coverage endpoint after the suite runs.

findings.title: Add points_ledger and reward_redemptions to write_payloads.json and the PHASE D zero-denial oracle in firestore_rules.test.mjs

evidence.quote: "_comment": "Canonical per-collection write-payload fixtures derived from Dart codec encode() outputs...",

findings.why: write_payloads.json's own header calls PAYLOADS 'the single source of truth for valid doc shapes, consumed by Phase D and E,' and PHASE D's comment claims 'a legitimate owner must be able to write every whitelisted collection without a single permission-denied error... the zero-denial oracle catches it before it reaches production.' In reality the fixture enumerates 12 collections and PHASE D enumerates 15 (ending at curriculum_scopes, line 767-768) — points_ledger and reward_redemptions are absent from both, and (verified in tool/emit_fixture_payloads.dart, not in this batch) the generator's payloads map has no entry for either, confirming the omission is systematic. Neither collection has a hasOnly whitelist today so nothing is silently broken right now, but this exact rules file has independently hit the 'hasOnly whitelist drops a real field → permission-denied in production' bug three times for other collections (profile_programs.updated_at, curriculum_tracks.purged/purged_at, bookmarks.track_type — all documented in this file's own comments). Since points_ledger/reward_redemptions are the most obvious remaining candidates for a future hasOnly addition (every sibling snapshot/ledger collection already has one), the safety net built specifically to catch that failure mode has a blind spot exactly where the next occurrence is most likely.
findings.recommendation: Add points_ledger and reward_redemptions payloads to tool/emit_fixture_payloads.dart's map, regenerate write_payloads.json via `make emit-fixtures`, and add both to PHASE D's oracle list and PHASE E's round-trip table.

findings.title: Assert update (not just delete) fails in the diagnostic_logs append-only test in firestore_rules.test.mjs
findings.rule: TQ-8 (assertion weaker than what source can do wrong)

evidence.quote: test('update and delete are denied even for owner (append-only)', async () => {

findings.why: The test's name and its own inline comment both assert the author's intent to verify update-denial, but the body only calls `deleteDoc` — no `setDoc`/update attempt against the pre-seeded doc is ever made. If a future rules edit accidentally changes diagnostic_logs's `allow update: if false;` to `if isOwner(uid);` (matching most sibling collections in the same rules file, which DO allow owner update), this test stays green. diagnostic_logs holds diagnostic event data for a children's-app account; losing its append-only guarantee unnoticed is exactly the class of regression this suite exists to catch, and here it doesn't.
findings.recommendation: Add `await assertFails(setDoc(doc(owner(), `users/${OWNER}/diagnostic_logs/e1`), { msg: 'changed' }));` against the pre-seeded doc inside this test.
acceptance_criteria: The diagnostic_logs 'update and delete are denied' test asserts both an update attempt and a delete attempt fail

findings.title: Fix no_feature_cross_import's _isBarrel to match the documented providers.dart crossing point (or fix the doc)

evidence.quote: The single allowed crossing point is `features/<feature>/providers.dart`, which is the deliberate, documented public surface.

static bool _isBarrel(String importedFeature, String importedPath) {
    return importedPath == '$importedFeature.dart';

test('does not recognise providers.dart as barrel', () {
        expect(_isBarrel('tracks', 'providers.dart'), isFalse);

findings.why: docs/coding-standards.md Rule 2 and this package's own README both tell developers/agents the only sanctioned cross-feature import is `features/<feature>/providers.dart`. No such file exists anywhere in the repo (grep confirms zero `providers.dart` under lib/features/); the real, consistently-used barrel across all 15 features is `features/<feature>/<feature>.dart`, which is what `_isBarrel` actually checks and what the parallel root-Makefile audit check 15 also accepts. A contributor who follows the written standard to fix a warn-only Rule-2 violation would create `providers.dart`, and the lint (once unbricked) would still reject it — the test file even asserts this outcome explicitly (`_isBarrel('tracks', 'providers.dart')` is `isFalse`).
findings.recommendation: Pick one source of truth and make all three artifacts agree: either rename the real convention to `providers.dart` project-wide, or update docs/coding-standards.md Rule 2 and packages/custom_lints/README.md to document `<feature>.dart` as the actual barrel. Cheapest fix: update the two docs (README.md Rule 2 section + coding-standards.md Rule 2, the latter outside this batch) to say `<feature>.dart`.

findings.why: AG-1 requires build/test/lint invocations to route through committed make targets so there is one place to change flags. hooks/pre-commit hardcodes the raw `dart format`/`dart analyze` commands a fourth time (root Makefile `analyze` target, learning_tracker/Makefile `analyze` target, and CI already each define their own copy). The anti-pattern has already bitten: root Makefile's own `analyze` target omits `--fatal-infos` that learning_tracker/Makefile, CI, and this hook all include — proof that hand-duplicated invocations drift out of sync over time even within this one repo.

findings.title: Automate hooks/pre-commit installation instead of relying on manual copy/chmod instructions
findings.why: The pre-commit hook only runs if a contributor manually copies it into .git/hooks/ — there is no `make install-hooks`/`setup` target anywhere in either Makefile that does this for them, confirmed by grepping both Makefiles for 'hook' and finding no match. This repo's own `.git/hooks/pre-commit` is absent right now, empirically confirming the gate is not installed even in the reference checkout. CI backstops the same two checks (format/analyze), so this is not a silent-corruption risk, but it means every new contributor's first several commits get zero local pre-commit feedback and the guardrail is bypassable by simply never running the two setup lines — exactly the 'check that can never fire by default' pattern this audit area was asked to hunt.
findings.recommendation: Add a `make install-hooks` target (or a postinstall step referenced from the top-level setup docs) that performs the cp+chmod, and reference it from hooks/README.md/CONTRIBUTING.md instead of raw shell steps.

findings.title: Wire the profileId-in-PK schema-check invariant into the CI-invoked Makefile

evidence.quote: ci: analyze validate-calendar test ## Run full CI pipeline (analyze + seed validation + all tests)

findings.why: tool/schema_check.dart (DNI-327) enforces the profileId-in-PK invariant that prevents a multi-profile data leak on shared devices — the digest's own rules table marks this rule [E]nforced. But it is wired ONLY into the root Makefile's `ci`/`schema-check` targets. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) only ever runs `make ci`/`make audit` with `working-directory: learning_tracker`, which resolves to learning_tracker/Makefile's `ci: analyze validate-calendar test` — a target with no schema-check step and no learning_tracker/tool/schema_check.dart to call even if it wanted to. No doc (CONTRIBUTING.md, learning_tracker/README.md, learning_tracker/CLAUDE.md) tells a contributor to run the root Makefile. Net effect: a new Drift user-data table that omits profileId from its composite key today would pass CI cleanly, and would only be caught if someone manually ran `make schema-check` from the repo root — something nothing in the documented workflow ever asks for.
findings.recommendation: Move tool/schema_check.dart's invocation (or a copy of it) into learning_tracker/Makefile's `ci`/`audit` target and add a dedicated CI step/job that runs it, matching how test-rules/arb-parity are wired. Retire the root Makefile's copy once the inner one is authoritative.
acceptance_criteria: learning_tracker/Makefile's `ci` or `audit` target invokes the profileId-in-PK schema checker and fails the build on a violation.

findings.title: Gate deploy-play-store.yml on a passing CI run for the exact SHA being deployed
findings.why: deploy-play-store.yml has no `needs:`/`workflow_run:` dependency on ci.yml and no step that checks the target SHA's check-run status. Its only steps between checkout and Play Store upload are checkout, codegen, and `flutter build appbundle --release` — no `flutter test`, `dart analyze`, `make audit`, or firestore-rules check. A maintainer who tags a commit that never went through review/CI (an emergency hotfix, a stale local branch, the wrong SHA) or whose ci.yml run is still red/in-progress can ship straight to Google Play production with nothing in the committed config to stop it — the only backstop is human diligence, which is exactly the kind of implicit, non-deterministic gate Rule 0 says not to rely on.
findings.recommendation: Add a job that queries the GitHub Checks API for the deploying SHA's required workflows before the build/upload steps run (or trigger deploys via a `workflow_call` from a successful ci.yml run instead of independent `push: tags`/`workflow_dispatch` triggers).
acceptance_criteria: deploy-play-store.yml fails fast if the deploying SHA has no green ci.yml run, before any build/signing steps execute.
A dry run against a SHA with a failing/missing CI run demonstrates the new gate blocking the deploy.

findings.title: Fix root Makefile's audit/analyze/test-all targets so they stop reporting false passes

evidence.quote:
cd learning_tracker && dart run custom_lint; \
	echo "audit PASSED."

findings.why: The whole `audit` recipe is one shell invocation (backslash-continued); its final two statements are joined by `;`, not `&&`, so the recipe's exit status is that of the LAST command (`echo "audit PASSED."`), never custom_lint's. Empirically reproduced: a `false;`-then-`echo` recipe in a throwaway Makefile prints the trailing text and `make` still exits 0. Since custom_lint is currently broken (crashes, per baseline), running `make audit` from the repo root today prints the crash output and then unconditionally declares "audit PASSED." Separately, root `analyze` omits `--fatal-infos` and `test-all` omits `--coverage`, unlike learning_tracker/Makefile's equivalents (which say "matches CI --fatal-infos flag" and are correct) — so `make ci` from repo root can go green on issues the real CI gate (which always runs from learning_tracker/) would reject.
findings.recommendation: Replace the trailing `;` with `&&` (or check `$?` explicitly) so a lint failure fails the recipe; add `--fatal-infos` to root `analyze` and `--coverage` to root `test-all`, or better, make the root Makefile's targets thin `cd learning_tracker && make $@` wrappers so there is exactly one place these flags can drift.
acceptance_criteria: `make audit` from the repo root exits non-zero when the underlying custom_lint invocation fails.
root `make analyze` uses --fatal-infos and root `make test-all`/`ci` produce coverage output, matching learning_tracker/Makefile.

findings.title: Correct learning_tracker/CLAUDE.md's false custom-lint enforcement claims

evidence.quote: Run `make audit` to execute every layering grep and lint check locally before pushing.

findings.why: Two independent falsehoods compound here. (1) custom_lint is currently broken and enforces nothing (baselined fact) — yet all five 'Enforced by: <custom lint> (DNI-38x)' lines assert active enforcement. (2) Even ignoring that, `make audit` (learning_tracker/Makefile:277-505) never invokes custom_lint at all — that's a separate `lint` target (lines 270-275) that this file never mentions running. An AI agent or developer reading this file (the FIRST and most authoritative guardrail doc for the app package) will reasonably skip manually checking Rules 1/2 (feature-import boundaries) since those are the two rules whose grep-based backstop is itself only warn-only (known backlog) — meaning Rules 1/2 currently have NO effective enforcement at all despite this file's confident claim.
findings.recommendation: Update the five 'Enforced by' lines to note custom_lint is currently non-functional (link to the tracking issue) and either fix `make audit` to also run `make lint`, or change line 87 to say 'Run `make audit && make lint`'.
acceptance_criteria: learning_tracker/CLAUDE.md's enforcement claims match what `make audit` and custom_lint actually do today, verified by re-reading the file against learning_tracker/Makefile after the fix.

findings.title: Replace make audit's dead literal-phrase TODO/FIXME/XXX grep with a real AG-6 check
findings.rule: AG-6 (every TODO/FIXME carries a Linear DNI-#### id) / Rule 0

evidence.quote: if grep -rn "TODO: refactor later\|FIXME: hardcoded for now\|XXX: temporary" lib/ --include="*.dart" | grep -q .; then \
// TODO: Add more integration tests as features are implemented:

findings.why: Audit check 10/15 ('No banned TODO/FIXME/XXX markers') matches only three exact, oddly-specific literal phrases. Verified: `grep -rn "TODO: refactor later\|FIXME: hardcoded for now\|XXX: temporary" learning_tracker/lib/` returns zero hits anywhere in the app, and always will — no developer writes that literal string. Meanwhile there are real, uncaught TODOs with no Linear id anywhere (`grep -c "DNI-[0-9]"` on all lib/ TODO/FIXME lines returns 0 of 4), and my own batch contains a live example the check silently misses: integration_test/app_test.dart:25. This grep gives the false impression that TODO/FIXME hygiene (AG-6) is enforced by `make audit`, when in fact it enforces nothing a real comment would ever trip.
findings.recommendation: Change the pattern to match any `// TODO`/`// FIXME`/`// XXX` NOT followed by `DNI-\d+` (e.g. `grep -rnE '//\s*(TODO|FIXME|XXX)' lib/ | grep -vE 'DNI-[0-9]+'`), which is what AG-6 actually requires.
acceptance_criteria: `make audit` fails on any TODO/FIXME/XXX comment in lib/ (or test/) lacking a DNI-#### id.
A regression fixture (one TODO with a DNI id, one without) proves the new grep distinguishes them.

findings.title: Consolidate the two divergent arb_parity_check.dart implementations
findings.rule: AG-1 (route through committed scripts; no ad-hoc variants) / Rule 0
findings.why: Two independently-maintained copies of the same nominal checker exist: root Makefile's `arb-parity` target runs tool/arb_parity_check.dart (repo-root paths, --en/--he flags, try/catch around JSON parse errors returning exit 2 with a clear message), while .github/workflows/ci.yml's arb-parity job runs `dart run tool/arb_parity_check.dart` from `working-directory: learning_tracker`, resolving to the DIFFERENT learning_tracker/tool/arb_parity_check.dart (learning_tracker-relative paths, no flags, uncaught jsonDecode exceptions crash with a raw stack trace instead of a clean exit(2)+message). Both currently pass because each is correctly paired with its own CWD, but a future fix to one (e.g. better error messages, a new --strict flag) has no reason to land in the other, and the two already silently diverge in behavior on the identical malformed-JSON failure mode.
findings.recommendation: Delete one copy and have both call sites invoke the same script (e.g. keep only learning_tracker/tool/arb_parity_check.dart and have the root Makefile's arb-parity target `cd learning_tracker &&` into it).

findings.title: Extract duplicated CI bootstrap steps into a shared composite action

evidence.quote:

# GitHub Actions does not support YAML anchors natively, so setup steps are duplicated per job.

findings.why: ci.yml's own comment justifies duplicating checkout/Flutter-setup/pub-cache/codegen/secret-decode steps ACROSS ITS OWN JOBS because 'GitHub Actions does not support YAML anchors natively' — true, but the actual GHA-native fix (composite actions / reusable workflows via `uses:`) is never used, and the same six-to-eight-step bootstrap sequence is copy-pasted a further two times whole across build.yml and deploy-play-store.yml (which the stated per-job-isolation rationale doesn't even apply to — they're separate files, not parallel jobs needing independent runners). findings.recommendation: Create `.github/actions/flutter-bootstrap/action.yml` (checkout+setup+cache+codegen+asset-prep+secret-decode) and reference it via `uses: ./.github/actions/flutter-bootstrap` from all three workflow files.

findings.title: Fix unverifiable Android App Link intent-filters for sign-in/invite deep links (AndroidManifest.xml)
findings.rule: Tier-2 correctness (no numbered rule ID; auth/deep-link infra consistency)
findings.why: Live verification (2026-07-03): https://torah-study-tracker.firebaseapp.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json returns HTTP 404, the domain root '/' returns HTTP 404, and '/sign-in' returns HTTP 404 — only Firebase's built-in /__/auth/action handler responds. Neither firebase.json (root or learning_tracker/) declares a "hosting" block, so nothing can ever serve assetlinks.json or these custom paths as currently configured. Android only honors autoVerify="true" intent-filters after validating that file, so it never marks the app as the verified handler for /sign-in or /invite. A parent tapping 'finish sign-in' in their email, or a tutor tapping an invite link (PP-7 wave-B, AndroidManifest.xml:57), gets sent to the system browser instead of the app — which then also 404s, since no Hosting deployment serves those paths either. Both flows dead-end on an error page.
findings.recommendation: Either deploy Firebase Hosting with a committed .well-known/assetlinks.json (declaring package name + release SHA-256 cert fingerprint) and add the "hosting" block to firebase.json in the same change, or drop the autoVerify/pathPrefix App Links approach for a mechanism that doesn't need host-level verification. Add a deploy/CI smoke check that curls the assetlinks URL and fails the pipeline on non-200.
acceptance_criteria: curl -f https://torah-study-tracker.firebaseapp.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json returns 200 with correct package_name/sha256_cert_fingerprints, wired into a deploy or CI check that fails the pipeline on regression.

findings.title: Fail fast on missing key.properties instead of silently debug-signing release Android builds (build.gradle.kts)
findings.rule: Tier-2 area note (security) — AG-11-adjacent CI guardrail soft-skip
findings.why: When KEYSTORE_BASE64 is unset (misconfigured secret, or a maintainer manually dispatches the 'Build APK' workflow with build_type=release before secrets are wired up), build.yml prints a warning but does not fail — it proceeds to 'flutter build apk --release'. Because key.properties was never written, Gradle's fallback here silently signs the 'release' APK with the shared, publicly-known Flutter debug keystore, then uploads it as a GitHub Actions artifact literally named learning-tracker-release-apk. Anyone who installs that artifact believing it's a genuine release build gets a debug-signed binary; since the debug key is identical across virtually all Flutter/Android-Studio installs, another developer's debug-signed build could later 'update' over it without Android's signature check objecting.
findings.recommendation: Make the release signingConfig fail fast (e.g. error("release build requested but key.properties is missing")) instead of silently substituting debug signing, or at minimum have build.yml's keystore-decode step exit 1 when build_type == 'release' and the secret is empty instead of only warning.
acceptance_criteria: flutter build apk --release (or ./gradlew assembleRelease) fails loudly when key.properties/keystore secret is absent, instead of producing a debug-signed 'release' artifact.
build.yml's release job aborts (non-zero exit) when KEYSTORE_BASE64 is empty and build_type=release.

findings.title: Commit gradle-wrapper.jar instead of excluding it in android/.gitignore
findings.rule: Tier-2 area note (correctness) — Gradle wrapper convention
findings.why: git ls-files learning_tracker/android/gradle/wrapper/ shows only gradle-wrapper.properties tracked — the bootstrap jar is untracked in every fresh checkout, contrary to standard Flutter/Gradle convention of committing it. Flutter Tool happens to self-heal this (GradleUtils.injectGradleWrapperIfNeeded in flutter/packages/flutter_tools/lib/src/android/gradle_utils.dart:256 copies its own bundled copy in before every flutter build/run), which is why day-to-day flutter build apk keeps working — but anything that shells to android/gradlew directly without Flutter Tool mediating first (e.g. Android Studio's Gradle sync on a brand-new clone, or a raw cd android && ./gradlew tasks) fails with ClassNotFoundException: org.gradle.wrapper.GradleWrapperMain.
findings.recommendation: Remove gradle-wrapper.jar from android/.gitignore and commit the jar (or regenerate via `gradle wrapper` and commit), matching the vanilla flutter create template.
acceptance_criteria: git ls-files learning_tracker/android/gradle/wrapper/ lists both gradle-wrapper.jar and gradle-wrapper.properties.
cd learning_tracker/android && ./gradlew --version succeeds on a fresh clone with no prior flutter invocation.

findings.title: Pin distributionSha256Sum in android/gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
findings.why: The wrapper properties file has no distributionSha256Sum key. Without it, gradlew's bootstrap download of the Gradle distribution has no integrity check beyond TLS — a compromised mirror/CDN or a MITM on a misconfigured proxy could substitute a malicious Gradle distribution that every subsequent local build and CI run would silently execute.
findings.recommendation: Run `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.14 --distribution-type all` (or add distributionSha256Sum manually from Gradle's published checksums page) so the wrapper verifies the download and fails closed on mismatch.
acceptance_criteria: gradle-wrapper.properties contains a distributionSha256Sum line matching the official checksum for gradle-8.14-all.zip.
A deliberately-wrong checksum causes ./gradlew to fail the download instead of proceeding.

evidence.quote: // This prevents anyone from claiming an invite not addressed to them.
// without needing the emailed deep link. Match the caller's verified email.

findings.why: Firebase Auth lets anyone register an account with any unverified email string. acceptTutorInvite, declineTutorInvite, and listTutorGrants({mode:'pending_for_me'}) all authorize 'is this caller the invited tutor' purely by comparing the caller's Auth email to grant.tutor_email -- none of them checks callerRecord.emailVerified (or the token claim), despite comments at both call sites explicitly (and incorrectly) claiming this 'prevents anyone from claiming an invite not addressed to them' / matches the 'verified' email. An attacker who front-runs registration of the invited tutor's email address can call listTutorGrants(pending_for_me) to discover the grantId, then acceptTutorInvite to gain ongoing read access (and any write permissions the parent granted) to the child's full learning profile -- without ever proving ownership of that inbox. The invite_token generated specifically to prevent exactly this (comment: 'single-use, per NFR-3') is stored on the grant doc but is never read back or compared anywhere in the file, so it provides zero actual protection. cf_grant_invite.test.mjs's own header comment confirms this exact gate is never exercised by any test.
findings.recommendation: Require callerRecord.emailVerified === true in acceptTutorInvite/declineTutorInvite before trusting the email match, and/or require the caller to supply invite_token and compare it against grant.invite_token (the mechanism already built for this). Apply the same emailVerified gate to listTutorGrants' pending_for_me query so an unverified account cannot even discover invites addressed to an email it doesn't own.
acceptance_criteria: A new Auth-emulator-backed test in cf_grant_invite.test.mjs seeds an unverified-email account and asserts acceptTutorInvite rejects it (e.g. permission-denied).
acceptTutorInvite/declineTutorInvite check emailVerified or invite_token before authorizing by email match.
make test-functions (or a new CI job per the companion finding) seeds Auth-emulator users so this path is actually exercised, not skipped.

findings.title: Close the update-mutation and create-validation gaps on append-only event collections in firestore.rules

evidence.quote: // deny `update` and `delete`. Snapshot collections deny `delete` and gate

findings.why: completions, streak_events, learning_ledger and points_ledger all `allow update` for the owner with no check that the update reproduces the existing document (no comparison against `resource.data`), so any client holding the owner's valid session -- a modified build, a tampered/replayed request, or a future client bug -- can overwrite an already-committed event with different field values. Three of the four (streak_events, learning_ledger, points_ledger) validate literally nothing on create either: no presence check, no `is timestamp`, no `<= request.time` bound, contradicting SR-3. Because points_ledger backs the reward-redemption economy, the append-only invariant this collection family exists to guarantee is not enforced -- a user could rewrite their own point-earning history to inflate reward-eligible balances. The file's own top-of-file comment ('deny `update` and `delete`') is simply false for the current rule bodies, which is itself a sign this drifted from the original design during the permission-denied-outage fixes documented inline at streak_events.
findings.recommendation: Restrict `update` on all four collections to a byte-identical replay of the existing doc (or drop `update` once outbox retries are proven to only ever hit `create`), and add `is timestamp` + presence + `<= request.time` validation on create for streak_events/learning_ledger/points_ledger, matching what completions partially does today. Fix the stale line-38 comment.
acceptance_criteria: functions/test/firestore_rules.test.mjs asserts that updating an existing completions/streak_events/learning_ledger/points_ledger doc with a changed field value is denied.
A create with a missing/non-timestamp/future created_at on streak_events, learning_ledger, or points_ledger is denied.

A malicious or buggy client can write a multi-megabyte string into any allow-listed field (e.g. goals free-text fields), bloating every synced device's listener payload indefinitely, or write the wrong type where the Dart codec expects a specific one, surfacing only as a runtime cast failure on every device that later syncs the doc.

findings.title: Split allow list from allow read in firestore.rules to cap request.query.limit

evidence.quote: allow read: if isOwner(uid) || hasActiveTutorAccess(uid, profileId);
allow read: if isOwner(uid) || hasActiveTutorAccess(uid, profileId);
allow read: if isOwner(uid) || hasActiveTutorAccess(uid, profileId);

findings.why: `allow read` grants both `get` and `list` under the identical condition on every match block in the file (learner_profiles, completions, streak_events, learning_ledger, points_ledger, and every other subcollection); none constrains `request.query.limit`, so nothing stops an unbounded query. This matters most for the tutor cross-user read path: a compromised or custom client authenticated as an active tutor can issue one unlimited `.get()` query across a child's entire completions/learning_ledger history.
findings.recommendation: Split `allow read` into `allow get` (unchanged) and `allow list` (same condition && request.query.limit <= 500) on at least the per-profile event collections (completions, streak_events, learning_ledger, points_ledger).

findings.title: Whitelist fields on tutor CRUD Cloud Functions instead of merging caller-supplied objects verbatim

evidence.quote: // Admin SDK bypasses Firestore Security Rules -- the permission checks above are

allow create, update: if isOwner(uid)
            && request.resource.data.keys().hasOnly([

findings.why: tutorUpsertGoal, tutorUpsertTrack, tutorUpsertStageDefinition, tutorUpsertStudyDayConfig, tutorUpdateGamificationSettings, tutorUpsertBookmark, tutorSetProfileProgram and tutorUpsertCurriculumScope all use the Admin SDK, which bypasses firestore.rules entirely -- the code's own comment says its permission checks 'are the sole enforcement layer for these write paths', but those checks only gate who may write and which collection, not what shape. Each function spreads the caller-supplied `xData` object straight into the child's synced document after only an object-vs-array/null check -- no field whitelist (unlike the `.hasOnly()` the same collections enforce for the owner's own direct writes) and no size cap. An invited tutor -- a distinct, deliberately lower-trust principal with fine-grained permission flags precisely because they're less trusted -- can therefore write fields the owner is rules-blocked from writing directly, or inflate a doc with an oversized field. None of cf_tutor_content.test.mjs / cf_tutor_goals_tracks.test.mjs / cf_tutor_settings_profile.test.mjs exercises this; every test fixture is a small, clean object. tutorEditProfile, in the same file, shows the correct pattern (explicit per-field validation with a length cap).
findings.recommendation: Give each tutorUpsertX function the same field whitelist as the corresponding firestore.rules `.hasOnly()` block (or one shared `assertAllowedFields` helper), mirroring tutorEditProfile's existing validation style.
acceptance_criteria: A tutorUpsertGoal call with an extra unexpected key (or an oversized string field) in goalData is rejected with invalid-argument, proven by a new test.

findings.title: Wrap tutorEditProfile's read-then-overwrite in a transaction to stop the lost-update race
findings.why: Every other stateful mutation needing read-then-write consistency in this file (acceptTutorInvite, revokeTutorGrant, resignTutorGrant, expirePendingInvites) wraps it in db.runTransaction. tutorEditProfile instead reads the profile doc, merges edit fields in application memory, then does a full-document `set(..., {merge:false})` with no transaction. If the owner's own device (or a second tutor) writes any other field to the same learner_profiles/{profileId} doc between the get() and the set(), that write is silently overwritten by tutorEditProfile's stale full-doc replace -- a lost-update race, undermining the very H2 fix comment that motivated reading the full doc first.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the read+write in db.runTransaction (txn.get + txn.set), consistent with the rest of the file, or switch to `profilePath.set(updates, {merge:true})` for the scalar fields being edited -- Firestore applies a merge write atomically server-side without a client-side read first.
acceptance_criteria: A concurrency test (a second writer updates an unrelated profile field between tutorEditProfile's get and set) shows that field survives.

findings.title: Make tutor audit-log writes idempotent and failure-visible instead of best-effort auto-ID writes

evidence.quote: /** Write an audit log entry for a tutor mutation (best-effort — errors are logged but not thrown). */

} catch (e) {
    logger.warn(`writeAuditLog: failed for grant=${grantId} action=${action}`, e);

findings.why: The audit log is the parent's only visibility into what an invited tutor did to their child's data (12-month retention, W3.42), but every write to it is swallowed on failure (the primary mutation still returns success:true even if its audit entry silently failed) and keyed by Firestore auto-ID rather than a deterministic key, so a client-side retry of a timed-out-but-actually-succeeded Cloud Function call produces a duplicate entry for the same real action. A parent reviewing the trail can see gaps or phantom duplicates with no way to tell which from inside the app.
findings.recommendation: Derive a deterministic audit_log doc ID from (grantId, action, target, an idempotency key) so retries coalesce, and consider writing the audit entry in the same batch/transaction as the primary mutation so both succeed or fail together.
acceptance_criteria: Calling the same tutor mutation twice with the same idempotency key produces exactly one audit_log entry, proven by a new test.

findings.title: Guard inviteTutor against silently resetting an already-active tutor grant

evidence.quote: //   1. Validate preconditions against the local [TutorGrant] aggregate.

findings.why: grantId is deterministic ({encodedEmail}__{parentUid}__{childProfileId}), so a second inviteTutor call for the same tutor+child pair overwrites the same doc unconditionally, even when the existing grant is currently 'active'. That silently resets state back to 'pending', issues a fresh invite_token/expires_at, and replaces permissions with the request-supplied defaults (which include can_bulk_prior_completion: true) -- while the already-active tutor_active_access index doc is untouched, so the tutor keeps live read access even though tutor_grants.state now says 'pending'. Neither the Cloud Function nor the Dart InviteTutorUseCase (whose own docstring claims it validates against the local grant aggregate, but whose implementation only validates email format) guards against this, so a parent re-sending an invite, or a duplicate form submission, can silently re-grant a permission the parent had explicitly turned off.
findings.recommendation: Before writing, read the existing grant (if any) and reject/short-circuit re-invites while state === 'active' (direct the caller to a permission-editing flow instead), or explicitly preserve prior permissions and keep tutor_active_access consistent with the resulting state.
acceptance_criteria: A new cf_grant_invite.test.mjs test: inviteTutor called twice for the same tutorEmail+childProfileId while the grant is 'active' does not silently reset state/permissions.

findings.title: test/helpers/golden_runner.dart and flutter_test_config.dart produce no usable golden-regression coverage — no fonts loaded, and every caller skips the pixel assertion
findings.rule: TQ-5 (goldens deterministic — fonts loaded in flutter_test_config.dart)

evidence.quote: Goldens are deterministic (fonts loaded in `flutter_test_config.dart`; pinned size/theme/locale; fixed clock; constant data)

findings.why: flutter_test_config.dart runs before every test file but never calls FontLoader/loadAppFonts — it only disables GoogleFonts network fetching. I built a throwaway probe (`goldenTest('probe', builder: (l) => const Text('Probe'))`) and ran `flutter test ... --update-goldens`: the captured PNG was 100% blank white — no glyphs at all. A second probe (`Container(color: red, child: Text(...))`) rendered the red container at full size (proving layout/paint itself works) but the text area was a solid opaque black smear, never legible characters. For comparison, test/golden/goldens/phone_1_dashboard.png (built by the separate store_screenshots_test.dart, which does call FontLoader itself) renders crisp real glyphs in the same sandbox — proving the blankness is caused by golden_runner.dart's missing font load, not an environment limitation. Because of this (or in anticipation of it), every one of the 11 current goldenTest() call sites across test/story_acceptance/ passes skipGolden: true, so matchesGoldenFile never actually executes anywhere today. The RTL/LTR visual-regression protection this helper's own doc comment claims to provide ('UI bugs that only manifest in RTL Hebrew layouts... cost the team a release window in E18') is not happening — if anyone flips skipGolden to false today to 'baseline' goldens per the tracked follow-up (DNI-380), they will commit blank/illegible PNGs as the accepted baseline without any test failure to warn them.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit font loading to flutter_test_config.dart (FontLoader per family declared in pubspec's fonts: section, mirroring what store_screenshots_test.dart already does locally) before testMain() runs. Re-run the probe pattern above with skipGolden:false to confirm real glyphs render, then un-skip and baseline the goldens that are ready (per the DNI-380 tracked follow-up).
acceptance_criteria: A goldenTest() call with skipGolden:false and real text content produces a PNG with legible (non-blank, non-tofu-smear) glyphs, verified by re-running the probe pattern used in this audit.

findings.title: Deduplicate seedProfile/seedProfileZero between test/helpers/drift_memory.dart and test/helpers/test_database.dart
findings.rule: Fowler duplication (test helper hygiene; no single named coding-standards rule ID)
findings.why: seedProfile and seedProfileZero are byte-for-byte identical function bodies defined independently in both files (same AccountsCompanion/LearnerProfilesCompanion literals, same email/tier/displayName defaults). drift_memory.dart's own doc comment already says 'Prefer this helper over the older createTestDatabase() in test_database.dart... it is the canonical entry point' — but nobody finished the migration, so both copies live on.
