findings.title: Remove flutter_test_config.dart's FlutterError.onError GoogleFonts filter — TestWidgetsFlutterBinding never lets it run during a test
findings.rule: Test-infra correctness (no direct coding-standards rule ID)
findings.why: The comment above this block claims it suppresses 'residual font not found errors... cosmetic rendering issues, not test logic failures' during test execution. I traced the installed Flutter SDK (3.44.1, matching this repo's `flutter --version`): TestWidgetsFlutterBinding._runTest() (binding.dart:1770) saves whatever handler is currently installed into _oldExceptionHandler, then unconditionally overwrites FlutterError.onError with its own handler that just does `_pendingExceptionDetails = details` — it never calls the previously-installed handler. postTest() (binding.dart:2131-2134) restores _oldExceptionHandler only after the test body has finished. Since _runTest() wraps every individual test()/testWidgets() body, the custom GoogleFonts-substring filter installed in flutter_test_config.dart is captured as 'the old handler' before the first test and is never invoked while any test is actually running — exactly the window in which a font-not-found FlutterError would fire. If such an error does occur during a pump, it is captured into _pendingExceptionDetails and fails the test outright, contradicting the file's own comment about what it does.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead FlutterError.onError override (lines 17-22), or replace it with a mechanism proven to run mid-test (e.g. wrap only the specific pump inside affected tests, or fix the font-loading gap in finding 'golden_runner.dart never renders real glyphs' so the underlying error stops occurring). Do not rely on a global onError swap in this file for anything that needs to suppress errors during pumpWidget/pumpAndSettle.
acceptance_criteria: A widget test that deliberately throws/renders a FlutterError whose message contains 'GoogleFonts' mid-pump either fails (proving the current filter does nothing) or is demonstrated to pass only via a mechanism that actually executes during _runTest's window.
The doc comment above the handler is removed or corrected to match what the code can actually do.

findings.title: infrastructure_test.dart's 'database is isolated between tests' only proves two objects aren't identical(), not that data is isolated
findings.rule: TQ-8 (assertions weaker than what the source under test can actually do wrong)

evidence.quote: test('database is isolated between tests', () async {

findings.why: createTestDatabase() is a plain constructor call with no caching, so identical(db1, db2) is guaranteed false for any two invocations regardless of whether UserDatabase has any shared/static state that leaks data between instances — the assertion cannot fail even if isolation were genuinely broken. Running this test (`flutter test test/infrastructure_test.dart`) confirms it passes today, and also prints a real Drift runtime warning at exactly this test's stack frame: 'It looks like you've created the database class UserDatabase multiple times... race conditions will occur and might corrupt the database' (createTestDatabase at test_database.dart:13, called from infrastructure_test.dart:134). Twenty-plus other test files in this repo (app_shell_test.dart, e2e_harness.dart, the sync/merge/* roundtrip suite) already know about this and explicitly set `driftRuntimeOptions.dontWarnAboutMultipleDatabases = true` when intentionally creating multiple in-memory DBs — this test does not follow that established convention, so it emits unnecessary warning noise on every run on top of not checking the property its name promises. A real cross-instance state leak (e.g. an accidental static/singleton in UserDatabase) would sail through this test undetected.
findings.recommendation: Replace the identical() check with a real isolation assertion: insert a row into db1 (e.g. via seedProfile) and assert it is absent when querying db2, or that db2's relevant table starts empty. Also set driftRuntimeOptions.dontWarnAboutMultipleDatabases = true here to match the repo's established pattern for intentional multi-instance in-memory DBs.
acceptance_criteria: The test inserts data into db1 and asserts it is not visible from db2 (or vice versa), not just that the two references are non-identical.
Running the test no longer prints the Drift multiple-database-instantiation warning.

findings.title: Delete the remaining tautological instantiation/fixture-echo tests in infrastructure_test.dart
findings.rule: TQ-8 (tautological tests — assert what the mock/fixture was hardcoded to return)
findings.why: This file (self-described as 'Example test demonstrating test infrastructure usage') contains 9 tests that cannot fail short of a compile error: 'MockAuthRepository/MockConnectivityService can be instantiated' asserts isNotNull on a non-nullable constructor result; 'can be stubbed with mocktail' asserts isA<MockAuthRepository>() on a freshly-constructed MockAuthRepository (necessarily true) and its body is otherwise a comment showing example usage that is never executed; 'creates valid mishna/daf/pasuk/container' and 'provides default curriculum' assert that ContentItemFixtures/CurriculumFixtures return exactly the literal defaults hardcoded into those same fixture files (content_fixtures.dart / curriculum_fixtures.dart) — they test the fixture's own defaults, not ContentItem or any production logic; 'creates test database successfully' asserts isNotNull plus `schemaVersion >= 1` (a comment notes 'current value is 23', itself now stale — actual is 32) which can only fail on a catastrophic schema-version regression. findings.title: privacy-policy.md falsely claims no analytics/crash-report collection while release builds ship FirebaseAnalyticsService + unconditional Crashlytics
findings.why: The App Store/Play Store-facing privacy policy tells a parent installing this children's app that it does not collect 'Analytics events or usage telemetry' or 'Crash reports.' In reality, release/profile builds wire analyticsServiceProvider to a real FirebaseAnalyticsService (analytics_provider.dart:22-29) that sends named events with a content identifier (sefaria_ref) and per-child identifiers (profile_id, at analytics_service.dart:56,82,87 — already a baselined PV-1 code gap), and firebase_bootstrap.dart unconditionally enables Crashlytics collection and forwards the numeric profileId as the Crashlytics user identifier. This is not merely stale prose — it is a live, false representation to end users (and, given the app's stated child userbase, a child-privacy-adjacent misrepresentation) about what data leaves the device. Anyone who reads and relies on this policy — including a parent deciding whether to let a child use the app — is being told something the shipped binary does not do.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the 'Data We Do NOT Collect' section to remove the false 'Analytics events'/'Crash reports' bullets, add Firebase Analytics and Firebase Crashlytics to the 'Third-Party Services' table with their actual purpose (event/crash telemetry) and a link to Google's privacy policy, and state what parameters are sent. This is independent of (and does not replace) actually fixing the underlying PV-1/PV-3 code gaps (consent-gating, dropping content/profile identifiers from event params) already tracked in coding-standards.md — but until those land, the policy must describe reality, not the target state.
acceptance_criteria: privacy-policy.md's collection list and third-party table match what analyticsServiceProvider/FirebaseCrashlyticsService actually send in a release build

findings.title: Delete dead AppLogger.setupFlutterErrorHandlers (logger.dart:85-94) — near-duplicate of the live crashlytics_bootstrap.dart handler wiring
findings.rule: Fowler-duplication (dead code / duplicate responsibility); EH-1 context
findings.why: Repo-wide grep for `setupFlutterErrorHandlers` shows its only 3 call sites are all inside logger_test.dart; bootstrap.dart never calls it, calling bootstrapCrashlyticsHandlers() instead. Git history proves this is not an oversight but a leftover: commit 78479109 (DNI-319/Story 24.4) deleted the `AppLogger.setupFlutterErrorHandlers();` call from main.dart and replaced it inline with the Crashlytics-forwarding block that is now crashlytics_bootstrap.dart:26-34 — but never deleted the method or its dedicated test group. Both implementations assign FlutterError.onError and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError unconditionally (no chaining), so whichever runs last wins outright. Because the dead method is public, documented, and sits in core/logging/logger.dart right next to AppLogger — exactly where a future maintainer would look to 'wire up error logging' — a single future call to `AppLogger.setupFlutterErrorHandlers()` (e.g. added to a new bootstrap path, a test harness, or a plugin init) would silently clobber the crashlytics_bootstrap.dart handlers and permanently disable recordFlutterFatalError/recordError(fatal:true) reporting to Crashlytics for the rest of the process, with no compiler error and no currently-existing test able to catch it.
findings.recommendation: Delete setupFlutterErrorHandlers() from logger.dart and its test group from logger_test.dart (see the paired TQ-8 finding). If a Talker-only path is still wanted for some caller, have crashlytics_bootstrap.dart's bootstrapCrashlyticsHandlers() be the single call site and inline the two-line Talker forward there — do not keep two independent implementations of the same two global handler assignments.
acceptance_criteria: lib/core/logging/logger.dart no longer defines a function that assigns FlutterError.onError / PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError outside of core/logging's own internal use.

New Rule-0 grep (wired into `make audit`) asserts `FlutterError\.onError\s*=` and `PlatformDispatcher\.instance\.onError\s*=` each appear in exactly one non-test, non-generated file under lib/, failing with file:line of any extra assignment site.

A regression test drives the real bootstrap.dart call graph (or bootstrapCrashlyticsHandlers() directly) and asserts the installed FlutterError.onError/PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError closures call both a fake CrashlyticsService and AppLogger, and that the PlatformDispatcher handler returns true.

sup-sm5.coverage: Read all 24 hand-written Riverpod Notifier/AsyncNotifier(-shaped) classes found via `extends _$`, `class .*Notifier`, `class .*Controller`, and `extends (StateNotifier|ChangeNotifier|Notifier<|AsyncNotifier<)` greps across lib/ (2 in core/, 22 in features/), plus callers (screens, .g.dart providers) where needed to confirm end-to-end error-handling behavior. 14 of the 24 are sync-only mutation notifiers (e.g. SelectedProfileId, ParentPinAuthenticatedProfileId, CompletionCommitted, JourneySortModeNotifier, ActiveTutoredProfileSelection, SchedulerGroupedView, _CelebrationInFlightNotifier) or plain-value/stream-driven function-style `@riverpod Future<T>`/`Stream<T>` providers (activeProfile, autoSelectedProfileId, journeyViewModel, allDailyTasks, profileList/profileListStream) where build() naturally propagates as AsyncError or there is no async I/O at all — SM-5 is architecturally inapplicable there; confirmed COMPLIANT, no findings filed. completion_feedback_controller.dart is a plain ChangeNotifier driving local widget animation state, also out of scope. Of the remaining 10 files with genuine async mutation methods, stage_providers.dart is confirmed the sole correct `AsyncValue.guard` user (the known baseline); the other 9 (pin_flow_controller.dart, reward_config_controller.dart, auth_state_provider.dart, sign_in_controller.dart, preference_providers.dart, notification_providers.dart, sacred_location_provider.dart, scheduler_providers.dart, add_track_controller.dart, onboarding_controller.dart) hand-roll loading/error state via bespoke sealed classes or bool/string fields, or omit error handling outright, yielding the 5 root-cause findings below (31 individual sites, 3 of which are live reproducible defects, not just style debt). The family is NOT architecturally inapplicable outside the DB-6 read-provider carve-out the assignment anticipated — it is badly under-adopted: only 1 of 10 mutation-bearing classes uses the compliant idiom.

ledger.note: Hand-rolled busy/error state (SM-5 family); 3 of 4 async branches catch only one specific exception type and the 4th catches nothing, so any other throw from PinService leaves state.busy stuck true forever and the keypad permanently unresponsive (appendDigit/backspace both early-return while busy).

RewardForm.loading/.error are fully wired into the screen's UI (dedicated spinner + error Scaffold) but the controller never sets them to true/non-null anywhere — confirmed via grep, only bootstrap() resets them to false/null. All 4 async mutation methods have zero try/catch.

build() fires _init() fire-and-forget with zero try/catch across multiple awaited DB/Firebase calls; any exception leaves state stuck at AuthState.initializing() forever, directly contradicting the AuthState doc comment 'Must not hang — see 19.6 startup hardening'.

SignInController hand-rolls a tri-state sealed class (Idle/Submitting/Error) with ~15 manual `state = ...` assignments across try/catch/finally instead of AsyncNotifier + AsyncValue.guard. Error handling is currently reasonably thorough, but the class's own DG-GAUTH-01 comment documents a previously-shipped bug from exactly this pattern (a missed state transition silently degraded to no user feedback).

5 Notifier classes (UseHebrewTerms, UseHebrewDate, ShowNikudPref, CurrentTransliterationVariant, CurrentFontSize) hold plain-value state and optimistically assign `state` before an unguarded `await` persistence write; a write failure is an unhandled Future rejection with the optimistic state left desynced from disk.

Same idiom as preference_providers.dart repeated across 5 classes (ReminderEnabled, ReminderTime, StreakAlertEnabled, StreakAlertTime, RewardNotificationEnabled) — toggle()/setTime() assign state then await an unguarded SharedPreferences write.

SacredLocationNotifier.detect (success branch)/setManualCity/setManualCoords and InIsraelNotifier.setInIsrael await unguarded persistence writes after assigning state, same family as preference_providers.dart; detect() otherwise correctly uses a typed LocationFetchResult union, which is the ONE part of this file done right.

SkippedTasks.skip/undoSkip repeat the unguarded-write idiom; note SkippedTasks._loadFromPrefs itself is a genuinely GOOD example (full try/catch + AppLogger.error) that the mutation methods failed to mirror. All other providers in this 1382-line file are plain-value/watch-driven and compliant.

_advance()/goBack() call the async _persist() without await/unawaited() or a catch, and tryRestore() runs jsonDecode on stored prefs JSON with no try/catch — a corrupt or unexpected persisted shape throws uncaught instead of falling back to a fresh wizard.

init()/advance()/jumpTo() await external OnboardingStep.save/load(ref) calls with zero try/catch anywhere in the file (grep-confirmed) and no loading/error state fields at all; the caller (learning_process_wizard_screen.dart) also does not catch and discards advance()'s one validation-error return channel.

Confirmed as the assignment's known-compliant baseline: StageEditorNotifier extends AsyncNotifier<List<StageDefinition>>, build() throws naturally, and all 5 mutation methods (addStage/updateStage/deleteStage/reorderStages/resetToDefaults) end with `state = await AsyncValue.guard(...)`. Not re-reported per instructions.

Same _mapAuthError gap and same now-unreachable local-collision detector (line 358) as sign_in_controller.dart. All 4 signOut() sites traced — each fires before any DB/session activation for the new identity, so AU-3 is clean in this file.

No getIdToken/forceRefresh pass-through exists (AU-5) — reloadCurrentUser() only refreshes profile fields via User.reload(), not the JWT. Everything else (no setPersistence, authStateChanges() correctly wrapped and confined per Rule 3) is clean.

showSignOutConfirmation's hard Firebase sign-out (line 190) makes AccountManagementService.signOut()'s documented 'soft sign-out for <200ms fast resume' unreachable from its only cloud-relevant caller (P3 doc/behavior mismatch). No sign-out path here deletes the local DB, so this is a UX/doc-drift issue, not data loss.

rollbackIfIncomplete/cleanupStaleOnStartup only delete the DB + signOut() when countProfilesForAccount()==0, so by construction no outbox rows can exist yet at that point (AU-3 clean). Not otherwise implicated in AU-2/4/5.

All 9 signOut() calls fire either pre-tier-flip (local-born profile untouched, never had outbox rows) or immediately after a failed post-flip email-verification check, and the one caller found (sign_in_controller.dart) pushes local data synchronously right after a successful flip — none strands unsynced cloud data (AU-3 clean). email-already-in-use is the only Firebase collision code reachable via this password-based path and has a full explicit merge flow (executeUploadLocalIntoCloud/executeKeepCloudDiscardLocal) satisfying AU-2.
Thin pass-through gateway with no session-routing, persistence, or token logic — nothing here to violate AU-2/3/4/5.

findings.title: account_lifecycle_service.dart removeCloudFromDevice() must verify the outbox is drained before deleting the local DB file

evidence.quote:
/// Firestore data and Firebase Auth are NOT touched — user can
  /// sign back in on any device and recover everything.
"accountRemoveFromDeviceBody": "Your cloud data is safe — you can sign back in anytime.",

findings.why: The outbox (tier-gated to cloud-born accounts, features/sync/presentation/providers/sync_providers.dart) queues Firestore writes locally until drained; those rows are the only copy of a mutation until push succeeds. removeCloudFromDevice() is reachable mid-session via swipe-to-dismiss in the Account Picker with zero connectivity check and zero OutboxDao.depth() check, then unconditionally deletes the account's entire local Drift file (which holds the outbox table) and the registry row. A child completing offline study sessions, then swiping 'Remove from device' while those completions are still queued, permanently loses that specific progress even though the confirmation dialog explicitly promises 'Your cloud data is safe — you can sign back in anytime,' and the method's own doc comment claims the same. This is exactly the credential-less/offline-account data-loss territory the standard calls out, just triggered by an explicit destructive action rather than a bare signOut().
findings.recommendation: Before _deleteDbFile in removeCloudFromDevice, sum OutboxDao.depth(profileId) across every profile under the account (the outbox is per-profile, the account can have multiple learner profiles) and block or force a bounded drain-and-wait when depth > 0, surfacing a clear 'N changes not backed up yet' warning instead of silently proceeding. Stop promising unconditional safety in the ARB copy until this is true.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: seed a cloud-born account with ≥1 undrained outbox row on any of its profiles, call AccountLifecycleService.removeCloudFromDevice, and assert it refuses/blocks rather than deleting the DB file.
Regression test: with outbox depth 0 for every profile under the account, removeCloudFromDevice still succeeds (no happy-path regression).
account_picker_screen.dart's swipe-to-remove flow surfaces the pending-outbox count (or blocks) before invoking removeCloudFromDevice for a cloud tile.

findings.title: AuthStateNotifier._init() must guard reloadCurrentUser() so an offline cold start cannot hang the session state forever

evidence.quote:
if (firebaseUser != null) {
      final refreshed = await authRepo.reloadCurrentUser();

/// App has not yet resolved the initial session (splash window).
  /// Must not hang — see 19.6 startup hardening.

findings.why: FirebaseAuthGatewayImpl.reloadCurrentUser() calls User.reload(), a network round-trip that throws FirebaseAuthException(network-request-failed) when offline — an entirely ordinary cold-start condition for an offline-first app (this exact file set otherwise engineers carefully around it, e.g. sign_in_controller.dart wraps every Firestore/Firebase call in try/catch and timeouts). Nothing in AuthStateNotifier._init() catches this; the exception escapes the fire-and-forget call from build(), so `state` never advances past AuthState.initializing(). AuthGuard never touches Firebase and lets onboarded users straight through to the app shell, which reads authStateProvider downstream — so a returning cloud-born user opening the app with no connectivity can be stuck on an unresolved session state indefinitely, directly violating the SessionStatus.initializing doc comment's own 'must not hang' contract (a lesson the codebase already learned once for the router guard per the '19.6 startup hardening' reference, but that didn't carry over to this newer Notifier-based path).
findings.recommendation: Wrap the Firebase-touching logic in _init() (at minimum the reloadCurrentUser() call) in try/catch; on failure, fall back to trusting the cached bare currentUser or the local-born row rather than leaving state unset, mirroring the defensive timeout/try-catch pattern already used elsewhere in sign_in_controller.dart.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: mock AuthRepository.reloadCurrentUser() to throw (simulating an offline reload()), build AuthStateNotifier, and assert state resolves to a terminal SessionStatus within a bounded time instead of remaining initializing indefinitely.
On-device check: cold-start the app in airplane mode with a previously-active cloud-born session and confirm no indefinite splash/loading hang.

findings.title: Handle account-exists-with-different-credential and credential-already-in-use for the Google sign-in / link-provider paths
findings.why: A repo-wide grep for 'account-exists-with-different-credential' and 'credential-already-in-use' returns zero hits anywhere in lib/. A user who already has a password-based Firebase account under an email and taps 'Sign in with Google' (or 'Link Google' in Settings) using the same address will hit one of these two Firebase codes; neither auth_repository_impl.dart's Google methods nor either screen's _mapAuthError switch has a case for them, so both fall to the generic default branch ('Sign-in failed' / 'Google sign-in failed') with zero guidance to use the existing password and no merge option — unlike the parallel email-already-in-use case in upgrade_to_cloud_service.dart, which has a complete EmailCollisionException-driven merge flow (executeUploadLocalIntoCloud / executeKeepCloudDiscardLocal). AU-2 explicitly names both codes as requiring an explicit merge flow.
findings.recommendation: Add both codes to both _mapAuthError switches with an actionable message ('this email already has a password — sign in that way'), and extend the merge machinery upgrade_to_cloud_service.dart already has for the password path to cover the Google-credential collision (e.g. capture the pending OAuth credential, prompt for the existing password, then link).
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: stub the auth gateway to throw account-exists-with-different-credential from signInWithGoogle(), assert SignInController/SignupScreen surface a specific actionable message (not the generic fallback).
Regression test: same for credential-already-in-use thrown from linkGoogleProvider().

findings.title: Local-born-account Google-collision detector can never match now that offline accounts use synthetic emails

evidence.quote:
final localMatch = await registry.findByEmail(googleUser.email ?? '');
      if (localMatch != null && localMatch.accountTier.isLocal) {

findings.why: Per the confirmed credential-less offline-account redesign, a local-born account is now keyed on a synthetic 'offline_xxx@offline.local' address, never a real user email (signup_screen.dart _createOfflineAccount). Both SignInController.signInWithGoogle() and SignupScreen._signUpWithGoogle() try to detect 'this device already has local-born data under this email' by calling registry.findByEmail(googleUser.email) — a real Gmail address can never equal the synthetic offline placeholder, so this collision branch (whose own comment says it exists to 'route to collision/upgrade flow instead of silently merging') is now permanently unreachable for any account created under the current model. A user with real local progress who later signs up/in with Google on the same device gets silently routed into a brand-new, empty cloud account with no merge prompt, leaving their offline progress orphaned in a separate account with no guided path to combine them.
findings.recommendation: Detect an existing local-born account on-device independent of email matching (e.g. check registry.getAllAccounts() for any untouched local-born entry whenever a new Google/cloud identity is being registered) and route into the upgrade/merge flow instead of relying on a field offline accounts no longer populate meaningfully.
acceptance_criteria: Regression test: seed a local-born registry account with the current synthetic-email shape, drive signInWithGoogle()/_signUpWithGoogle() with a real Gmail identity, and assert the user is offered the offline-to-cloud merge/upgrade path rather than silently landing in a second, empty cloud account.

findings.title: Add a getIdToken(forceRefresh) primitive so a synced write hitting permission-denied/unauthenticated can recover

evidence.quote:
if (user == null) return null;
    await user.reload();

/// Delegates to the auth gateways in `lib/core/auth/`. Per layering rule 3,
/// this file MUST NOT import the firebase_auth SDK

findings.why: AU-5 requires exactly one getIdToken(true) forced refresh plus a single retry when a synced write fails with permission-denied/unauthenticated. A repo-wide grep for 'getIdToken' returns zero hits in lib/. Neither FirebaseAuthGateway/FirebaseAuthGatewayImpl nor AuthRepository/AuthRepositoryImpl — the only classes layering Rule 3 permits to touch FirebaseAuth for this feature — expose any way to force-refresh the cached ID token; the closest method, reloadCurrentUser()/User.reload(), only refreshes profile fields (displayName, emailVerified), not the JWT/claims. A stale token (e.g. after a custom-claims change) therefore has no dedicated recovery path; a failing synced write can only retry against the same stale token via the outbox's generic exponential backoff until it dead-letters, and the only user-facing fix is a full sign-out/sign-in.
findings.recommendation: Add Future<String?> getIdToken({bool forceRefresh = false}) to FirebaseAuthGateway/AuthRepository as a thin pass-through to User.getIdToken, and wire the outbox/push-pipeline's permission-denied handler to call it once with forceRefresh: true plus a single retry before falling through to the existing backoff.
acceptance_criteria: FirebaseAuthGateway/AuthRepository gain a getIdToken(forceRefresh: true) method with a unit test against the fake/mock gateway.
Outbox/push-pipeline regression test: inject permission-denied on first attempt, assert exactly one getIdToken(true) call plus one retry occurs before falling back to normal backoff.

findings.title: Wire AuthStateNotifier to authStateChanges() instead of leaving a shadowed, unused stream-based authStateProvider
findings.why: auth_providers.dart defines a genuinely stream-backed authStateProvider (Stream<AppUser?> authState(ref) => ref.watch(authRepositoryProvider).onAuthStateChanged()) — exactly the AU-4-compliant primitive. But the provider that actually drives session routing everywhere (AuthGuard, AppShell, this screen) is the differently-implemented, identically-named authStateProvider generated from AuthStateNotifier, which never watches or listens to that stream — forcing every screen needing both to hide/alias one of them (see the 'hide authStateProvider' import here and the 'as auth_state' alias in sign_in_controller.dart/signup_screen.dart). If Firebase invalidates a session server-side (disabled account, revoked refresh token, forced sign-out elsewhere) while the app is running, nothing re-derives AuthStateNotifier's state from that change — the app keeps believing the user is signed in until an unrelated explicit action happens to call reload/signOut. account_picker_screen.dart:274 shows the same non-reactive pattern at tile-badge granularity: hasValidSession is a one-shot ref.read(...).currentUser snapshot, not derived from the stream.
findings.recommendation: Either delete the dead stream-based authState/authStateProvider if genuinely unused, or have AuthStateNotifier subscribe to it in build() so live Firebase-side session changes propagate into routing state, removing the need for every consumer to route around the name collision.
acceptance_criteria: authStateProvider resolves to exactly one declaration reachable without hide/as workarounds across the codebase.

Regression test: emit a value on the mocked authStateChanges() stream after AuthStateNotifier has already resolved to signedIn, and assert the notifier's state updates without requiring an explicit signOut()/mutation call.

findings.title: Reconcile AccountManagementService.signOut()'s documented 'soft sign-out' with its always-hard-sign-out callers

evidence.quote:
/// Soft sign-out — clears the in-app session so the user sees the
  /// account picker on next launch, but leaves Firebase's cached

// Hard sign-out: clear Firebase session so the user must re-authenticate
    // on next launch rather than being silently resumed via cached token.

findings.why: AccountManagementService.signOut()'s doc comment claims it deliberately keeps the Firebase token cached specifically so Epic 21.9 AC2 (tap an account tile → dashboard in <200ms) keeps working. Its only two callers (showSignOutConfirmation, showDeleteLocalAccountFlow, both in account_actions.dart) immediately follow it with a genuinely hard authRepositoryProvider.signOut()/authStateProvider.notifier.signOut(), so the fast-resume behavior the comment describes is unreachable from Settings > Sign Out today. This is a stale/misleading comment rather than a functional bug (the actual hard sign-out is arguably the safer choice for an explicit Sign Out action), but it risks a future edit assuming the token survives this call, and no sign-out path anywhere in this batch tells the user whether unsynced changes are pending before ending the session.
findings.recommendation: Update the doc comment to reflect that Settings > Sign Out is always hard, and note where (if anywhere) the soft path is actually exercised — or restore the soft path for the scenario it was designed for.
acceptance_criteria: Doc comment on AccountManagementService.signOut() matches an actual, tested call path, or the soft/hard distinction is removed from the comment.
